George Douglas Papers annotated transcription

Version 2.0 · September 2026 · 932 source scan pages

AI-assisted contribution for review. Tentative and unreadable passages remain marked. Unresolved readings.

Editorial guide and limitations

Scope

Version 2.0 adds the four newly supplied PDFs, sources 07–10, containing 545 scan pages. Combined with the earlier six sources and 387 scan pages, the collection now accounts for 932 scan pages. Covers, later labels, envelopes, duplicate images, blank leaves and fragments count as source pages. Coverage does not mean every word is legible. Earlier volumes I–IV retain their version 1.1 text and layout; new volumes V–VIII and the combined reading files carry version 2.0.

Preparation and independence

Prepared for Volney Douglas with AI assistance in September 2026. Every new scan page received an initial visual reading, with selected enlargement, rotation, contrast adjustment and comparison against related passages within the source collection. Local Apple Vision OCR was run at four orientations on all 545 new pages as a reading aid. OCR agreement alone did not establish a reading. The other agent’s transcription was excluded as a source for this addition. Reference and family readings of the new pages were prepared together from the scans; they are not independent of each other. No independent human verification or ACU endorsement is claimed. The earlier version 1.1 has its own disclosed comparison history, preserved in the previous guide and review records.

Reference and family editions

The annotated reference edition preserves readable original wording, spelling, grammar and abbreviations. Ordinary prose wrapping may be reflowed; poem lines and ledger groups are retained. Capitalization, punctuation and word division sometimes require judgment. Superscripts are generally lowered; raised numbers in the convivial journal are retained. Underlining and decorative marks are not systematically encoded. This is a direct reading transcript, not a facsimile or fully diplomatic edition. The family edition modernizes wording and explains abbreviated forms where secure. Very damaged passages sometimes receive an explicitly identified fragmentary reading rather than an invented continuous text. Financial figures remain as read and are not silently reconciled.

Uncertainty and interventions

Double square brackets identify editorial intervention. [[word?]] is a tentative reading; [[illegible]] marks unread writing, with no implied word count. [[lost: description]] records missing material and [[obscured: description]] records an obstruction. [[deleted: text]] and [[inserted: text]] distinguish readable revisions. [[separate block: description]], [[blank]] and other descriptive markers explain layout or non-textual material. Original single brackets and question marks remain part of the source. A gap is not filled solely to make a fluent sentence or to match a related copy.

Order and evidence

The reference volumes retain PDF scan order. Editorial notes link displaced continuations and clearer related versions. The family edition also retains source-page locators, with reading-order guidance beside the relevant text. Later identifying slips remain distinct from the manuscript and may disagree with it. A name in an account does not establish kinship, ownership or parentage. Poems may use fictional speakers, aliases, satire and imagined events. Letters preserve their writers’ assertions, rumors and opinions, including offensive historical language; a transcript does not verify those statements.

Locators and corrections

A page ID such as 09-003 means source 09, PDF scan page 3, counting the cover as page 1. A block ID such as 09-003-P02 identifies the second transcript block. These locators are not original manuscript page numbers. Earlier IDs are unchanged. New uncertainty IDs append U001, U002 and so on to their source-page ID. Please propose corrections with the locator, existing wording, proposed wording and supporting image evidence. The original scans remain authoritative.

Source credit

Original documents and scans: George Douglas Papers, 1830–1939, Center for Restoration Studies MS 5, Abilene Christian University Special Collections and Archives, Brown Library, Abilene, Texas. Collection address: https://digitalcommons.acu.edu/george_douglas/. This family contribution acknowledges the university’s preservation and scanning work. It does not claim university publication, approval or a transfer of copyright.

Earlier scans and review history

The replacement PDFs for sources 01–06 add no manuscript pages. Folders 1–3 matched the earlier copies pixel for pixel at the comparison render size; the sermon and endorsement contain the same decoded scan-image pixels with altered page dimensions or margins. The finding aid is visually unchanged, with small render and text-extraction encoding differences documented in the comparison report. The older 1,200-item review remains a historical review of sources 01–06; it is not a review of the 545 new pages. New marked doubts require further source or human review.

Reuse files

The combined HTML, UTF-8 text, structured JSON, source manifest, page inventory, uncertainty register and PDF page map cover all ten sources. The new per-page records also contain the family readings and notes. Existing volume files remain available alongside four new volumes in each edition. Original source PDFs are identified by filename and checksum but are not duplicated in the public package.

02-003 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 02 - L. Douglas Sermon Notes, 16 Feb 1883.pdf · Scan page 3

02-003-P01 Of all the thoughts enclosed in the language of Inspiration [[lost: left edge]] its laws its precepts its promises what is there that conveys more, to our minds and hearts than is expressed in this short sentence? Jesus wept. Let us look a moment at the character of Jesus: who, and what is he? If we accept the truths of the Bible, he is the son of God, The King of the Jews, The bright and morning star! A ruler of the Jews came to Jesus and said, "we know thou art a teacher come from God for no man can do the miracles that thou doest, except God be with him." Look then at the power of this man: by his word water is turned into wine. The blind receive their sight, the lame walk. By His word the tempest is stilled, and He walks the waves of the wild Galilee. By His word the dead are called back to life again. Truly He was the son of God.
02-003-P02 But it is not from the Bible alone that we have testimony in regard to the greatness of this man. Renan in his Life of Christ says "All ages will proclaim that among the sons of men there were none born greater than Jesus." His goodness, [[greatness?]], his omnipotent power, we cannot doubt. We stand in awe as we contemplate them, and our hearts acknowledge him as King of Kings and Lord of Lords. But while we contemplate all of this glorious majesty our eye falls upon this simple sentence Jesus wept. What do we learn by this? by these two short words. We learn that He had a heart that could be touched by the sorrows and Suffering of our frail humanity: that Sympath[[lost: torn edge]]

Editorial note. First word and left edge of the second line are damaged. The terminal word is torn; it has not been completed from context. Text continues on scan page 4.

02-004 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 02 - L. Douglas Sermon Notes, 16 Feb 1883.pdf · Scan page 4

02-004-P01 the power to "make e'en the wretched blessed" had its abode in His breast and that He could be touched by a feeling of our infirmities. How our hearts thrill with emotions of Love and thankfulness when we think of this blessed truth, that He was in sympathy with the sorrows of frail humanity.
02-004-P02 More than eighteen hundred years have been measured by the revolving Earth since Jesus walked the shores and waves of Galilee, but the influence of His words and life, are still felt. And down through the vista of the coming Ages they will be felt till time shall be no more. And with all the records of His wonderful life this simple truth will descend with the others, Jesus wept.
02-004-P03 L. Douglas. Sylvana Feb 16th 1883

04-007-P01 into the Service, Where it Seems we all arrive at the Same, now in October Col Burleson having become famous as a “Rosin Heel” catcher was Sent to this State on the Same business, Where we were mortified [[illegible]] Texas Contained quite a [[illegible]] of the above Character. I joined the Command in Hopkins County the Last of Nov & Soon after was detailed to take Some prisoners to Tyler — was then detailed to deliver them at Shreveport — Was there ordered to take Some [[illegible]] Guns to Bonham. This [[illegible]] to me [[illegible]] thinking the [[illegible]] would not admit [[illegible]] home — we Concluded to go on to Bonham. Our Co was permitted to Spend the “Holidays” in this County & Staid at home Some 15 days — then reported at Crockett & from there has gone to San Augustine. I will prefere not to be [[illegible]] at this business As it is by no means agreeable to my feelings. Our Brigade is ordered to be at Hempstead Tex by the 10th of Feb — It moves by Way of Shreveport & I hope our detachment will be permitted to [[illegible]] it on the Way.
04-007-P02 I leave Monday for the Command. I first recd a 20 days furlough before its expiration was detailed to transact some business here. Those [[illegible]] to the Co are given Every 2 mo — I have not drawn a [[illegible]] leave yet. Jim Lowder of Ross' Regt is home on furlough. The Squad he came With brought Some Arms across the “Trans[[illegible]]” [[illegible]] 6 millions in Confed. Money. He reports the Miss Army — Well supplied & buoyant in Spirits. We have not heard from [[illegible]] & James Since the middle of Oct. James was [[illegible]] Wounded [[illegible]] in the Chickamauga Battle. I am very anxious to know how They came off at the Chattanooga fight. Capt Bledsoe left Lancaster a few days Since to resume the Command of his Company — which will be very gratifying to them as they were not pleased With the Capt put over them at the instigation of [[illegible]] Command. The last [[illegible]] of the militia has been called out too & are now enroute for Galveston All (too) were mustered into the Service and those unable to go now have received furloughs from one to Six months in length

04-010-P02 Cousin George
04-010-P03 Dear Sir

04-012 · verse

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 12

04-012-P01 The River of death
04-012-P02 Beautiful world! I've trusted long To your gilded show, your Syren Song; I thought the joys you gave would last But one by one they have hurried past; Till now the last you could give has flown, And I stand by the River, Alone! Alone!
04-012-P03 I was merry once, and to music sweet Kept tinkling time with dancing feet; I crowned my hair with roses red, But the lute is shatter'd, the roses dead; Music and blossoms are long since gone, And I stand by the River, Alone! Alone!
04-012-P04 And once I loved; 'twas a dream of bliss, Could earth give more to her child than this? Rapture so great it was almost pain, A girdle of flowers with a silken chain; But love like a vision of night has flown, And I stand by the River, Alone! Alone!

Editorial note. Manuscript copy of a poem. The title and verse lineation are retained. Continues on scan 13.

04-013 · verse and letter

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 13

04-013-P01 Then madly I quaffed the cup of fame, And smiled when thousands lisp'd my name, My brow was bound with a wreath of bay, But it faded quickly and drooped away, Leaf after leaf until all are gone, And I stand by the River Alone! Alone!
04-013-P02 And what have I done O Christ! for thee? Drear the visions my dim eyes see! Have I given a cup of water cold To a single Lamb in Thy precious fold? Time for working is past and gone, And I stand by the River Alone! Alone!
04-013-P03 O Christ! have mercy! The waters wild Are sweeping away Thy erring child; Wilt Thou not listen? O, take my hand, And guide me through to a distant land; All that I trusted on earth has flown, Must I sink in the River, Alone! Alone!
04-013-P04 The River! The River! tis dark and wide, But I see a light on the other Side! My heart no longer is faint with fear, For Heaven has help; my God is near! With joyous footsteps I hasten on No more in the River, Alone! Alone!

04-017 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 17

04-017-P01 [[Yellow?]] Branch [[illegible]] Sept 18th 1863
04-017-P02 Cousin George. I have written Several times to you but Silence has been the result. My uncertain Whereabouts perhaps have been the Cause — for I cannot think you so ungenerous as not to have Written to me Since Sept last year. I have thought my letters of last Spring may have Contained something not acceptable — if so I cannot conceive what it was — for if you are like the majority of Soldiers — your Feelings could hardly be ruffled — I will try you another Effort and if Silence is the response I may know Something is wrong in Denmark, & will call off my hounds. But as I am floating in rather a dull atmosphere I will not promise to be very interesting but trust I may for a while relieve you of the monotony of the Camps.
04-017-P03 I am home on a detail after Clothing for our Co. having reached Sat Evening. I find things moving on in this vicinity about like they did before the War began save the absence of Young men. Plenty Seems Smiling at every door — and were it not for absent ones I believe the people here would be happy. [[illegible]] quite warm weathering Carried on in North Carolina. As yet I have visited but Little. I have visited Waxahachie twice — a very important case being under Consideration in the Court — To wit; The murder of a Mrs Claunch by her Daughter — The case has not yet been decided but from the evidence I have heard believe she will come clear — but not in the Eyes of the people — as innocent of the offence. From Waxa on Monday I went to Red Oak Camp Ground — Camp meeting being on hand — and have remained till Tuesday — The meeting not so largely attended as in former years — Especially by the Sterner Sex — but there has been no discount on the other Side. The eating part received marked attention on my part. I indulge freely in those Substantials that keep Soul & body together — but did not Labor very hard to make myself agreeable — or to create a Contagious Sometimes Called a “palpitation of the heart” — My observation teaches me That the germs of this malady are in an [[illegible]] State and only need Sunshine to bring them to bloom, Expand & Captivate —
04-017-P04 They had Shouting times that night — Some things done rather disorders — Some Singular movements. Amongst them was a Soldier friend — who yielded to the Solicitation of an Old Gentleman who has a Daughter that has [[illegible]] Claims upon him — I think the meeting is Still in operation — If Shoutings are an indication of Godliness — This is Certainly the most Christian people in the range of my knowledge. Possibly this may be attributable to the fact of the abundance of Preachers — who Claim exemption by reason of their vocation and fearing if they do not all Preach they will have to Shoulder their musket & Battle Some

Editorial note. Letter in a small, closely written hand with a fold and scattered reproduction damage. The first word of the place-name and several clauses remain uncertain. Continues on scan 18.

04-018-P01 I will now tell you Something of the operations of our Command. In June it was ordered West & have just returned to about where we! The [[illegible]] was Countermanded & it with another [[illegible]] returned to the vicinity of [[illegible]] Remained in the Same about a month recruiting our horses. About The 1st of Aug. We moved to the Miss. Valley near Natchez — remained there a Couple of Weeks & then were ordered to Our former field (Ark). On the 31st of Aug the Brigade Started on their way rejoicing. We had Seen the Elephant in La & the Boys were willing to go any where. They will doubtless See Some other large Animal in Ark for they will have to ride it as they Left it. [[deleted: illegible]] The Division will be home before there — and they will have a tough time of it with Genl Steele. Majors' Div is also gone to take the [[illegible]] of Walker's [[illegible]] — Had taken up line of march for [[illegible]] & it was believed they would follow also — So now you may listen to hear of Stirring times this fall.
04-018-P02 Whilst Scouting on the Miss Our Squad turned over about 30 fine Horses their arms &c to the Yankee Sent [[illegible]] of them went down to New Orleans to get some Crackers. The others made their Escape Swimming & hiding in the [[weeds?]]. They were Completely Surprised at 3 oclk AM on the 28 of Aug — and a great Wonder all did not get [[killed?]]. Capt [[Vardeman?]] again Got into [[illegible]] Some Candy — He & the dismounted men are now at home [[illegible]] the election — I was not in the Regt yet & Some [[illegible]] of my mess but [[illegible]] had not come out on [[illegible]]. Bob got to Camps the day before I left — I had had chills for a month in the Summer was Sick last Evening & Expect them returning — Jeffie was down last week.
04-018-P03 We Learn Lizzie spent Sunday with you & she Returned to John on Monday. [[Laura?]] Spent last night here. Mother has had a very Sick Spell is getting over it. Had a fine Rain day before yesterday. [[Br?]] Sam Austin Called in today Returning from the meeting — The same is Still going on [[illegible]] the Camp but has been dispersed with only 7 professions So far — We recently Recd a Letter from Lafayette of [[date?]] 1st of Aug. Their Brigade had a heavy fight on the 22nd of July — their Regt went into Battle with 320 & Came out with about 80 — James who was in the [[illegible]] had a narrow Escape [[illegible]] All are Stout & healthy — They are [[illegible]] in high hopes of Early End of the War. I hope their [[illegible]] may be realized.
04-018-P04 [[margin]] Since [[illegible]] — Those of their Co that was not killed had to Surrender & while They were Stacking arms Hage [[illegible]] through [[illegible]] & Clem [[illegible]] was found at hind [[illegible]] My paper is full — I hope to hear from you before I leave for the army — Yours Truly H D [[/margin]]

04-019-P01 Cold Springs Texas Sept 19th /63
04-019-P02 Mr George Douglas
04-019-P03 Dear cousin
04-019-P04 Perhaps you will think strange of receiving a letter from me as you have in all probability forgotten your old hunting companion and school mate it has been A long time since we used to meet down on old Brushy and give the old gobblers a round. and I fear it will be a longer one Still before we can have that blessed privilege again. nearly Four years have pass Since I Saw you and I imagined that you are the Same old george you used to be. I have not changed in the least, only from the big to the bigger. I weigh 175 pounds and the largest Devil in co. (F.) I was ordered to report to the Brigade Quarter [[Mr?]] for fatigue duty this morning. got half way turned round and came back and now looking for the guard to arrest me and if they do I will lye out of it Some how.
04-019-P05 We are having A very pleasant time at this camp duty easy Drill Four evry day except Sundays [[as wet foots?]] we also have a chain guard around our camp wont let a fellow out with his Saddle. you ought to See the boys riding all over the Country bare back There is a big meeting going on in camp. There was about forty mourners last night. They haven't got me yet but I dont know how Soon they will for evry time the old fellow preaches Scare [[there?]] is A [[frog?]] in my throat as big as your fist

04-021-P01 Tupelo Mississippi Jan 25th/65
04-021-P02 Dear Brother
04-021-P03 As Brother Lafayette will Start home in a few days on furlough I will write you a few lines to let you know how I am getting along I was painfully wounded on the 22nd of July while Charging the enemys works The ball Struck me on the the left wrist and passed throw my hand my wrist Bones was badly fractured also the Bone of the middle finger I have Suffered a great deal with it about the middle of August I took the fever and for too months and for two months I were hardly able to get off of my bunk with out assistance — I Received 60 days furlough in October to go to mobile to See our relatives — When I arrived at Demopolis my hand was paining me very much and I was very unwell So I Concluded to Stop a few days untill I could get better I Stoped with an old Lady By the name of Brassfield Thair I had all the attention a confederate Soldier Could wish for. By the [[time?]] I was able to go on I had Concluded [[to spend?]] my furlong in that neighborhood & go to Mobile

Editorial note. The repeated “the” and repeated “for … months” are in the manuscript and are retained. The last two lines are crowded and partially obscured. Continues on scan 22.

04-022 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 22

04-022-P01 Some other time. I spent the time very pleasantly & only Regreted that I Couldent Stay longer I Shall never forget the kind people of Ala.
04-022-P02 At the expiration of my furlough I Started to the Command. But learning that I Couldent get to it. I turned my course and went to Columbus Miss. with the intention of getting my furlough extended and go on to Mobile. Before I Could get off from that place the Federals Destroyed the R Road So that I Could not get thair So I went in to the Hospital and remained thair untill a few days ago.
04-022-P03 My hand is not well yet. it has healed up on both Sides untill the Sear is the Size of a pea and it not heal any more it is running all the time The Doctors Say that is Caused by deceased Bone or by Some pieces of Bone that aught to have been removed My wrist will be entirely Stiff I think I will have the use of all of my fingers except the middle one.
04-022-P04 I Returned to the Command last week found the Boys all in good health Thair is very few of our Brigade left only about 4 hundred out of five Regiments

04-027-P01 Monday Morning.
04-027-P02 Dear Zella,
04-027-P03 Of course you would like to know of the meeting. While there has been no further additions, yesterday was a “big” day. According to announcement there was dinner on the ground. And such another dinner. About the finest ever spread at Sylvana. Among visitors present was White Stirman and [[deleted: illegible]] wife, (who sends her love to you) and Nellie Russell. They left after preaching last night for Ennis, White and family going to move right away to Marlin, where White has a job of running a “Watkins” Medicine wagon.
04-027-P04 From Oak Cliff were three carloads of people, Jeff Barclay among the number who kindly remembered you, the wife of J. C. Estes, the preacher, Bro. Stevens, mother wife and sister, Bro. Melton and family and Bro. Holsenback, and wife.

Editorial note. Continuation on scan 28. Personal names are transcribed as read; no attempt has been made to identify these visitors from outside records.

04-028 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 28

04-028-P01 These enjoyed themselves finely, and were profuse in their invitations for me to visit them when in Dallas.
04-028-P02 Mrs. Dr. Mitchell and family, and Bro. Dunn's family were out from Waxahachie. These comprise the major part of the visitors who took dinner. After dinner Mrs Howard and family came in and remained until after night preaching. She was showered with attentions by all who knew her while she was with us, and last Cliff Stanford came much to the delight of his many friends.
04-028-P03 The meeting may close tonight, and maybe tomorrow night. Bro. Dunn being something of a revivalist is blue over his work here, he is disappointed.
04-028-P04 No change to report in Lucile's condition but I expect to finish this letter at Red Oak this evening; and will give latest dates.
04-028-P05 Larkin is much worse; the disease taking a malignant form day before yesterday. I will hear from him this morning. All company has been forbidden. The prospect is most serious.

Editorial note. Continuation of scan 27.

04-029 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 29

04-029-P01 We will have to hedge on expenses. The Ellis Co. cotton crop is a failure today the eleventh of August. The worms have completely destroyed all the bolls and squares, and blooms are scarcer than I ever saw — if anything is made it has to be made in the future, there is nothing now. Worms are of all sizes and this argues that they will be with us some time yet.
04-029-P02 I hope you will continue to do well, get some weight and strength and hold both. I am feeling fine, batching must agree with me; but I am not stuck on it.
04-029-P03 Am getting from two to eight eggs per day.
04-029-P04 At Kate's. I found Lucile not so well as last Sunday — She seems quite unwell, suffering considerably. Kate says: “Her stomach has gone back on her.” Poor Child, she looks badly. Larkin is about the same as [[illegible]] (Saturday) If he has strength to stand it he may pull through all right.

04-030-P01 Sermon to the Church to day — Ila Duncan and Mayfaire made the confession and will be baptized this evening — meeting will close tomorrow night.
04-030-P02 Came up today and had a real civilized dinner with [[Bros?]] Duncan. I dont see why all women can't cook. Its so much nicer —
04-030-P03 Jesse Ligon and family have returned to Red Oak, bag and baggage. I am glad they have come back as Jess is the best Ligon of the whole bunch — Did I tell you that the old wooden center of Red Oak burned out from brick to brick? Well the old rat traps are gone. Some loss heavily —
04-030-P04 This covers the ground to date — Affectionately G. D.
04-030-P05 Do the best you can for yourself while you are there. Dont bother about me. My peach preserves were highly praised
04-030-P06 [[margin]] some of everything is made it has to be [[lost: reproduced line ends]] [[/margin]]

04-032 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 32

04-032-P01 Wednesday Eve
04-032-P02 Dear Zella, Just got your letter. I staid with Clarence & Kate Sunday night and saw you in the car window Monday morning as you passed.
04-032-P03 Came on home in the evening, and today went back for the laundry and the young lady. Had a puncture coming home and got mighty hot and dirty fixing it. Delivered the young lady at her home and in a few hundred yards returning the same wheel went down again. Had a time. Some men came along and all of us put together could not fix it, so I drove to Rockett on the rim, and with the help of Sid Farrar soon had it righted up. Came on and spent three hours with Kate. The children surely look bad. Glenn was not well, but Kate looks much better than I expected.

Editorial note. Letter continues on scan 33.

04-033 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 33

04-033-P01 They will have to give up that place the first of August. Will likely come to Roland's house in the pasture.
04-033-P02 The letter to you from Paris I opened to see if it should be forwarded. Find it enclosed. Will send yours to your Aunt Nannie by way of explanation.
04-033-P03 I do hope your appetite will stay with you and that the girls will see to your wants. Dont be a burden and dont overdo yourself.
04-033-P04 Dont worry about me. I boiled me two potato's and six eggs yesterday evening, and Ruth gave me a glass of plum jelly and I have plenty of bread, and I reboiled the Molasses and strained it through the new sifter. So I am prepared to get fat. Elmer Carter is very glad to get all of the Cow. Rain plenty since you left. Tell Edwina I enjoyed reading her good letter hugely.
04-033-P05 Affectionately G. D.

Editorial note. Closing continuation of scan 32. “get all of the Cow” is retained as written; the wording has not been expanded into an inferred meaning.

04-034 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 34

04-034-P01 [[deleted: Monday]] [[inserted: Tuesday]] Morning.
04-034-P02 Dear Zella —
04-034-P03 Yours written Sunday came yesterday. I am glad you did not have a bad time last week, and hope you will do better this week. I know Ed's expenses must be enormous; but be sure you do not add any to them. Our house keepers packed up their goods Saturday, and Sunday Evening loaded them on two wagons, and Monday morning pulled out for Bartlett Texas. At Waxahachie they shipped their effects, and by now are at their destination.
04-034-P04 So my prospects for baching grows brighter from day to day. Sure I live better, and my next cook must look refined. My nieces cant understand why I persist in staying at home, and there is not much use for it except I hate for the house to be unoccupied at night. Elmer Carter has taken the Cow to his house, and there is nothing to do but gather up a very few eggs of an evening.

Editorial note. The weekday was corrected above the original “Monday.” Continuation on scan 35.

04-035 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 35

04-035-P01 The hens are on strike mostly. They mainly water just below the Feterita patch at a swamp spring, and the feterita furnishes them fine picking.
04-035-P02 Our meeting crowds are small, and the preaching not much bigger. It chafes Bro. Dunn very perceptibly, but he has a poor way of helping himself, as the job of building up a large audience is a big one. The crowds will be apt to grow later on.
04-035-P03 Word came down last night that Olaf wished to be baptized, so Bro. Duncan returned immediately to Red Oak to make preparation and Bro. Dunn and others went up after Church was over to attend to it. I have no word from them up to this writing. Dr. Stoker told the friends that apparently he had [[deleted: only]] only a few days to live. This is hard on Kate but not unexpected. Lucile can sit up in a rocker an hour or so each day. I will close this when I hear from them after awhile.
04-035-P04 At Kate's Tuesday Eve. Olaf is resting fairly well now. Looks bad, and very much emaciated. Plenty of friends here, which [[inserted: makes]] them feel that they are not neglected. Do not note any change in Lucile —
04-035-P05 Affectionately G. D.

Editorial note. Closing continuation of scan 34. A repeated canceled word and an insertion in the pencil postscript are recorded.

04-036 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 36

04-036-P01 Thursday Morning
04-036-P02 Dear Zella,
04-036-P03 Olaf died yesterday evening at six thirty. I am just ready to start up there. Was there a couple of hours yesterday morning. They had all the attention from the outside that was needful for their comfort.
04-036-P04 Lucile is still able to sit up a little while every day.
04-036-P05 Larkin is sick with [[deleted: bl]] blood poisoning. Was there a couple of hours yesterday evening. To begin with a hen scratched him on the thumb some days ago, this inflamed and was very painful. That got some better and now he has a large red spot on top of his right foot with red streaks running most up to the knee, he has some fever but is not suffering much. Mrs. Wadley, the Dr's mother died yesterday evening.

Editorial note. Letter continues on scan 37. The partial canceled start of “blood” is recorded.

04-037 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 37

04-037-P01 Red Oak Thursday Evening — Just back from Olof's burial at the Rawlins cemetery — Many friends and sympathizers were present. Bro Dunn made a good comforting talk at the tabernacle. Twas very hot but I stood it pretty well — I cannot say what effect all of this death and funeral will have on Lucile yet — She seems to have considerable vitality and may linger for quite awhile — Hattie Stanford is to be baptized this evening. Quite a lot of the Patrick Chapel people were down today, and quite a lot are reported coming from Oak Cliff Sunday —
04-037-P02 I hope you are doing finely this week.
04-037-P03 Affectionately G. D.

Editorial note. Closing continuation of scan 36. The name spelled “Olaf” on scan 36 appears as “Olof” here; the difference is retained.

04-038 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 38

04-038-P01 Thursday Morning.
04-038-P02 Dear Zella,
04-038-P03 I am still Baching and doing fine. Somehow I do not expect my housekeepers any way soon.
04-038-P04 Mary Roberts sent down and got all the Fruit jars she wanted some days ago, and yesterday Evening Edna came and got seventeen for her Mother.
04-038-P05 I got some of the peaches from the tree up by the mustang vine, and yesterday I put up a gallon and a quart of preserves all by myself. I had 12 pounds of peaches, and 9 pounds sugar, began at sun up and got through by noon. I did not use a single drop of water. Have disposed of 13 dollars worth of potato's and have plenty left. Kate and children are doing as well as could be expected.
04-038-P06 Nothing new. Affectionately G. D.

Editorial note. The name in the salutation has a flourished initial, read here as Zella, as in adjacent letters. No date other than the weekday is supplied in this entry.

04-053-P01 I would love for you to be here, for I get very blue and lonesome at times, and you are all I have that is best to live for. With the number of my years I cant stay here long, so your company is that much more precious. I may survive this trouble and may not. At all events my physical strength will be greatly weakened, and for this reason I wanted the car sold, as my car cranking days are over.

The healing process is doing nicely, the only trouble is I have to keep my jaw still, and this cuts out the Eating act to two meals a day. I told the Dr. I was willing to cut it out to every two or three days if it would help matters. My general health is as good as it ever was.

04-079-P01 Palestine, Sept. 8th 1851 Dear Father, Your letter of August 16th came to hand a few days ago, and I was much gratified to hear from you all again. I have just been writing to sister Rebecca, and scolded a good deal with [[her?]] for none of you writing to me, but I see from your letter that the fault lay entirely with the mail, so I shall not send it. I am glad to hear of the good health of the Family, and it gives me some hopes that health may be enjoyed in Brushy, as well as other places. This County although reputed to be one of the healthiest in the State, has been very sickly for two months past, more so than I ever saw it in Ellis Co. I think that Old Mr Benson is nearly willing to try the [[illegible]] again for he has not bettered himself so far as health is concerned, by moving down here. There has been a great many deaths in the county, & five Doctors living in this place have had their hands full of practice, tho' now it is becoming [[margin]] more healthy [[/margin]]

Editorial note. Heavy show-through from the reverse interferes with several readings. The place name following “enjoyed in” reads Brushy after image review.

04-080 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 04 - Folder 1, Correspondence and Loan Papers.pdf · Scan page 80

04-080-P01 My own health never was better than it has been since I have been in this place. I still get plenty of work to do. I quit working for Mr Dale about a month ago & have been picking up little jobs round ever since. Were it not so expensive to live here I could make a tolerably fair living. I am now helping build a large Livery Stable, my wages are $1,50 cts pr day, but after subtracting $10 pr month for board & washing, the amount is considerably diminished. There is going to be a very good opening for carpenters here this coming Winter and Spring, and I am somewhat at a loss whether to continue journeywork or turn out undertaker, I think I could get plenty to do either way. The Christian Church at this place have resolved to build a house of worship as soon as lumber can be procured. It will be 56 ft long & 34 wide and will present a very neat appearance when finished. It has not rained here for so long that I forget when it did rain last, every thing is very much parched up. Corn crops are tolerably good, but Cotton will not make more than a half crop

04-083-P01 Jan. 12 1862 Dear Sister Lizzie I received your letter last week. Beck was here and we had the pleasure of reading it together it had been sometime since we had herd from you. we looked for some of you up Christmas. I had plenty of cake and pies at my cabin Christmas day and a big Egg nog. I envited some of the near neighbors to come and dine with me. and about ten oclock I looked out and saw 14 young men and girls riged out comeing I did not know that they were comeing so you see they stormed me. you may depend the youngsters about here had a lively time of it all the week after which most all the young men left for the war. I wish you and Laura had been here. I have not been any where since christmas week for I have been sick ever since was not well for a week before I am chilling now and have the old [[razzle?]] as heath calls it. [[Gaskin?]] had a chill last week and now has very sore eyes he is walking and is as pretty as any bodys boy he can talk now as good as Angus. Maggie is growing fast and will be another Sister Fleming

04-088-P01 Red Oak Tex Sept 6 1892 Dear Sister Lizzie. The reason why I have delayed so long in answering your letter is not indifference or want of affection for a dear absent sister, but rather the dazing effects of some of the contents of yours. I thought silence much easier & more prudent than to say things that, to say the least, might do no good. I do not now wish to say anything only to regret, nay lament such a condition of irreligion as portrayed in your letter Surely California & Sodom & Gomorrah are not unlike A day in the courts of the Lord is surely worth a thousand in such a place & I surely would make haste to get out, were I there, lest I too might forget God. "Be ye also

The time of my going home seems to be so uncertain that I shall make no promises about it this time. The principal reason of my delay is, that I have, incurred more expences than I anticipated, & shall have to work longer in consequence. I hoped to see Warren, down here last week, but was disappointed I had however the pleasure of meeting with David Gaslin, at Bonners ferry on Trinity, last monday evening & also on Tuesday morning. I learned from him some of the particulars about home, & amongst the rest, that Jepse & Warren had gone out on

05-002-P01 To N. L. Douglas from Henry Douglas Palestine, Tex. Jan. 12, 1855

05-003 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 05 - Folder 2, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 3

05-003-P01 Palestine Tex. Jan. 12 1855 Dear Father: I have been looking for a letter from home; for a long time, not having heard from any of you since I left there in Oct. But as I have not heard I [[illegible]] to write again [[illegible]] I think it rather uncertain [[illegible]] you would hear from me Lest you might have failed to get any of my late letters, I would say that I have written several times since November, & this must excuse me if such be the case I much desired a letter from you before making arrangements for the present year, & I waited until New Years day for that purpose. Being then left entirely on my own judgement I concluded to remain here one year longer, & risk the consequences. Dr Kendrick & myself have formed a partnership for the year. I get ⅓ of the accounts, & am at ⅓ the expence, pay my board & furnish my own horse The advantages of this arrangement are, — his experience — a share in a practice which is firmly established — and a division of responsibility in bad cases, which is not the least of things to be considered. The disadvantages are,

Editorial note. Abrasion or fading at the folds interrupts the opening paragraph. The shares are read as one-third; the second is faint.

05-004 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 05 - Folder 2, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 4

05-004-P01 — a probability of making more money elsewhere — the greater incentive to study, by being thrown on my own resources — & it may be the loss of a good field of operations by being 1 year later. — Have I done wisely, or not? We have great opposition here both from [[numbers?]] & prej[[illegible]] This latter is, however giving [[illegible]] in the minds of the people; & as for the Doctors, it makes but little difference what they think, say, or do. Dr K's practice has been regularly on the increase, for some time, & will continue to do so. Old Mr Ransom, (whom I take to be a man of strong prejudices) has declared his intention to try Dr K when next he wants a physician. Others, the same. I mention him, as he is known to you I wrote to Warren, of a Cancer case we have on hand, which was considered doubtful, & is probably so yet, but it is now doing well & we have more hope. It was a great risk, but will be a great triumph, if a cure is effected. — My health is good. I think I can venture to promise you a visit in the Spring, say April. I could come sooner, but the winter winds & sleets are too bad. If you have not written please do so immediately. My love to all Yours in all affection Henry Douglas N. L. Douglas

Editorial note. Two faded phrases near the top remain unresolved. Medical claims are transcribed as the writer’s historical statements.

05-005-P01 To Mrs. Mary Douglas from Henry Douglas Palestine, Texas April 8, 1853

05-006 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 05 - Folder 2, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 6

05-006-P01 Palestine Tex. Ap. 8, 1853 Dear Mother: The letter from yourself & Susannah, came by last mail, & lest you be somewhat disappointed by my delay in my promised visit, I now drop you a line I recd a letter from Uncle Sam a short time ago, suggesting the 1st of May, as the most suitable time for me to come up, in consequence of his engagements, at court in April & also Jepie's & Warrens absences, he, thinking it probable that they would not be at home until about that time. As it was of no material difference to me, I wrote him immediately that I would be up the last week in April. & lest the letter should miscarry, I write this. Your letter was nearly 3 weeks on the way & if this makes no better speed, & nothing should hinder, I will be with you soon after you get it. I am pleased that Susannah has consented to come down with me, & hope there will be no disappointment, in any way; but that the step shall prove entirely satisfactory to all concerned. I think you are disposed to praise my humble self entirely too highly in this matter; for I have only done, what seemed to me, a reasonable duty. I feel that I have been blessed beyond my expectations, in whatsoever

05-007 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 05 - Folder 2, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 7

05-007-P01 I have laid my hand to, since I left your roof to seek my fortune in the wide world. I know that while memory lasts I shall never forget the day when I parted from Father, in the wide lonely prairie, near the Willow pond, his parting advice, & the loneliness of the subsequent hours in walking to Porters Bluff. Never till then had I felt so isolated; never had I felt what it was to be homeless, houseless, & in effect, friendless, for I was going amongst strangers, & I knew not whither I took everything upon trust; & have not been disappointed. I have been blest with health & plenty; not so abundantly as some, but as much as I had any right to hope for. I repeat then, that I deserve no praise, but if I can render any service to others I am only doing my duty. You may, then, expect me up about the last of April, (of course I can't say precisely) & I hope to remain with you a week or 10 days, maybe longer. The weather has been very dry with us, for a long time, & crops are suffering greatly for rain. Corn has been badly frostbitten & much of it will be to plant again. I fear the wheat has been ruined, with you. I remain as ever, your affectionate Son, Henry Douglas. Mrs Mary Douglas
05-007-P02 [[margin]] P.S. Give my love to all. Remember me to [[Un.?]] & aunt Cynthia. &c &c H.D. [[/margin]]

Editorial note. The postscript is inverted at the top of the image. The abbreviation before “& aunt Cynthia” is uncertain.

05-008-P01 To N. L. Douglas from Henry Douglas Mississippi County, Missouri June 23, 1860 — re driving herd of sheep to Texas

05-009 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 05 - Folder 2, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 9

05-009-P01 Missisipi County, Missouri June 23d 1860 Dear Father: After a long lapse of time I now find an opportunity to write you. I have nothing encouraging to write. I have had to pay from 1 to 2 dollars for sheep & have been at a great deal of trouble to find them & expense in collecting my drove. Mr Willis Helm sent $500 by me to get him some sheep & with the 1500 I have bought 750 head & do not know that I will have money enough to get them to Tex. as I only have some 200 left. I bought common sheep in Callaway & Graves Co's Ky purchase lambs at 1 & Ewes at 1.25 per head but could not get enough & so went back to Christian Co & got some 250 head at 1.75 & 2 per head These are finer sheep & I would now prefer that all my funds were invested in such sheep I crossed the Mississippi at the Iron Banks last Sunday & had to pay 8 cts per head ferriage then after driving two days I had to stop on account of the sheep taking a disease from poison or some thing else. Several have died & altogether I have lost near 50 head since I started, mostly however by their dodging in the thickets the first few days

05-010 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 05 - Folder 2, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 10

05-010-P01 driving. I learn that every drove of sheep that has passed through here has suffered severely in the same way that mine has. Last year about this time a Mr Long passed through with 1000 & lost 150 to 200. A Mr South, Methodist preacher, with 3 or 400 lost only a few. He passed through about the last of July. A few days ago a drove of 7 or 800 passed from Rutherford Co Tennessee & lost a great many. The people here say that I have escaped better than any of them & they say, further, that after leaving here all the droves did well which I greatly hope is true. I now have my sheep in a large crabgrass pasture free of charge, & will remain till I think it prudent to start which I hope will be in 3 or 4 days. Nearly all are doing finely but probably 50 show a diseased condition. The symptoms are, first a drooping & swelling of the ears, which thicken up the cellular tissue being filled with yellow serum. The sheep becomes dull & stupid & in some cases the head swells — under the jaw the skin will hang in a pouch & I have stuck my knife into several & the yellow serum would flow freely. I know that I have lost 5 since I crossed the river & one more will die, probably. I forget to say that, after the head swells the sheep suffers from an intolerable itching, judging from its actions, & the hair will come off when the swelling goes. I have 2 toll gates

05-011 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 05 - Folder 2, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 11

05-011-P01 to pass before I get clear of the swamps & then no more I suppose till I get to Fort Gibson ferry on the Arkansas. I have 4 hands hired at 15 dollars per month each & taking all together I cannot make the drove profitable if I do not lose by it. I have not heard from any of you since I left Texas nor have I heard from Ellen since I left Lincoln County. Taking everything into consideration I cannot feel otherwise than "low down" but win or lose I am bound to go through. My health is still good & if I dont get sick I think I can stand it. Now I have written this I do not know that it would be best to send it, but you had better know the truth than to be in suspense. I suppose I will reach Springfield Mo. in 30 or 40 days & you must write me at that place & also at Fort Gibson, & write to Warren to do the same as I am very anxious to hear from all of you. I have been much disappointed & perplexed by men who engaged with me for the trip, failing to come up at the appointed time & some not coming at all. This required me to hire hands temporarily & higher prices & to pay them off when they quit, which has been a heavy draw on my pocket. I will write again — for the present this is enough. Love to all. Your affectionate son. H. Douglas

05-014-P01 Murfreesboro Ten April 18 /54. My Dear Sir It has been about two years since I heard from you in relation to our business — it has been I believe nearly three years. I should be glad to have a letter from you — giving me full accounts of every thing, and I hope you will write to me immediately on the receipt of this. I have bought lately of Gen. A. Sublett the balance of the Littleton White tract of Land — the purchase embraces about thirty two hundred & fifty acres — You know where it is situated & I want you to see to it. See whether the Taxes are paid, and give me any information you may be able to obtain in relation to it. I would be obliged to you to write me fully about the Louis Dickson tract of Land on the Trinity River (I believe it is called the Louis Dickson tract) — Gen. A. Sublett owns it & I am thinking about buying it. I believe the Land is at the mouth of the five mile [[deleted: branch?]] [[inserted: creek]] Write me what the Land is worth & give me any information you may have, or can get, in relation to it.

05-036-P01 Bardsdale, Sat, 29th, 1893.
05-036-P02 My Dear Aunt:—I finished up my morning work pretty well this forenoon, so now I will take time to write to you. I am still better—haven’t had a “break down” since I wrote last.
05-036-P03 I have every room swept nicely—I still have a bed in my sitting-room two rockers, two footstools, nicely covered, the stand-table, Mr. [[Curren?]] made, two tea-baskets on the mantle-piece, my vases, & two advertisement pictures, which makes the room presentable.
05-036-P04 I try to keep the door opening in to the hall closed, so as to have the room ready to receive anyone; for they come, at any and all hours, being as Bruce
05-036-P05 [[margin]] This afternoon I made 4 glasses of preserves out of the last quart of my black berries—I haven’t much fruit left. Wont I have a siege filling my jars by and By. [[/margin]]

05-037 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 05 - Folder 2, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 37

05-037-P01 says “togezzer” (together) with the store. One day he came from the P.O. & said “Grandma Chadsey's house isn’t togezzer is it Mamma?” “Ours is though” He noticed that her Post Office doesn’t join her dwelling, while our store does—dont you think him quite observant? Mr. Headrick has been down with his back, for two weeks, till he could scarcely move, but is much better now—last week he wasn’t able to help me work, at all, so I did it (a small washing) alone as you know I am better, I sat & rinsed them in a bucket. 05-047-P01 Bardsdale August 8th. Dearest Aunt:—I have just gotten dinner over. Mr. Headrick has gone to work, Elmo is seated on the table, and Bruce by it with a slate, and talking more. I am as well as usual. Mr. H. helped me wash yesterday. Grandma Humphrey’s growth increases, and is so bad she has difficulty in breathing—consequently has consented to have an operation performed; which, I greatly fear she will not undergo. Dr. [[Hinckley?]] is back now and he Drs. Bard and Mott, are to do the work. I saw Dr. H. passing, once since his return. I spoke, told him I was glad to see him back, and expressed lasting gratitude for his kindness. Could hardly keep from saying if he thought half as much of me, as I did of him, he would have called to see us sooner. but of course we can’t express ourselves thus freely, to strangers.
05-047-P02 We had our picnic at Mr. Grimes, last saturday, which was quite a success. I prepared a good dinner in case I should get a chance to go; but the hour came for starting, and no opportunity presented itself. How fully I realized that if I was back there, or even you here it would be different. Had I acted on my own feelings, I would have put forth no effort to go; but the children were so anxious to go, they said, if I didn’t go down and ask Mr. Wigmore for his cart, they would. I knew they couldn’t bring it alone, so I went with them but fortunately for my “brazen face” it had been spoken for, and I found it out before I had to ask. I found Mrs. Pickering hardly able to be out of bed, and still fixing to go off camping, in hopes ’twould enable her to stay a little while longer with her children. So I swept her house, cooked her two jelly cakes, and came on home about noon. Mr. H. took his dinner so the children and I sat down and ate picnic dinner alone. After we had finished, and I had sat down, to read a little, down came Mr. Henry Chadsey in Mrs. [[Curren’s?]] surrey, for us. Lillie Chadsey had inquired of several why I wasn’t there, and

Editorial note. No year is supplied in this page’s heading. Several personal names have uncertain letter forms.

05-048 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 05 - Folder 2, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 48

05-048-P01 the answer of all was of course, “I guess she didn’t have any way”. She told them there was no reason I shouldn’t have a way, when there were so many conveyances there, so she started Henry in a hurry. I was thankful on account of the children especially. They had a large table heavily loaded, with choicest food. Mrs. Grimes took up nearly all her dishes, and every one else took plenty so it was a set table just like you would have at your own home. But just such a mixture of dishes, you never heard of. It took them quite awhile to get them straightened out. They had lemonade and ice-cream. two swings a set of croquet, and a game of baseball. And [[no part?]] of the pleasure was due wholly to Lillie Chadsey. I was amused to observe, as she came down in the afternoon, to see Elmo running her. Imagine him handling (or rather attempting to) over Two hundred pounds. But you know he always rather liked her. That was the 4th, and little [[Beckie’s?]] birthday, and what think you, she went to Santa Paula with Mr. [[Reck?]] [[Lehock?]] and married him unbeknowing to her father. The old gentleman is quite wrathy over it. ordered her off the place, when she went back for her clothes, and threatened to disinherit her. It was her 18th birthday. The [[Wilmot?]] [[Hagarts?]] are not all dead yet. Grandma Roberts spent last sunday night with us. I am always so glad to see her. I forgot to say, I heartily wished for you to dine with us, when we sat down to eat our picnic dinner all alone. Elmo said to me one day “when a girl marries a young man, she takes his name, doesn’t she”, to which I said yes, and he continued how many Headricks will there be then? Bruce was standing by, and put in, I’m going to marry a “dutch girl”. Well I must tell you that I earned $4.50 pitting fruit. A handsome amount for me.
05-048-P02 Expecting an account of the meeting soon, I am as ever, S. G. H.

05-066-P02 I seek not for devoted dears.— “Platonic friendship at my years,” Most surely will suffice, Impassioned hours have long gone by— The furtive glance—the pensive sigh— [[Was as for lovers nice?]]. Give me a strong and helping hand While adverse clouds hang low, A friend in danger’s hour, who’ll stand Then onward will I go I’ll meet cold fate, with heart elate And smile at fortune’s frown, I’ll bare my breast, to its rudest blast, Altho’ I may go down,
05-066-P03 “Beauties newblown” will Nature bring With each returning vernal Spring And I enjoy these, The flowrets on the prairies wide The murmuring streams which sweetly glide The grand and lofty trees, Altho’ I am an Anchorite Absolved from humankind Some joys will stop with me o’er night And leave a pledge behind, That in after years, thro’ changeful cares They’ll call around once more And bring with them, some nameless gem “From the distant Aiden shore,
05-066-P04 Thus Hope is still the harbinger Of many a blissful coming year Which fortune may deny.

05-078-P01 Of all the thoughts enclosed in the language of Inspiration [[lost: left edge]] its laws its precepts its promises what is there that conveys more, to our minds and hearts than is expressed in this short sentence? Jesus wept. Let us look a moment at the character of Jesus: who, and what is he? If we accept the truths of the Bible, he is the son of God, The King of the Jews, The bright and morning star! A ruler of the Jews came to Jesus and said, "we know thou art a teacher come from God for no man can do the miracles that thou doest, except God be with him." Look then at the power of this man: by his word water is turned into wine. The blind receive their sight, the lame walk. By His word the tempest is stilled, and He walks the waves of the wild Galilee. By His word the dead are called back to life again. Truly He was the son of God.
05-078-P02 But it is not from the Bible alone that we have testimony in regard to the greatness of this man. Renan in his Life of Christ says "All ages will proclaim that among the sons of men there were none born greater than Jesus." His goodness, [[greatness?]], his omnipotent power, we cannot doubt. We stand in awe as we contemplate them, and our hearts acknowledge him as King of Kings and Lord of Lords. But while we contemplate all of this glorious majesty our eye falls upon this simple sentence Jesus wept. What do we learn by this? by these two short words. We learn that He had a heart that could be touched by the sorrows and Suffering of our frail humanity: that Sympath[[lost: torn edge]]

Editorial note. Also reproduced in source 02, scan page 3. Damaged line beginnings and the torn final word remain unresolved. Continues on scan page 79.

05-079-P01 the power to "make e'en the wretched blessed" had its abode in His breast and that He could be touched by a feeling of our infirmities. How our hearts thrill with emotions of Love and thankfulness when we think of this blessed truth, that He was in sympathy with the sorrows of frail humanity.
05-079-P02 More than eighteen hundred years have been measured by the revolving Earth since Jesus walked the shores and waves of Galilee, but the influence of His words and life, are still felt. And down through the vista of the coming Ages they will be felt till time shall be no more. And with all the records of His wonderful life this simple truth will descend with the others, Jesus wept.
05-079-P03 L. Douglas. Sylvana Feb 16th 1883

05-081-P01 The beauty of female culture. There is nothing more important than the cultivation of our minds there is given to each of us a mind some superior to others but it matters not what degree of intellect we possess it is the common duty of all to improve it If we do not do this what will be the result? why it will be as a field that is not in cultivation and grows up in bryars and weeds.
05-081-P02 The greater mind we possess the more we are expected to accomplish. I think there is more in the cultivation of the mind than there is in the mind itself.
05-081-P03 We must also cultivate the heart kindness of feelings and gentleness of disposition.
05-081-P04 There is also a great importance attached to the cultivation of our manners for what makes a young lady appear to better advantage than gracefulness and politeness of manners all true politeness originates in kindness of heart for if we feel kindly towards anyone then it is no trouble to act kindly to them.
05-081-P05 Then let us all [[deleted: illegible]] earnestly strive to accomplish this so that we may make ourselves equal with those that now so far surpass us.

05-084-P01 Parting From Friends O! how sad we feel when we part from our dear friends! This is the case when we part a short time only, and expect to meet again soon, but how much [[inserted: illegible]] sad it is to part with them when we know that we will meet them no more in this world! Who can discribe the feelings of them who stand around the death bed of a loved father or mother, brother or sister, and hear from their dying lips the last fond words of love they will ever be permitted to utter. And then how agonizing to follow their lifeless bodies, and see them placed in the cold, and silent grave. No one can imagine the feelings caused by such a trial [[deleted: expept]] [[inserted: except]] those who have experienced it. All should be prepared to die, for we know not how soon we may be called upon to leave this beautiful world, and all our dear friends and loved ones. We should ever be kind to our relatives and friends for we do not know how soon they may be taken away from us, and then it will be a sad parting, indeed if we have ever treated them with unkindness.

05-087-P01 Murfreesboro Tenn Dec. 6–1883. Mrs. Douglas and Mrs. Orr. Ferris, Texas. Dear Friends: I send you an advertisement of the land sale which explains itself. During the Term of the Court, Chancellor Burton was sick and died. While he was sick a Circuit Court Judge held his Court and decided the case as to who the land goes to, but seemed very much tangled in the case.
05-087-P02 He decided that 180 Acres of the land that descended to Mrs. Alexander from her father, Jacob Wright, goes to or is inherited by the nephews and nieces of Jacob Wright, and to the children of his deceased nephews and nieces, or their representatives, and as he had about forty nephews and nieces, seventeen of whom are living, and about twenty three dead would make about forty shares into which the estate would be divided. As to the McGlothlin tract of 230 Acres, descended to Mrs. Alexander from her mother, to use his language he said this tract “ascends” to the heirs of Mary Wright from her daughter, the said Rebecca, and the father and mother being cousins, that the heirs of the father and mother of Mary Wright, related to her in equal degree, or representing those in equal degree, take equal moities of said tract of 235 Acres – if such heirs or those they represent

Editorial note. Continues on the following scan. The tract acreage appears as 230 and later 235 on this page; both readings are retained.

05-088 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 05 - Folder 2, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 88

05-088-P01 do not stand in equal degree to the said Mary Wright then the heirs nearest in blood to the said Mary, or them representing those nearest in blood to her of the whole and half blood will take the whole of said 230 Acres in preference to those of more remote degree.” I appealed from the whole decree to the Supreme Court as also did the McGlothlin claimants of the 230 Acre tract. I am in no way discouraged by the decision of the Court, and feel satisfied that I am correct in my construction of the law that Mrs. Alexander’s first cousins, living at the time of her death, inherit her whole estate from her, and that it does not ascend to the heirs of the Father, or Mother. About the time the case will be finally ended in the Supreme Court, the land money will be ready for distribution. Very Respectfully, B. F. Lillard. Per Ida.
05-088-P02 Criminal and Chancery Courts to day are both in session and I have no time to write. B. F. Lillard

05-092-P01 Murfreesboro Feby 26th 1883. Mr Geo. Douglas Ferris Texas – Dear Sir – Mr Lillard our Attorney has shown me a letter from you in answer to two letters that I requested him to write to your Mother and Cousin Cynthia Orr, and in reply to your letter I have this to say. There is no other Attorney representing any of the heirs of Rebecca Alexander and there is no necessity for any other, I have conferred with Cousin Docia Bivins, she stated that she was going to leave her part, I have also conferred with Isaac N. Wright who joined me in employing Mr Lillard to investigate and take charge of the whole matter and we gave him to understand that he would represent all the heirs, I have had letters written to all from a distance, and he has recd a letter from Mrs Nance – which has been answered and we are looking for a Power of Attorney from her, as the whole matter has been explained to her, and she stated that she wanted her part – Isaac Wright recd a letter from his sister Mandy requesting him to act for her. We want all the parties

05-093-P01 to join as Complainants in the bill to save costs to the Estate. and we thought it just to give all a chance to unite in the bill – The costs and Attorney’s fees will of course come out of the proceeds of the land and you need have no fears on that, and I assure you that Mr Lillard who is competent and has the reputation of an honest lawyer. and whom I have-known from infancy will treat all parties justly – Mr Alexander has told several parties that he will not litigate the matter – that he would do what was right about it – Our Attorney is running the case as smoothly as possible so as to avoid litigation, but the bill has to be filed to sell the land for division of the proceeds, and to settle the rights of the parties,

05-095-P01 Murfreesboro Tenn Dec. 30/82 Mrs Mary Douglas [[deleted: Ennis]] [[inserted: Ferris]] Texas. Dear Madame I suppose that you have heard of the death of your Cousin Mrs Alexander daughter of your uncle Jacob Wright. She did not make a will and her real estate descends to her next of kin consisting of her first Cousins now living being 3 of the Goodloe family, three of the Dill, two of the Brasher and six of the Thompson Wright family as I have been informed by Messrs Wright & Dill, I have been employed by a good many of the heirs to represent them in the matter and at their request I write to you, as it is very desirable that I should be the Attorney for all the interested parties and I want authority to act for you, I have written to Mrs Orr Post Office [[deleted: Ennis]] [[inserted: Ferris]]. Please notify her of the fact. We desire [[inserted: to]] act as smoothly as possible, and when I am clothed with the proper authority I will make the demand for the possession of the real estate consisting of 680 Acres of land assessed at $8500.00 but of course land generally brings double the assessment. [[inserted: also for possession of the 640 Acre tract hereafter referred to]] If possession is not given on demand an ejectment suit will become necessary. After possession a bill will have to be filed for partition or for sale for partition, There may-be more real estate besides the 680 Acre tract, probably 300 Acres in Ark.

05-096-P03 The conveyance is defective – I have made a thorough investigation and am satisfied that the sale can be declared by the Courts null and void and the land can be recovered. B. F. L.
05-096-P04 [[separate block: lower note]] Whatever the law gives you is right and if Mrs Alexander had not wanted the land to go to her kin she could have willed it otherwise So she left the law of the land as her will,

05-098-P01 Murfreesboro Tenn. March 22nd 1883 Mr Geo. Douglas Ferris Texas – Dear Sir – Your letter of March 15th has been recd. I think that you have been under a misapprehension about several things – In the first place you certainly must think that after I recover these lands that I want to handle the money that may arise from the sale – In this you are mistaken I simply wanted to represent you in the litigation (I mean your Mother & Aunt) I never draw the funds of a party unless specially requested to do so – it is too much trouble to keep receipts &c, but then at the same time I want you to understand that I am thank God far ahead in this world’s goods, and I don’t know of a human being to whom I owe a cent, or whom I ever wronged, You do not understand the law in this State applicable to Attorneys – If an Attorney collects money and fails to pay it over his License [[deleted: was]] [[inserted: is]] taken from him, he is forever prohibited from practicing law, fined a thousand dollars, and imprisoned in jail 12 months, If you remember my first letter to [[deleted: you]] [[inserted: the ladies]] I stated that a letter instructing me to represent them was sufficient, but the Powers of Attorney that I sent was a more formal way and was preferable, and that I did not care about them acknowledging it [[inserted: before a clerk]] [[deleted: illegible]] your first suggested the acknowledgement, showing that

05-099-P01 that all I desired was simply to do the [[lawing?]] and this was at the request of those whom I represent here, This litigation so far has I regret to say exhibited no small amount of bitterness of soul on the part of some persons, who are not even interested in it, except to try to injure me, and to aid Alexander – They have tried to get some of my clients who live at a distance to discharge me and employ Alexander’s Lawyer [[inserted: & so far have failed]] – Now if they can succeed in getting all the parties who do not reside here on Alexander’s side that are made defendants as I was compelled to place your Mother & Aunt at the time of filing the bills, and then buy out my resident clients of Course the bills would be dismissed – It looks like a blind man ought to see through this – And again Alexander I learn wants to buy the land (which at one time he said was willed to him and now abandoned on account of my persistent efforts against him and others who did not want “to disturb their Cousin Andy or make him mad as they expressed it) and now if, in the bill that I have filed to sell it [[deleted: illegible]] he succeeds in getting most all of the parties on his side, he thinks that he could control to some extent the division of the land into lots, and buy at his own price – Can’t you see into this – These are stubborn facts and I have thoroughly posted you in the whole matter, You have the recommendation of Albert Jetton of me as an Attorney, the editorial of the Free Press that I sent to you, also the certificate of Judge Burton the Chancellor before whom the case will be tried, of John Woods Chairman of the County Court

05-102-P01 whisky for neuralgic rheumatism, and like every body else who uses whisky of any temperament, I sometimes used too much, but I never did use it regularly – and now for a great while I have abandoned the prescription, and I do not use any intoxicating drinks, not even berry wine, or cider, as the whole citizens of this Town will testify, and if any man says that I ever neglected my professional engagements on account of whisky he tells that which is absolutely untrue, I do use two cups of Coffee per day, I smoke tobacco and sometimes a little Mullein prescribed by a Methodist Preacher several years ago, but my respect for ladies is too great to allow me to chew tobacco, and this is the extent of my stimulants, Isaac N. Wright, Col. Brashears & Mr Dill & others who reside here are my clients – they have known me from infancy & ought to know what is best, One other party said that she would have nothing to do with it – her and her husband both told me the same, and the latter lately – the other resident party employed a Counsel who came and wanted to join me in the bills, but said he also represented a lot of second Cousins, I told him that his clients interests conflicted, that my bills denied second Cousins having any interests, and that I should comply with the rules of the Bar, that is, when parties originate a suit, and some in interest don’t want to employ their Counsel in a partition, they are made defendants & I would do so in this case, as I did not want to practice Law for persons who did not desire me to – he said he had not investigated the rights of the parties – I replied “that I had” And now I do not desire to take a Lawyer on the cases with me and teach him the law and pay him for the privilege by a division of my fees. Let me hear from you immediately and if you desire further inquiries I will cheerfully answer you – Very Respectfully B. F. Lillard
05-102-P02 [[margin]] caused from Army wounds [[/margin]]

05-103-P01 P. S. In addition to what I have said I will state that I have been informed by one of your true friends, that you have been written to, to turn your back on me and to employ a certain other Lawyer here – I will now proceed to give you the origin of that – Mr Alexander sent for the old Gentleman to meet him in Murfreesboro one day this week – he did so – they went to the Office of Mr Alexander’s Lawyer, and the three held a long [[deleted: Counsel]] [[inserted: Consultation]], the result of which was, that he went from that Law Office, and consulted with another Lawyer, and then he wrote his letter suggesting to you to employ that Lawyer – Against this Attorney I have not a word to say, nor will I be so uncharitable as to say aught against any brother Lawyer – but no Lawyer is infallible, and a Lawyer is as liable to be imposed [[inserted: on]] as any one else, when the case is stated to him from the opposite side, and that too by an old person whose prejudices can be worked upon – Why did not Mr. Alexander bring into the Consultation your Cousin Albert Jetton whose store is within 75-ft of that Law Office, It seems to me that you ought to be able to see through all this, My bills and work have won the battle unless trickery turns the tide, but I am determined to head off any such warfare, and if any party gives aid and comfort to the enemy to defeat their own rights they shall do so with their eyes open – If Captured by the enemy of this Lawsuit they shall be willing Captures – I further learned that Mr Alexander’s Lawyer said that he could not

Editorial note. Postscript continues on 05-104. Scan is inverted.

05-104 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 05 - Folder 2, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 104

05-104-P01 represent your Mother and Aunt, “but he did not say that about one of my clients, Mrs. [[N?]] last week who resides in West Tenn, Her son, down there had been worked upon by some one defaming me, and recommending to him Alexander’s Lawyer, and he accepted, but I overtook the parties, and Alexander’s Lawyer has been discharged by them, and I have been retained, and her son writes to me that in a few days he will have sent to me a regular Power of Attorney, – just as soon as [[inserted: he]] can have it properly acknowledged. I have set out to defeat these parties & I intend to do it, by every thing that an honorable man can do, nor do I intend to permit unjust and wrongful impressions to go out against me, I have as many diplomas from as good Universities as this Country affords, my Law Diploma was signed 25 years ago by Judges Green & Caruthers of Cumberland University, the ablest Jurists Tennessee ever had, and I defy any living man to point to a single stain of dishonor on my character – You yourself ought to be able from what I have informed you to understand all these matters – I would suggest that you lay all of my letters before some good Lawyer of your County, and I know what advice he would give you – There is nothing in this letter intended to reflect on your conduct towards me, Everything is written with the kindest of feelings – because I appreciate fully what has acted on your mind – Very Respectfully B. F. Lillard

Dill which explains most of the matters about which you made inquiry, I would be as free from bringing a suit against any one to defraud them of their just rights as any person who would decline to receive the rewards of such litigation, The 640 Acre Tract of land was conveyed by deed to D Travis for the Consideration of $6400.00 to be paid in three equal payments Augst 1882, 83, 84 – It was not dated but that is obviated by the date of the acknowledgement before the Clerk July 15–1881, by A. Alexander to take the Privy Examination of Mrs Alexander which he certifies to the next day, This deed was registered Sept, 1882, and she died Nov, 11 1882,

05-108-P01 any agreement between Alexander & wife as to the reinvestment of the proceeds I am not as yet advised – If this deed had been properly executed the sale would have converted the land into personalty and it would be absolutely the husband’s money,
05-108-P02 My remark in my letter was simply the conclusion of one of my clients as to the purpose of the Conversion – One of them related to me that he was at Mr A’s house on one occasion when Mr A. argued the propriety of selling out and purchasing property in Town and appealed to him for approval and he did not seem to like his answer or rather seemed displeased at it, which was against Town property &c, As to fees and the costs we are not allowed as in your State to take Contingent fees, it would be champertous and a suit so taken by an Attorney would be dismissed, but of course Lawyers do not charge so high where there is no recovery – we look to amount involved &c, I can say this much that we will have no Controversy about the fees, and as Mr. Dill’s letter indicates we may avoid litigation, and simply have partition bills, and if it becomes necessary to litigate about the 640 Acre Tract of land I will notify you of all the particulars and await your advice before using the ladies names as Complainants – The parties are very much scattered, and I desire to commence proceedings in time for next Court and hope you will answer me immediately, Very Respectfully B. F. Lillard.

05-115-P01 P. S. J. N. Spence the soninlaw of Mrs Bivins informed me that Mr A. M. Alexander about two weeks ago said that if they found no will that he did not want any lawsuit and that he would give up the lands, It is reasonable to suppose that a will conveying such a large estate and disposing of it would not be hid way in a corner – None has as yet been found and you may rest assured that none will be produced,
05-115-P02 Now as to my opinion about the recovery of the 640 Acre Tract of land – I have fully investigated the question and I am fully satisfied that the deed can be declared null and void, but whether the parties will seek to do this is a subject for their own consideration, it is my duty as a Lawyer to point out the rights and it is the clients privilege to exercise it, Mr Alexander is rich outside of this – If he was needy and to take from him the benefits of this 640 Acre tract of land would leave him poor I think the moral question would enter and I am free to confess that I could not very zealously prosecute a suit to recover it – I do not think any such considerations apply – We do not know what induced her to join in the deed, but we do know that for years she had refused to sell it, we further are informed that she said that her Father on his death bed told her that he made no will, and asked her to promise the same and that she said that she had so promised and that she did not want Mr Alexander’s kin to have her property – So the law of the land was her will – If she had desired it she could have determined it otherwise, I do not even suppose that she knew her personal estate would go to her husband, and the taking of her Privy Examina
