05-123-P01 Cross Creek Travis Texas August the 30th 1869
05-123-P02 George & Lizzie, your letters were duly and gladly rec, for I am ever anxious to hear from home, or Brushy and its vicinity — I've nothing very interesting to offer at present. The weather is extremely hot and dry in this section since the ((flood)) as I term it and in consequence a great deal of sickness below this Mostly Chills and fever
05-123-P03 I was riding, three days last week trying to rent Me a place nearer Austin But failed All occupied for another Year. and the people not all But a great many sick for the season
05-123-P04 I have become a little dissatisfyed with the Mountains Oweing to the roughness of the road and distance from Austin I was fully determined to move to Arkansas this fall. But I must Confess that the grief and tears of a good Old motherinlaw is a preventative, at least as long as She lives and possibly She may out live Me.

06-013-P01 Readyville March 20 1883 Miss Lizzie Douglas My Dearest Cousin Your very kind letter was recieved in due time and I was very glad to learn that you were all well and know that you have not forgoten me. Willie & myself are both as well as usual The Kin & friends are tolerble [[inserted: well]] at present. Mary Lees Babe little Granville has been very sick but is better to day Paps health has improved very much I think he looks [[inserted: now]] better than he has in Several months Adele spent Several days with me last week she is looking well and is very much pleased with her new home Bro Mcguffy has moved to his new home they have a very nice house & Yard and are

06-014-P01 much pleased with their Surroundings I am very glad to have Jennie So near me it is only a half a mile to her house and we visit each other often Aunt Sallie is still in west Tenn I dont [[inserted: know]] whether She will come back this Spring or not we [[inserted: have]] not heard from her in Some time I [[inserted: have]] been gardening Some but we have had So much Cold weather our vegatables are not doing much good we had quite a Snow Storm yest but the Snow is all gone this morning and it is very pleasant out of doors in the Sun I have Such a lonely time here only a little negro with me Willie is at home of nights but gone every day he is working land over at his Gran Paps this year and is either over there or off with his Waggon hauling for
06-014-P02 Some one [[inserted: all the time]] he never misses a day if he Can help it So you See I am very much confined at home and consequently very lonely. You wished to know the particulars of Cousin Rebeccas Alexanders death I did not know She was Sick until the night before She died I was at the funeral and learned there that She exposed herself getting up very early of mornings to look at the Comet which She was very much interested about She took a very Severe Cold and died from the effect of it I think She was in her right mind all the time during her Sickness Sat up eat her breakfast and talked with her friends in the morning and died that evening a few a Clock, As to the Lawsuit I know very little about it only you know just what I hear [[inserted: hearsay]] other People Say

Editorial note. Two facing pages, transcribed left then right. The account of Rebecca Alexander’s illness and death is the writer’s report, not a medical determination.

06-015-P01 The latest and most reliable I have heard is from Charlie he and Pap were at Cousin Andys last Satterday they found him in very poor health and in a great deal of Trouble he told them Cousin Rebecca will was stolen out of her draw two weeks before her death he is willing to give up the land does not wish to have a law Suit but wants to buy the land of the heirs has already made arangements to get the interest of Several of the Wright family The Jacob Wright Estate is said to be worth about $[[26000?]] and my own opinion is the heirs ought to have it as Cousin Andy will be a rich man without it My best love to you all write soon Most affectionately your Cousin L A Jetton
06-015-P02 [[margin]] Lizzie please dont let any one read this poor Scribled letter I am ashamed of it but have got so out of the habit of writing I cant write fit to be seen [[/margin]]

06-017-P01 Readyville Tenn March the 3 1878 Miss Lizzie Douglas My very dear Cousin Your kind and interesting letter came to hand in due time and I hasten to reply. This leaves the family in rather poor health, Pap & Mother are both Complaining and the Children all have the Whooping Cough. Willie has it very bad and besides that he has had a spell of billious fever is sitting up a little this morning for the first time in Several days. Adele is quite sick with the Cough She has it the second time. Cousin Nellie is getting better but Charles Children are very bad off. Well the wedding Came off at the appointed time we had nice Crowd a good supper and every thing passed off quietly. Adele Willie and myself all went to the reception At Cousin Miriams they had a splendid dinner and all seemed to enjoy it very much Jimmie & Mary are going to live with Cousin Miriam as She is almost alone having only one Child single and he is hardly ever at home Jimmie and Mary Came over yes evening they are both well they have [[inserted: gone]] to Church to day at newhope We had Some fun out of them this morning
06-017-P02 [[margin]] you must excuse all errors as the Children have kept up such a noise and talking I could hardly write at all will try to do better next time Yours as ever L A J [[/margin]]

Editorial note. Continues on scan 18. The postscript is inverted above the opening date.

06-018-P01 about their kin they both call their motherinlaws Cousin they say the kin is so mixt up they dont [[inserted: know]] how to claim it So they will just call them all the same they did before they were married. Well Lizzie Jimmie was a boy sixteen years old when we came here and the first time I met him I told may beth I had picked him out for my Soninlaw (just in fun you know) She was very indignant about it vowed She wouldnt have him I laugh at her [[deleted: now]] [[inserted: now]] about [[deleted: her]] Changing [[inserted: her]] mind she says people often do that it is their privledge The kin and friends are generaly well so far as I know We have had a great deal of bad rainey weather this winter we hardly ever [[inserted: have]] more than [[one or?]] good days at a time The farmers are getting discouraged about not getting to plough any Wheat Crops looks very fine. Dear Cousin you have my deepest sympathy in your great afflictions I loved Cousin Sue on earth I hope to meet her in heaven where Sorrows and partings are unknown I [[inserted: will]] have to Close for the present Tell uncle Jimmy Mary is going to write to him before long and Send him hers & Jimmies pictures Give my best love to the kin and please accept a large share your self I want you to write to me as often as you can as I am always so glad to get a letter from you Adele says tell [[Cousin S he?]] will write to her before long when She gets well of the whooping Cough the Children all send much love to you most affectionately your cousin L A Jetton

06-041-P01 with the health of the family and friends There has been a great deal of sickness in the community but we have been richly blessed Pa had one right severe spell but recovered from it before the sickliest part of the season came and Charlie had a light spell of fever which lasted only a few days with this exception we have escaped, that is, our immediate family. Cousins C. & L. Walker came out to spend some time with us and were both taken sick at once and stayed very sick for about two weeks They were carried to town as soon as they were able Since then they have been very sick, since they left, there was about a week that I missed but two evenings from visiting the sick Bud J & D have gone to sit up with a sick neighbor tonight. 06-050-P01 Mosshead Ala. Wednesday night Aug. 29th 1867 Dear Lizzie Your very welcome letter of the 25th July reached me about two weeks ago I read it while in bed I have been quite sick was in bed nearly a [[illegible]] it [[illegible]] caused from billiousness being sick when I got your letter and very busy since I got well I hope you will excuse me for not answering it sooner I have only partially regained my strength I am greatly reduced in flesh and very much reduced in color My sickness has served to make me look like an Ala. girl the first morning that I was able to fill my seat at the table some of them said “Cousin Lizzie your sickness shows right smartly on you” I said “Oh! it is only helping to make an Ala. girl of me” it seemed like they were going to [[inserted: quiz]] me they all commenced “yes you never have any sickness in Texas” said I “we dont have as many pale faces there as you do here” I was sick two weeks last summer but it didn't take
06-050-P02 [[separate block: left-hand page; concluding page of this letter]] it out I would have liked so much to have gone I dont know whether there is an organized church and regular preaching down there or not if there is I hope we will get to go yet I havnt met up with any one yet who is a member of the Christian Church Pa and I are alone it makes me feel right badly I do wish there were a church in this neighborhood or even if it were not in this neighborhood if it were near enough for us to attend once in a while that would be better than not to go at all we have very good Methodist preaching here as there are none but Methodists living here we dont have series of doctrinal sermons like they do at Liberty Lizzie do you ever hear anything from Mr. Goodman these days poor man I reckon he will move and move until he settle in his grave and leave his family helpless it is a pity that he cant be contented to stay in one place I feel sorry for him and family Where is Mr. Austin and what is he doing any thing? he is very much related to Mr. goodman Lizzie I have written a letter to Jane and Mary which I hope you will pardon me for sending in yours give it to any of or all the boys and they will get some person to read it for them you can read it if you want to before you give it to them I hardly knew how to begin or how to end please write me a long letter I have written two [[illegible]] this contains more to write with much love yours Lizzie

06-053-P01 Mosshead May 10th 1867 Dear Lizzie I expect some of the family will go to town tomorrow and I will try and scratch you a few lines I would have written before now but I received Mollie's letter about two weeks ago she said you had received my letter I have been looking for the reply I had much rather answer a letter than to write before receiving one I heard last week that there were letters in the office for me but when we sent for them [[deleted: illegible]] we couldn't get any So I supposed one of them was from you so I will try and write you something if only enough to bring you in debt to me you will therefore excuse this uninteresting letter for I know I shall fail to interest you as there is no news afloat and but little family news none of the Cousins married yet and not probable that any of them will be soon we are all well at this time except Pa he has had sore eyes very bad but they are improving now I very much feared he would entirely lose one of them at least but now they are so much better I hope he will save both of them When I wrote to Mollie last I was not quite well had two or three chills but broke them up with red pepper

06-057-P01 ever saw. Sanfrancisco is far a head of Montgomery in the fashions if not ahead of New York a person has to be rich to move in the first circle there My cousins found it too gay for them, so they moved about 500 five hundred miles south of that to Los angeles, it is a very quiet and flourishing place. 06-069-P01 Brushy April 21st 1865 Dear George:
06-069-P02 We were somewhat surprised last tuesday evening — the 18th by the arrival of Joda; we were all truly glad to see him you may be sure. I was a little disappointed in not getting a letter from you, but suppose you have written by mail since your return from Velasco. I am anxious to hear something about Dock, and the something you would tell of next time which you spoke of in yours of the 5th inst. has accomplished its purpose — excited my curiosity. The thread you sent by J. M. was very acceptable, it will save me many a turn of my “Piano.” The pins — although I had plenty you left before — do not come amiss. I have a little speculation in my head, which, if I was sure it would turn out right, I would write you several little articles to buy that you might keep your eyes open for such bargains: but, as I am not sure of accomplishing it, I will just tell you my plan. It is to send down some flour by Joda that Laura and I have. There is only six hundred pounds of it, and Joda says if he gets Transportation at all, he will take it. But he does not know yet whether he will get any thing to transport, untill he hears from Mr Bell. If he takes a waggon we will try to send you a little something to sweeten your tooth. I would like for you to look around a little, and see if a side saddle could be got in Houston. Laura is very anxious to get one, and if the flour speculation succeeds she might stand a chance to get one, as Joda says waggons are continually passing from Houston to Dallas

06-070 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 06 - Folder 3, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 70

06-070-P01 I recd a letter from Laura this evening. she seems to be very well satisfied in her new situation. says she has from 16 to 19 schollars, with a prospect for more. I suppose it is better than to be carding and spinning but take me from friends and Home, and place me among strangers, and I would feel that I was left to pine neglected, and to “perish in forgetfulness” — to be poetical. Cousin Mollie has just returned from school and is going to stay all night with me so I must quit.
06-070-P02 Saturday evening 22nd Today has been bright and clear, quite an uncommon thing: the wind has been from the north since day before Yesterday, and last night we had frost enough to kill most of our beans, though I do not think the fruit is injured. Cousin M. amused me last night by relating some of her school exploits, and altogether the time was passed off quite pleasantly. She is going to Liberty; A mrs. Bishop is teaching there now. She is from Dallas, and some rather quiter, I mean — could teach almost every thing the Dead Languages included. But May says it is with difficulty she can find the answers in old Kirkham, so I suppose the Living have become Dead to her. Some foul play has been carried on, up here of late. Several horses have been stolen, and two Stiles boys who lived over in the neck and were deserters, were suspected. A company of men got after them, and caught one of them — the Youngest; he acknowledged to stealing and said his brother was concerned in it. They hung him on the same limb Stanley was hung on — so we have heard. They tell various tales about the other. one is that they shot him and broke his arm but did not take him. Another, that they took him, and hated to shoot him while a prisoner, so they guarded him loosely so he would try to make his escape, which he did. and then they shot him and broke his arm but he made his escape

Editorial note. The account of violence explicitly includes hearsay (“so we have heard”) and alternative stories. These are the writer’s reports; no independent verification is implied. Text continues on scan page 71.

06-071 · manuscript

06-071-P01 Last Sunday morning a party of 8 or 10 men passed Mrs Campbells — aunt [[Bats?]] house — with one of the Stileses. Jim Floyd was one of the party. a young man who was at Mrs Campbells asked Floyd what they were going to do with him. He replied, they were going to take the left hand road with him. The same day Jennie Bell saw a party enter the big thicket at their wood yard. They either took him in there and hung him, or went in to hunt him, after he made his escape. One thing is very certain to my mind, that is if they ever captured him, he never made his escape. Perhaps they merited death, but I dread the consequences of this mob law. We know not, but this is the beginning of terrible times. I hate the thought that Brushy [[deleted: should]] should be the place of the beginning of such things. I would feel a great deal better if I knew that man was not hanging over in that thicket.
06-071-P02 Fayette has not yet returned; the last news from them, Bob was having the chills, and was trying to get a furlough to come with F.

Editorial note. Continuation of the letter begun on scan page 69. The writer distinguishes belief from knowledge in her account of the suspected hanging.

06-072-P01 Henry and Ellen went up last wednesday, so we are once more by our selves. Henry helped Father to sow his grass seed before he went away. They have got the stove set up, but the weather is pretty cool now to be without a fire place. They got the top of the well, a good many old shoes and large rocks and a Young possum out of the well.
06-072-P02 Tomorrow, brother Methodist Jones, will hold forth at Liberty. I will try to attend as I have not heard a discourse since the 1st of March.
06-072-P03 Joda says tell you he is at home safe, and a plowing. We will try to keep him busy while he is at home. There are so many of us here now that we are almost obliged to have some more room. We recd two letters from [[Fran?]], last dated 26th of March. He is very anxious to come home, but thinks it uncertain about getting to come. There is one thing I would like very much to have, a pair of Scissors if you can get them cheap, but do not inconvenience yourself about them.
06-072-P04 With best love to Warren and yourself I remain Lizzie

06-087-P01 [[Wednesday?]] night 15th This beautiful day has been passed very busily and pleasantly by me, we have been putting in a piece of cloth, and this evening [[Colburn?]] and Henry R. came over. [[Colburn?]] came to stay all night to go a turkey hunting with Joda in the morning, but was disappointed as Joda went to Dallas to day to see Watts having failed to see him at Ingeville as he went to Johnson; but they have let their plans to have a good hunt while Joda stays. You ought to be here to hear the turkeys gobble of a morning and see some of our beautiful pet deer. They are very gentle, since you have ceased to torment them. We also have another pet up in these western thickets, which [[illegible]] we suppose to be a panther. There are a kind of pets I would rather would be a little more distant. On the subject of John Turneys, the people of [[Tennessee?]] are anxious that he shall get a six mule team if he can, if not two four mule teams; They seem anxious to send plenty up there to the Co.
06-087-P02 Yours of March 30th we recd last Sunday. You say dont get too fast on the peace questions I will not, for I never was as sanguine as Father and [[Louisa?]] we all told them they were too fast. But I always have and always will think there is something wrong about this cotton trade. You have seen before this the account of the threatened invasion of Tex. from Ark. of twelve thousand men with a train of four hundred waggons. I rather reckon you have not seen the accounts of the wise disposal Genl McCullough has made of his men of late; or such items as these seldom go through the Telegraph. He appointed a day for them all to rendezvous at a certain place. Some of them being at home on furlough two hundred of them had arrived when they were surrounded by a Regmt and taken prisoners and then sent off to their respective commands where they had originally belonged, or to their enrolling officers. just turned out as I always expected it. un-fortunately a great many had not got there when the two hundred were captured. [[deleted: among them William Duff and his]] nephews Jno Smith who have returned to this section and report the [[illegible]]. They have joined Co. with [[illegible]]. This movement on the part of McCullough has rendered these men desperate. Rome has now gone to Wax. with a waggon master who he is acquainted with and who he thinks is his best friend, to try to get to drive a team from San Antonio to Eagle Pass. they say the Govt wants men who will bring their own teams. It will suit with R. if he can get into it but I cant help but think it is a trick to get him into the Service, though it may turn out that my fears are all groundless.

Editorial note. The weekday is tentative; it has not been changed to agree with the preceding page’s Thursday heading. Several personal names remain unresolved. The writer reports McCullough’s actions without independent verification.

06-089-P01 Brushy Nov. 13th 1864 Dear George
06-089-P02 You will have to forgive my delay, my excuse is busy times. This morning Lou and I went to meeting to Liberty to hear Mrs Justins funeral preached; it was to have been preached at the Colony last Sunday, but Mr Haynes had been sick and was not able to preach. To day the house was cramed jamed and running over. A goodmany of the Colony were up and a greatmany from about Shilo. Five preachers: Haynes, Justin, Maley, White, and Berry. Mr Haynes gave us a long tedious discourse from the last clause of the 4th vs. of the 11th ch. Hebrews. He spoke fully two hours, and a good portion of his sermon was about the depreciation of the currency (I am not talking about the “old” and “new issue”) but the money itself. The “old issue” was fully represented to day; and judging from the display have no idea of being repudiated soon. Em. and Liz. were there I just got to speak to them, had no time to talk. I wish you had been there to see all of the people. Times are about as they were when you were here; a good deal of work to do and not much time to visit. We assisted aunt Bettie in getting ready to move, she did not get her thread ready for me to weave, but got some jeans from Ellen, and we made the little boys coats. She got off on the morning of the 10th

06-090 · manuscript

ACU CRS MS5 - 06 - Folder 3, Correspondence and Legal Papers.pdf · Scan page 90

06-090-P01 She took Betsy and chickens, left the spinnack and what few cows she had. I think [[her will intend?]] coming back to attend to them. Father bought a sow and five shoats from her for ten dollars specie, so I reckon we are safe in the meat line for another year. — that is if we can get corn raised to feed them on. Father has reserved twenty acres for [[corn?]] and hungarian. Laura wrote to you, Gibson was to fix the fence; she was mistaken that was not in the bargain; he was just to raise the wheat, cut it and thrash it and put a fourth in the granary. How the old fence is ever to be fixed up is more than I can tell but I hope it will all come out right. The well holds out finely about a dozen mules and horses are watered out of it twice and three times a day. It gets down pretty low, but hardly gets muddy, and by the next time is as full as ever. If I had any hopes of the war ending soon I would feel so much better but from the tone of the papers, we need not look for peace in four more years. Old Abe is elected in all probability and [[Childsy?]] thinks it is best for if Mc. Clelland is elected says he, propositions will be made which some of the States will accept, and then we are ruined. So it seems he is for four more years warfare.
06-090-P02 The wind was blowing cold from the north on last monday evening we were all sitting round the fire, when we heard [[coo a night owl?]] we looked out and sure enough there she was. [[Childsy?]] was nearly frozen, but a warm fire soon set him to talking, and he and Mr Grounds (a soldier that came with him) kept us laughing nearly all the time they were here.

06-091-P01 I was right glad to see [[Childsy?]], you and Joda had talked so much about him, that he seemed like an old acquaintance. I never saw any person more anxious to get home than he. I suppose Joda must have drawn you some shirts, by you sending that one home, draw every thing you can, for that is all the pay you can get. The shoes you sent Mr Grounds told us would not come up, he says they have been recalled.
06-091-P02 Henry and Ellen started home on the 8th, all well and hearty. we have not heard from Warren but look for him and Beck down. Griffin or somebody else must have a particular spite at Warren. If he did not get his furlough lengthened, his stay at home will be short. We recd a letter from Dock [[Wyrman?]] not long since, dated 10th Oct. He had just got Fathers letter and the socks we sent by Ed Dickson. Said he was very glad to get them as he needed them. He belongs to Co. G. Bates’ Reg which is stationed at Velasco, he says he expects they will remain there this winter. He winds up his letter by saying “I am a peace man, let it come as it may.” Ed Dickson is now at Tyler guarding prisoners. He deserves some credit for taking the trouble to send the socks over to Dock. Many a soldier, these scarce times would have kept them. [[Rome?]] it seems has a notion of hanging on to the service. The last letter Sister got from him he told her to buy two more waggons (a horse and an ox waggon) and come to him in the spring. Sister is mightily pleased, she has been wanting to leave here a long time. She thinks she can rent a house in San Antonio and send the children to school

06-092-P01 Wednesday [[eve?]] 16th When I commenced writing I expected to send this to the office before now, but it seems like a hard matter to get a letter to the office these days. I am perfectly furious this evening; at some future time I will let you know what it is about. If I can collect my senses sufficiently, I will try and fill this page. Jeppe got here yesterday he will only stay down a few days, as he is going to San Antonio with a load of wool as soon as he returns. Henry and Ellen [[inserted: had]] got back safe. Warren not got down; he can get no conveyance to bring Beck down while he stays; he wrote he would be here on the 10th of Dec. on his way back to Sabine. I suppose he got his furlough lengthened. On last monday Mr. Marshalls family [[deleted: was]] rolled in from Ark. composed of two sons and six daughters. They are greatly dissatisfied down on the old man for marrying, and wish they were back in Ark. they say they had plenty there of every thing and a good house to live in. The jayHawkers were the only ones that pestered them much. They say the feds treated them better than our folks. The old man has rented Lous house for them, he is going to build a chimney in it before they move there.
06-092-P02 As an other item of news I will tell you about [[Lidda?]] Bakers nose. Dr. Mc. [[Curdy?]] is making her a new one; he made a gold nose and then cut a piece of skin out of her forehead and twisted it around and covered the gold. when it knits at the sides he is going to cut it loose at the top and straighten it out: He says he is going to make her a lip when her nose gets well and then take her for pay. My paper is full and I will have to quit I reckon you are wishing I had. I cant send this to the office before Sunday. Affectionately Lizzie
06-092-P03 [[margin]] Jane Green died last Saturday night with pneumonia. [[/margin]]
06-092-P04 [[margin]] Aunt Bettie told me to tell you to write to her [[illegible]] Ark. [[/margin]]

06-094-P01 Brushy Texas No. 4 Feb. 19th 1864. Brother George:
06-094-P02 Yours of the 7th and 8th came to hand this evening, and although short, gave us great satisfaction. When the Sundays mail fails to bring us any letters, as it did last Sunday, we are always uneasy until we do hear from you. Brushy has been in the receipt of various news to day; Laura got a letter from Fayette, M Orr one from Fayette, Mary and I one apiece from Jim.
06-094-P03 They have come safely through all the fights except the slight wound Jim rec. at Chickamauga. They both say they are tired of it. Jim says “he can stand the fatigue and hardships all very well, till it comes to the fighting fighting, and then when he sees his comrades falling around him, it is all he can do to persuade himself not to run.” Tole Hamilton fell at Ringold, in the retreat. he was shot through the breast, and only lived a few minutes. Poor fellow he has gone like many another from home and kindred, never more to return. He leaves a widow and child. The boys write home that two Goodloes (Aquilla’s sons) have deserted. And whose name do you expect to hear [[illegible]]? Tell no other than Squire. but uncle [[Givans?]] says this must [[illegible]] out of the family I know not why unless his boys wrote it home is the reason. But Squire is safe over the Border, where a many another poor Dixie boy wishes he was I expect. But Squire is not the only one of your acquaintance. The boys say that Charly Brown has written to them, that Will is safe with his kindred in a Northern Clime, hearty and well. Now dont you reckon that Will G. and Will Brown are having a happy time? Mary G. is perfectly satisfied about Billy. From the tone of Jodas letter, he seems to think your Batt. is disgraced worse than any other body of men in the Army, but he is behind the times, and had as well quit his noise. Tom [[Warthen?]] writes home that they have to keep a guard round Gurleys reg. to keep them from deserting. We hear there all of Murrays Texas Co. have left but Sixteen. I just give that at what it is worth. I am mistaken about Will G. being with

06-097-P01 No. 13. Brushy, June 28th 1864. Dear Brother,
06-097-P02 I have sorrowful news to tell you this morning. Uncle Alfred is dead. Mr Orr recd a letter from Henry yesterday, confirming what we had heard before. He died late Sunday evening the 5th of this month, just 18 days after he was wounded. Poor Aunt Bettie is allmost crushed beneath the blow. As soon as she heard it was really true, she fainted away, and they thought for a while she would never revive again. Ever since, she has had cramping spells, and sometimes loses her breath. I have just returned from there, Mary Orr and I staid with her last night. I fear she will have a severe spell of sickness first — if she ever does get over it.
06-097-P03 He writes that the Drs made a good examination of his wound just a few days before he died, (which they had not been permitted to do previously, on account of the swelling) and discovered that the bone had been considerably fractured, just below the knee cap, and upon pressing it a good deal of matter run out with the oil of the knee cap.

06-098-P01 [[separate block: left-hand page]] So you see it was a good deal worse, than was at first thought. Poor Uncle Alf. when he told Lou and me goodbye he said “I just want to get into one big fight, that will do me.” But now he sleeps between two comrades in arms — John Morgan, and [[deleted: illegible]] [[inserted: Docter]] Gardner. Bob [[Head?]] and his lady called upon us yesterday morning; he is rapidly recovering from his wound and will start to his command next week. He says Uncle A. was a good soldier — he watched him during the fight and he appeared to be the coolest man in the Co. Henry writes that cousin Gran is able to walk some, is in fine spirits, and will be able to start home in a few days. Bob has drawn a furlough and will come with Gran. Thos. Harper got in the other day, he says Parsons men have been ordered to Houston. By the by Who is Coz G’s correspondent.
06-098-P02 Well the Methodists are having another grand time at Liberty; their meeting commenced last Thursday night, and will probably end to night (tuesday). I have not attended except Sunday, there was so many people there that day, they had to move the seats out under the trees. I did not know half the people that were there. Parson Sansom preached in the morning, [[Coltr V.?]] in the evening. Had a splendid dinner on the ground and pretty girls were plenty, but thats no news to you.
06-098-P03 [[separate block: right-hand page]] “But as in the days of Noah they shall marry and be given in marriage” Last Sunday night Old Mrs [[Liz?]] Hawkins and Old Mr Love were united in the bonds of matrimony; and not long since, Old man Durst and a widow Smith of Johnson Co; It is reported she has a hundred negroes. All I can say is [[illegible]] her. Since the old people have gone to marrying I suppose the young folks will think they have full licence now. I saw Sweet Sunday, it is reported that Jim has gone to the Feds, but I hardly think he would marry and go right straight off and leave his wife. I recd two letters from Fayette yesterday which Henry had recd and sent home. He appears to be in fine spirits says all the men over there are and that the most of them have reenlisted for 50 years or during the war. He says Jim is as lazy as he can be, just lolls around camp, and he accuses him sometimes of being in love, but cant tell how it is as he never gets any letters and he is sure he never sees any of the girls, unless it is in his sleep.

06-103-P01 Ann & Cynthia have just passed by going from aunt Catherines and say Warren Payne is dying he has been sick for some time. Lizzie and I will go up to sit up to night.
06-103-P02 Warren Payne is the youngest child of Preston Payne whom aunt [[inserted: Catherine]] took when he was only nine days old and has kept him ever since. Had he have lived seven more days he would be seventeen months old. His disease was chronic diarhea. Lynn Norman is at home on furlough; he has been out on the RioGrande for some months but is on his way to La. He has to report at Sabinetown on the eighth of Sept. He says the Reg. to which Eppa belongs has been ordered to Arizona. Another wildgoose chase like that of Sibleys Brigade. Gran Jetter is still at home. I dont think he is in much of a hurry to return to his command as he has been digging a well for two or three weeks past and intends to finish dig and [[wole?]] it with white rock before he thinks about fixing to go back. His furlough has been out a long time and he says when he is in the army all he thinks about is how to manage to get another. His patriotism has cooled down several degrees below zero. Mr. Chappell and his son Bob were in fifty miles of their home the last that has been heard of them. They are now violent secesh, but doubtless have got home and taken the oath to the feds long ago to keep out of the service in Dixie. Miss Ada Chappell is living at Gran Jettons and she is so patriotic that she says she had rather her father and brothers would all be killed than for this confederacy to go down. but she knows they are all out of danger now for Dock deserted and went home from La. last fall you can now form some idea of what kind of folks they are. Sue
06-103-P03 [[margin]] I wont write any more while Lizzie is at home I am not well [[illegible]] [[/margin]]

Ellen and Laura [[Coffy?]] Mrs [[Graithwaite?]] Jennie Bell and uncle Johny Joe Witherspoon and Mr and Miss Anthony were at uncles Joes. Allen was shot on the 5th but as you said nothing about it in yours of the 7th I suppose it is not true. Mother and Sue have gone to Mr [[Grames?]] Father to Mr Grounds to take some socks to send to Cousin Dock by Ed. Laura did not come home so I am here by myself, except Ruth, sisters black girl whom we have hired for two or three months. I must go down and stay with May to day; and am in a hurry so excuse this botched up letter.

06-106-P01 No. 9. Brushy April 30th 1864 Brother Geo.
06-106-P02 Saturday evening has again arrived and brought the time for me to write. I have sad news to communicate this time; Jeppe is again a widower. Gail died last Saturday (23d). Mother got home yesterday and brought the little baby with her. It is the poorest least one I ever saw, though now it fattens up I think it will be very pretty. Mother says Jeppe told her he would give it to Sue and me, poor little orphan, we will all do all we can for it. It seems that Jeppe is fated to a life of trouble. Henry brought Mother home, and left all the balance well on Hack.

06-109-P01 No. 16. Brushy Texas, Sept. 6th 1864 Dear Brother
06-109-P02 I will again attempt to write. Last thursday I went up to the Office, and got yours of 10th ult. also the knife you sent by Mr. Collins, he passed a little while before I got to the office. I was sorry I did not get to see him. On yesterday I recd yours of 21st August; Lou, Jodas of the 25 which is the latest from you. I also received one from Frances Blair, who by the way is as good at letter writing, as conversation, and if you have ever been in her company much you know she is interesting. They were all well. Thomas has not yet gone into the service.
06-109-P03 Jeppe arrived this evening. He brings no news, left all well on Hack Creek though there is a good deal of sickness in the neighbourhood. Henry has had a gooddeal of practice of late; he has lost two patients, one of them was Daniel H. Willbanks, Warren [[deleted: knows]] [[inserted: knew]] him. Sallie Willbanks married Dr. Orr, and they have parted.
06-109-P04 Jeppe gathered his corn before he came down, made a hundred and thirty bushels. There has been several very sudden deaths in this section of late. Nancy Hancock, (Stout that was) was taken sick on Sunday and died on the next wednesday. They say after she died her eyes poped out of her head. While they were going to bury her, her little brother was taken suddenly, and died [[deleted: illegible]] in two hours he had had a chill or two before, but got up and helped to catch a chicken that morning and ate a hearty breakfast. It is a strange disease. They did not complain of any pain.
06-109-P05 [[margin]] Father has sold old Toby to Mr. Martin, for twenty three dollars in specie. [[/margin]]

06-110 · manuscript

06-110-P01 Mr. Telly — Nancy [[Culphers?]] husband — has been in bad health for a long time: on last Sunday morning a small red spot made its appearance on his arm, it spread rapidly and his arm swelled all over, mortification took place and he died on monday. I have heard of other sudden deaths, it is all thought to be the same disease, in different forms. J. Bell is now suffering severely from his wound. His shoulder is greatly swelled, and there is a place six inches long, in which he says he can feel the ball working back and forth. They think the ball will have to be cut out, but the Dr. thinks he had better not do it till the weather gets cooler.
06-110-P02 Wednesday evening, 7th At 10 oclock this morning, Mr. L. Evans called on us, and left the books you sent, also the letter from Joda. You better reckon we were glad to see some one from the boys. He came riding up through the rain, which had been falling nearly all morning; he was in such a hurry he did not stay more than fifteen minutes, we wanted him to stay for dinner but he was in such a hurry he did not want to [[deleted: illegible]] talk about it. I reckon thats the way they all are when they get pretty close home. He will get home to night, says he left Sabine on the 31st thats only seven days on the road. Dont you call that pretty good traveling.
06-110-P03 Mr Evans says your time will not come before Feb. he also says you could get leave of absence the same as he did. Now you know more about the matter than I do; but had you [[inserted: not]] better not come now, than wait till Feb, when perhaps the furlough business will all be stopped, or you sent off to La. or some where else? Thirty days is a short time for a man to come so far, he would not have long to stay at home but a short time is better than none. I am glad old Magruder is gone.
06-110-P04 [[margin]] The little baby is five months old and weighs nine pounds. We thank you for the book [[inserted: you sent me]] [[illegible]] [[/margin]]
06-110-P05 [[margin]] [[illegible]] says tell uncle [[illegible]] to see him [[/margin]]

06-111-P01 I will now have to tell you something more about the meetings which seem to be the most engrossing events of the day up this way. Every one preaches his own doctrine with all his might, consequently discussion [[inserted: is]] [[deleted: illegible]] rife. You wondered in one of yours, whether the good feeling which seemed to exist between different parties would continue to exist. I will give you a few items and you can draw your own conclusions: At our meeting in August it was announced that at the next appointment the meeting would be protracted, several eminent preachers were expected, and of course good preaching anticipated. Now this was not exactly in accordance with the feelings of our Methodist friends, so after studying on it awhile they appointed a meeting in Mr. [[Batakers?]] neighborhood embracing the same time! Not exactly as warm towards us as of yore, think you? The saying of Parson Hill, “now if me and my neighbor dont agree I just let him alone, dont go about him,” had sunk deep in their hearts, so union meetings were forgotten. Our meeting commenced at the appointed time, thursday night before the 1st Sunday. the congregations were small untill Sunday when, notwithstanding their efforts at “hedging” there were so many there, they had to move the seats out and preach under the grove. It is only the methodists that are so hostile. the presbyterians are not so afraid of the truth.
06-111-P02 Bro Jones was [[inserted: the]] only preacher from a distance, he did most of the preaching. By request Parson Austin addressed the people Sunday evening, [[inserted: he preached]] from the words “It is finished”. He made a very good talk. There were no conversions, but four united with the church — Milton Rawlins, his wife, Sarah Selby, and Lizzie [[Burnard?]]. The meeting closed on monday night at which time Bro Jones preached one of the best sermons I ever heard on the unity of the church. The house was full and I hope a good

06-112-P01 impression made. Parson Austin was not a regular attendant but heard several good sermons. In his own language he says “I tell my brethren that they (the christians) have the bulge on us and we had better let them alone”. This is an odd expression. I dont know why it was done, but an other protracted meeting was appointed for the [[deleted: illegible]] beginning friday night before the first Sunday in Oct. Bro Goodman told us several preachers would be there we had never heard of before. How I wish you could be with us at that time. I know you would enjoy yourself.
06-112-P02 Parson Austin was [[deleted: illegible]] waiting on Lis. Gibbs last Sunday, and [[gave?]] Saturday night. Dont you think that is right early? his wife has only been dead a little over two weeks. Father has just returned from the widow Mc Knights; he went down to get an auger to bore for water. He brings two items of news; one is that Fayett and Jim have either been taken prisoners or killed. A letter has been recd stating the whole Brigade was captured. F. and J. have a hard time of it. The other item is, that Mary Morgan is to be married to night to Mr. [[deleted: illegible]] Phipp. And so they go. You wish to know if I would not like to partake of your cobler. It would be a treat indeed. I have only tasted one this year. But I would gladly take supper with you some night, if it consisted of bread and water only. I saw Walk Hatter the other day, he looks about as he used to. He was a prisoner four months, and says he fared well while in N’s hands. He says the Soldiers he talked with sayed the would fight us ten years but what they would whip us; that old Abe gave them plenty to eat and wear, and that is all they care for. You see I can write you long letters now; I have
06-112-P03 [[margin]] done so this time, but I fear it will not be interesting to you. Lizzie [[/margin]]

07-003 · Lizzie fears for George’s safety and the missing letters

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 3

07-003-P01 No 10 Brushy Wednesday Night April 15th /63 Dear Brother: Again I take my pen to write, though I will not promise to be very interesting. Laura received your letter of 21st March last Saturday, the first letter we had got for three weeks. Lou got Joda’s letter last Sunday with yours of the 12th inst. enclosed which gave us great satisfaction; as we did not know whether you had left Galveston or not. I hope your new situation will prove a healthy, and agreeable one, though, fear it will not be so much so as the one you left. Do you think there is any probability of your being attacked there, in that inland place? it looks to me [[deleted: to a curious place for]] soldiers. I fear you will not remain there long, but be ordered along untill you get to the Mississippi and there be trapped up like the Post prisoners were or perhaps receive a worse fate.
07-003-P02 You cannot imagine how uneasy we were when we could not hear from you; how many causes were assigned for not getting letters. Who knew but what some of your letters had been read, or some of

Editorial note. Continues on 07-004. Deleted wording in the inland-place sentence is partly awkward and is reproduced rather than silently repaired. Post prisoners is the writer’s phrase; the event is not identified on this page.

07-004 · Mother’s fears, Lizzie’s request to burn letters, and farm work

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 4

07-004-P01 mine to you, and something dreadful been done to you; for you may have been careless with them, leave them lying about, and who knows how much treason might be found in some of our uncongenial ideas. So reasoned Mother and what truthfulness there was in her logic time alone could determine. I know you will smile when you read this, but you must remember how scary we allways are when any thing unusual happens. Moreover, Mother has enjoined upon me, to be careful what I put on paper, in these perilous times: and, by the by just while I think of it, Beck told us she found several of my old letters in Warrens trunk. had, nt you better, after you have perused them to your hearts content, just commit them to the flames of your camp fire; they will only raise the blaze a little higher and then settle down and be out of mischief.
07-004-P02 After hoeing so hard all day, and then brought a buckett of water from the head spring and then milked the cows (we have six young calves in the pen) I feel right smartly fatigued so for the present, hopeing you are not on guard to night, I make my best bow and retire.
07-004-P03 16th This is a very pretty evening, the clouds that obscured the Sun for a while this morning, have been driven away by a strong southern breeze.
07-004-P04 [[separate block: closing written upside down above the main text]] This leaves all well on Brushy no more at present Affectionately Lizzie

07-005 · Good crops, furloughs, and a sister’s wish for peace

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 5

07-005-P01 and left the sky clear and bright. We have had a very seasonable spring so far, consequently every thing looks well. Fathers six acres of corn happened to be planted just before a big rain; it has come up beautifully, scarcely a missing hill. Mr. Graves did not do quite so well, he had to replant a good deal.
07-005-P02 Cousin Gran got home on the 4th inst. on a sixty days furlough; it appears to me, Gran must be born to good luck; this is the second time he has been home for sixty days since they all went to Arkansas. I mean being married goes a long ways in his favor in getting furloughs it appears. There is Lambert Pace, has been sick for a long time, and has been trying to get to come home, but had not got permission at last accounts, just because he is not married I suppose. Joda writes he expects to [[lost: small tear]] to come home about the middle of May; You say nothing at all about coming, so I suppose there is no chance for you to come.
07-005-P03 But I do hope, and trust, and pray to our heavenly Father, that this cruel war will soon come to a close; and you again be permitted to return to us. Be sure to watch and guard against the temptations which surround you, so you may return to us greatly improved in those qualities of mind, and body also I might add, which when

Alas! I fear but few will come out of this awful this soul trying scene of wickedness and confusion, unscathed and pure: but I think that some will, and among that number I may my brother be, so that they may return to their homes and grace Society as its brightest ornaments of virtue and Christian character.

Father got his grass sown last week 4 acres and there has been a fine rain on it since. George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 8

07-008-P01 Saturday Night April 4 Dear George: Warrens stay is about over with us, as he starts tomorrow; and I thought I would write you a few lines to let you know we are all stirring. We have not received a line from you for about two weeks, I cant tell why it is we dont get letters unless they have stopped you from writing; yet I hope this is not the case. We were filled with sadness this evening by hearing of the death of Mrs Payne. Poor woman to die and leave her little children to meet the worlds cold frowns without a mothers kind and tender care there is five of them one an infant of one week old. Preston is at home now though as a matter of course he will have to go back to the army soon

Editorial note. Continues on 07-009. Year not written; the later slip suggests 1863.

07-009 · Cotton socks, medicine, and longing for the family to reunite

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 9

07-009-P01 We send you two pairs of socks and some pills and a fine [[deleted: comb?]] comb. I wish we could send something else but I have been studying and can think of nothing else that would be of any benefit to you; as you seemed to like the cotton socks Ellen gave you we thought we would knit some more thinking they would be more pleasant for summer. If you do not like them I suppose you have woollen socks enough to do you till we can send you more. Sister is over and Warren being here it only lacks your presence and Jodas to make us seem as we used to seem. Oh! I do hope the time will come when you can again be with us; but if you have gone east I fear it will be a long time first. As I wrote you a long letter by last yesterdays mail I can write no news of interest to nite. Your Sister Lizzie

07-011 · Lizzie waits for letters and reports deaths near Brushy

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 11

07-011-P01 Brushy Tex. Jan. 22nd /1863 Dear Brother. Again I take my pen to write you a few lines, though I dont promise to be very interesting. I have written you four letters, and never have received a line from you yet. We have been looking anxiously for letters for the last week and none have come. Laura went to the Post Office this evening and I thought sure we would get a letter but as usual we were disappointed. I attribute not getting letters partly to the mail for I think surely you do write. The last date we have is the 7th, your letter to Mary Orr.
07-011-P02 This leaves all well on Brushy, except Father he has a spell of the headache. But Death has again visited our neighbourhood. Eliza [[Andrews?]] died last Sunday morning. Lizzie D. is still mending slowly. I forgot to mention in my last the death of Dr. Burkhart; he has been dead about
07-011-P03 [[separate block: side margin]] Dont you get enough to eat? Your health is always better as if you were hungry [[illegible]]

07-012-P01 a month. There has been two weddings up the Country since you left Miss Becy Branson and a Mr King, Miss Ellen Branson and Mr Sam Earl. Perhaps you know Sam Earl he belongs to Deals Co. was at home sick.
07-012-P02 [[Granite?]] is also at home sick I have not seen him; he told Father he thought he [[deleted: was]] poisoned. (Perhaps with dead [[illegible]]). No late news from Mr Orrs boys. And from no where else. Indeed this is a dull time. A [[goozy?]] came a long the other day; Father asked him if he had any late news. He said had heard [[Hymiman?]] had taken Galveston but for his part he did, nt believe it. I seldom go to meeting now consequently dont see the girls often; therefore cant tell you any thing about them. Jeffie has just returned from San Antonio He is well. Says every thing is as high there as it is here. We received a letter from Beck to day stating that Capt. Burns Brother had been killed by the Feds, in sight of his own house.
07-012-P03 I suppose you have heard all about it. Your Sister Lizzie

07-014 · Typed copy: news of Aunt Rebecca and the missing soldiers

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 14

07-014-P01 Letter Number 9/ Tuesday night Feb. 10, 1863 Dear George, I recieved your letter of Feb. 1 this evening, letter, map, and all very interesting. Ellen was delighted with her letter. She has had us read it for her at least ten times this evening, you must write her another, it does her so much good as it does me to get a letter. I recieved your letter of 25 Jan. a week ago to day, and by a continuation of dates will try to answer them both in the same letter.
07-014-P02 I believe we have never written to you about hearing from Aunt Rebecca Hymann’s folks. As Jessie was returning from Ark. he camped with a man just from Miss. who told him, the Federals had overrun aunt Rebecca’s neighborhood destroyed her farm, and had taken her house for a hospital; her boys were all in the army or had been. Henry was at home on account of his having been wounded at Ft. Donaldson(?)
07-014-P03 Mollie O. Sue, Laurer, and myself all went over to hear parson Austin last Sunday. He gave his views on the Millenium made a pretty good talk I suppose; but I didn’t understand much of it; came home and heard Mr orr had recieved a letter from Henry so we ate a few bites and went down to see what he had written: his letter was dated 21 and 23 Jan. they were at Pine Bluff had been there only a few days, they left the White River country in a hurry, he said their cooking utensils were strown from Brownsville to Little Rock their teams having given out so they could not pull them. We have not heard Fayett’s and Jim’s fate. Henry wrote he had talked with several who had made their escape, who told

07-015 · Typed copy: escapes from Arkansas Post and work at the loom

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 15

07-015-P01 him they had seen Fayett and Jim late in the evening on the first day of the fight in the rifle pits, all right then; that is the last account we had of them.
07-015-P02 Wednesday night, 11 Henry allso wrote that cousin Granville had seen Jack Chappell he had made his escape from Ark. Post he said he was detailed to dig ditches, and when he saw the Federal flag waving over town he got out; he was on his way to Little Rock and was going to try to get from there home. Burdet Weatherford and John Porter have got home, they say they were detailed to wait on the Dr. at the hospital and as soon as they saw the Federal flag flying they allso left. Porter says he lay in the bushes near there for a day and a night perhaps, and that after the Feds. got possession, the men in the rifle pits kept firing at them, so one of the gunboats moved a little further down the river, and just raked the ditches and our officers had to call out, Stop men stop! before the rifle men would desist. Aunt Cynthia is very uneasy about Jim and Fayette. We have been spooling our thread today for our dresses tomorrow we expect to mark it, and as Mr Tilford is to bring our loom home tomorrow we expect to get out cloth in next day. it is now eight o’clock so I must quit as they have all gone to bed but me.
07-015-P03 Saturday 14 Feb. Your letter of the sixth just came to hand this morning: glad to hear you are enjoying good health. Well, I find I must try to lengthen my epistles, draw them out, spin a longer thread in other words, try to compose a little. As for my ever becoming a newspaper correspondent, it is something ti which I never hope to attain: my brain is not full enough of ideas to try to communicate them to the masses, even if I had language at my controll, by which to do so. but can’t is a word that should be in no ones vicabulary. Therefore in th future

07-016 · Typed copy: criticism of military authority and a plea for peace

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 16

07-016-P01 I will try to be more interesting.
07-016-P02 You ask “what I think of such opinions” as are advanced by your leader, I answer to say the least, They are arbitrary, unjust and tyrannical. Let such minds as these go into ascendency and have controll and where is our liberty, our privilege as rational beings? I answer gone! and gone forever! I am sorry you are under command of one, who has so little feeling, so little humanity, and has so much tyranny of opinion about him; if he really thinks what he says, if he does not, I detest his moral principal as a man, and think him unfit for the position which he occupies. If he was to see this, I suppose he would be more of the opinion than ever, THAT correspondence should be stopped between the “utencils” of war and their equally worthless friends at home; for my part about all the good I wish him is, that he may never rise to higher command but sink to the position of one of the lowest high privates and then let him tyrannize over whom he can.
07-016-P03 As for peace, it is what we cannot hope for, as long as the North choose to prosecute their present undertaking and the South holds out with it’s stubborn resistance. Oh! that the ruling powers would stop! Stop and think for what this strife is for! for what this stream of blood continues to flow. But no, of this they do not think: the love of power is stronger than any other, and all must Subserve to this. We cannot stop it, we can only move along with this vast current and trust to providence to bring us safely through. May the time speedily come when peace shall again smile upon us is my prayer.
07-016-P04 Saturday night, my usual time for writing to you, has again arrived. Sue, Laura, and myself all writing, Mother is knitting. Father and the Children in bed.

Editorial note. Later typescript included among the university’s scans, not an autograph manuscript. This is an independent reading of that typescript. Typewriter correction strokes and visibly cancelled miskeys are omitted when the replacement is clear; substantive wording and remaining typographical errors are retained. Continues 07-015. The leader is not named here. A separate loom paragraph at 07-018 may belong with this text, but scan sequence alone does not prove it. 07-017 · Typed copy: sickness at home and uncertainty after a lighthouse fight

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 17

07-017-P01 Brushy, May 7, 1863 Dear George, Laura being sick it falls to me to write to you again this week. We were fixing to go to preaching last Sunday, when Laura was taken with sick stomach. She has been right sick ever since till this morning. She is able to sit up some, and thinks she will be able to write some this evening; the balance are all well except myself; I waked up this morning with swimming in my head [[a line of question marks in the typescript]] FURTHER sickness. I recieved yours of the 8 to 15 the day I mailed mine no. 12; Laura allso got yours of the 16 and 17 the same day; as Laura’s was written just the day before the light house fight, which we notice on account of in the Telagraph, we were anxious to recieve your next letter, to learn whether you and Joda were in the engagement or not; if you were I hope you were unhurt, as the paper gave no account of any wounded on our side. We are very much in hopes you have not been sent to La. I suppose troops will have to be kept at Sabine, and as you are there we think perhaps you will be kept there: though it is very uncertain, for it seems troops are ordered one direction to day, and tomorrow are turned right around and sent to an entirely different place. Stones Reg. was ordered to the frontier and travelled three or four days when the order was countermanded, and they were sent to La. We have heard when they got the orders to got to La. about four hundred refused to go, and there was about to be a burst up how much truth there is in this report I cannot tell. That regiment appears to be composed of not very sound matierial any how from all I can learn, it is doubtful whether the Confederacy is ever benefitted much by thir service.

Editorial note. Later typescript included among the university’s scans, not an autograph manuscript. This is an independent reading of that typescript. 07-019-P01 If Joda gets to come home on furlough, we will look for him in anout ten days from now: how I do wish I knew you were coming with him, but I have not any hopes of it, or I would not be writing this letter. 07-021-P01 hearing of [[Harmans?]] death, and her girls will keep going to frolicks. She told Mr Orr to day, that her children at home gave her more trouble than those in the army. Jeffie brings word, that Jack [[Shaws?]] wife is dead. — Laura forgot to number her last letter: it was the seventh, (not counting these scraps) so you see we have done most as well as you. 07-023 · Lizzie’s Sunday visitors and a plea for a letter

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 23

07-023-P01 Sunday night Feb. 1st Dear George: It doesnt seem hardly natural for a letter to go off and nothing in it to you therefore I scribble down a few lines, though dont promise to be very interesting. Mother went to Sisters to day. Laura has just returned from there, says they are all well. They have heard from War once, since he left, he only traveled from seven to eight miles a day. Rob and Nancy were over to day; also Mr Orr aunt Cynthia [[Claray?]] and Laura. Jim, poor fellow had no person to talk to but Ellen and Jimmie I know he missed you. Nancy is fat and can laugh as loud as ever. Mrs [[Swann?]] is in a great deal of trouble [[just?]]
07-023-P02 [[separate block: side margin]] Hope you will find time to write to little me.

07-024 · Ellen delights in George’s letter; news of Aunt Rebecca’s farm

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 24

07-024-P01 Letter Number 9 / Tuesday night Feb. 10th 1863 Dear George: I received your letter of Feb. 1st this evening, letter, map, and all very interesting. Ellen was delighted with her letter she has had us to read it for her at least ten times this evening; you must write her another, it does her so much good as it does me to get a letter. I received your letter of 25th Jan. a week ago to day, and by a continuation of dates will try to answer them both in the same letter.
07-024-P02 Well I believe we have never written to you about hearing from Aunt Rebecca [[Hymanns?]] folks. As Jeffie was returning from Ark. he camped with a man just from Miss. who told him, the Federals had overrun aunt Rebeccas neighbourhood destroyed her farm, and had taken her house for a hospital; her boys were all in the army or had been. Henry was at home on account of his haveing [[deleted: been]] been wounded at Ft. [[Donelson?]]

07-026 · Henry’s letter and uncertain news of Fayette and Jim

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 26

07-026-P01 Mollie O. Sue, Laurer and myself all went over to hear parson Austin last Sunday. He gave us his views of the Millenium made a pretty good talk I suppose; but I didn't understand much of it; came home and heard Mr Orr had received a letter from Henry so we ate a few bites and went down to see what he had written; his letter was dated 21st and 23rd Jan. they were at [[deleted: illegible place]] [[inserted: Pine]] Bluff had been there only a few days; they left the White river country in a hurry; he said their cooking utensils were strewn from Brownsville to Little Rock their teams having given out so they could not pull them. We have not heard Fayette and Jims fate. Henry wrote he had talked with several who had made their escape, who told him they had seen Fayette and Jim late in the evening on the first day of the fight, in the rifle pits all right then; that is the last account we have of them.
07-026-P02 Wednesday night 11th Henry also wrote that cousin Granville had seen Jack Chappell he had made his escape from Ark. Post
07-026-P03 [[separate block: inverted upper margin]] Rec'd 20 Feb — 63

Editorial note. Continues 07-024 and is followed by 07-027. A place name before Bluff is cancelled and Pine is inserted above. Henry’s report is secondhand news of Fayette and Jim, not confirmation of their later fate.

07-027 · Escapes from Arkansas Post and preparations for weaving

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 27

07-027-P01 he said he was detailed to dig ditches, and when he saw the Federal flag waving over town he put out; he was on his way to Little Rock and was going to try to get from there home. [[Burdett?]] Weatherford and John Porter have got home, they say they were detailed to wait on the Drs at the hospital and as soon as they saw the Federal Flag flying they also left. Porter says he lay in the bushes near there for a day and night perhaps, and that after the Feds got possession, the men in the riffle pits kept fireing at them, so one of the gunboats moved a little farther down the river, and just raked the ditches and our officers had to call out, Stop men Stop! before the riffle men would desist. Aunt Cynthia is very uneasy about Jim and Fayette. We have been Spooling our thread to day for our dresses to morrow we expect to warp it: and as Mr Tilford is to bring our loom home tomorrow we expect to get our cloth in next day. It is now eight O Clock so I must [[separate block: side margin continuing sentence]] quit as they have all gone to bed but me

Editorial note. Continues 07-026, followed by 07-028. Opening given name is uncertain. The manuscript reads warp it; the later typescript’s differing word should not replace it.

07-028 · Lizzie’s reply to the opinions of George’s commander

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 28

07-028-P01 Saturday 14th Feb. Your letter of the 6th inst. came to hand this morning: glad to hear you were enjoying good health. Well, I find I must try to lengthen my epistles, draw them out spin a longer thread; in other words, try to compose a little. As for my ever becoming a newspaper correspondent, it is something to which I will never hope to attain: my brain is not full enough of ideas to try to communicate them to the masses, even if I had language at my controll by which to do so: but can't is a word, which should be in no ones vocabulary, therefore in the future, I will try to be more interesting. You ask, “what I think of such opinions” as are advanced by your “Leader”, I answer to say the least, They are arbitrary, unjust and Tyrannical: Let such minds as these get in ascendency and have controll, and where is our liberty? our privilege as rational beings? I answer gone! and gone forever!

Editorial note. Continues 07-027, followed by 07-029. The Leader is unnamed on this page; do not assign a specific officer without corroboration.

07-030-P01 To George Douglas from Sister Lizzie Douglas Brushy May 7, 1863 — Refers to Lighthouse fight — (mentions darkies) also note to Joda Bell from wife Susanna Douglas Bell
