07-031 · Laura is ill; the family waits for news of the lighthouse fight

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 31

07-031-P01 Brushy May 7th 1863. Dear George: Laura being sick, it falls to me to write to you again this week. We were fixing to go to preaching last sunday, when Laura was taken with sick stomach she has been right sick ever since till this morning she is able to sit up some, and thinks she will be able to write some this evening; the ballance are all well except myself I waked up this morning with swimming in my head [[lost: line at fold]] further sickness. I received yours of the 8th [[deleted: and]] [[inserted: to]] 15th the day I mailed mine No 12. Laura also got yours of 16th and 17th the same day: as Lauras was written just the day before the Light-house fight, which we notice an account of in the Telegraph, we are anxious to receive your next letter, to learn whether you and Joda were in the engagement or not; if you were, I hope you are unhurt, as the paper gave no account of any wounded on our side. We are very much in hopes you have not been sent to La. I suppose, troops will have to be kept at Sabine, and as you are there, we think perhaps you will be kept there: though it is very uncertain; for it seems troops are ordered one direction to day, and tomorrow are turned right around and sent to an entirely different place. Stones Reg. was ordered to the frontier, and traveled three or four days, when the orders were countermanded, and they were sent to La. We have heard, when they got orders to go to La. about four hundred refused to go, and there was about to be a burst up. how much truth there is in the report I cannot tell. That regiment appears to be composed of not very sound material any how from all I can learn, it is doubtful whether the Confederacy is ever benefited much by their services. If Joda gets to come home on furlough, we will look for him in about ten days from now: how I do wish I knew you were coming with him, but I have not any hopes of it, or I would not be writing this letter. You must take good care of yourself

Editorial note. First autograph leaf of the May 7–8 letter; continues through 07-034. One line at the horizontal fold remains unreadable. The typed counterpart at 07-017 also leaves a gap. The claim about four hundred men is explicitly unverified by the writer.

07-032 · Wool, harvest labor and news from Johnson County

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 32

07-032-P01 while Joda is away for if you were to get sick you would not have any person to wait on you unless Warren gets back. Directly after I finished writing to you last Friday Jeffie arrived: he left all well in Johnson except Maggy and Larkin. Maggy had been very sick, they were both better when Jeffie left. He left Warren on Buck Creek. Warren intended to start to camps the first of this week, I expect he will be there before this reaches you and can tell you all the news of Johnson County. Jeffie brought us about 90 lbs of wool from Henrys which will keep us very busily employed untill we [[inserted: can]] get it [[lost: words at fold]] for the carding machine. Jeffie intends running his reaper this harvest, he never reported for enrollment and he has never been pestered yet and I hope will not be for he will let every body else alone if they will let him alone; he has bought a very nice little pump since he has been up there, which [[paces?]] like a cradle rocking he says. This is a beautiful day the wind is from the north quite cool for this time of year the sun is shining very brightly every thing looks so green and pretty, though I suppose I need not expatiate on the beauties of nature, as you are now in sight of trees and vegetation, and not surrounded by a waste like you were on the Island. This good weather is very appreciated, we have had such a wet spring and the wheat had a little rust: I wish you could see Jims wheat it looks so fine. Some of it comes up to Jeffies chin, the birds are eating it some now. Harvest will soon be here, some talk of cutting this week (the Becketts and Lemmons) but ours will not be ready before two or three weeks yet: I hardly know how people will get their grain saved unless the men are furloughed there surely are not enough of men here to save all of the grain. I have just been out to get Laura some dewberries. They are very scarce as the prairies are nearly all plowed up. Our garden looks very well plenty of mustard lettuce and radishes now and we will have plenty of beans peas squashes and tomatoes we planted a good many onions but they are not doing well
07-032-P02 [[separate block: inverted upper margin]] Laura is better this morning May 8th

Editorial note. Continues 07-031, followed by 07-033. Manuscript reads Jeffie and Buck Creek where typescript 07-019 has Jessie and Brick Creek. A word describing the pump’s motion is uncertain. Lost text concerning preparation of wool is not supplied.

07-033 · Reported death of Robert Jetton; Lizzie’s political views

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 33

07-033-P01 Mr Orr got a letter from Mr Dyer the other day. He writes that John says cousin Robert Jetton died in Miss. three of Uncle Louis's boys, he says, were taken prisoners at Ft. Donaldson but had been exchanged and were back in Tennessee when he left there. John Jetton from inability, had never been in the army. I think John Orr must be mistaken about three of uncle Louis's boys being taken prisoners, for I do not think there were but two at Ft. Donaldson. But all is now hid behind the “vail of futurity”; when that is raised the picture may be sickening to look upon: how many may then be dead whom we have known since childhood, time alone can tell. O that this awful war would cease, and let those who are yet alive return to their homes. It appears to me, there has lives enough been sacrificed to gratify the ambition of any man that has any heart at all but I suppose Lincoln does not care if the lives of every man in the South are sacrificed if he gets his beloved colored [[deleted: citizens]] liberated, and he can rule this Southern land. It is for who shall rule and who shall not they are fighting for, and not for the love of the union; but I think I would be willing to live under the rule of the Czar of Russia to get peace. Most any thing would satisfy me, but the setting of the negroes free here among us, that would be more than human nature could stand: if (old Lincoln) intends to make us and the negroes equals I want the South to fight him till he gets out of the notion, and then take him and make him serve in the capacity of one the ballance of his days. It seems all hopes of foreign intervention has failed entirely; and it remains now to fight fight till one side gives it up, or the other is conquered. I hope it will not be the latter for I do not think a conquered people could be happy: just think of a standing army over us to keep down insurrection. Should we gain our independence would it be desirable or not, I mean would the independence gained be desirable, there would be a standing army to support, a conscription term to serve if our president could carry out the views advanced before the Miss. Legislature.
07-033-P02 [[separate block: inverted upper margin]] I got a letter from aunt Jane the other day. She and the children were well she said she had got a letter from you a short time before

Editorial note. Continues 07-032, followed by 07-034. This page was inverted in the scan. Cousin’s name reads Robert Jetton, not Jackson. The writer distinguishes reported information from her doubts about the number captured. The racist and proslavery arguments are preserved as her historical views, not editorial assertions. Uncle Louis’s identity and precise kinship are not independently established by this leaf.

07-034 · Local marriages and Susanna’s hope that Joda will come home

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 34

07-034-P01 “Between two evils choose you the least:” but as I said before most any thing would be better than war. I expect you will be tired of this letter before you get done reading it so I will write a few more items and quit. Well I'm going to tell you somebody is married; and who in the world is left to marry, these war times [[deleted: there]] you begin to think? It is no other than Mr George Clayton and Livinia Andrews, after being engaged Seven years they have at last made out to marry; But he still is not ready to take her home I hear, he has to go down to where his tanyard is and fix up a house and prepare two months the report is before he is ready to take her home. Don't you think he might have got ready in Seven years? I do. Don Weatherspoon says Lizzie Chapman dared her Father to bring his wife there so Old Grady has gone to live at his wifes house. The report is Ed and Lizzie have bought the home place from their father. With an other item of gossipp if you wish to call it that I will quit and that is [[deleted: that]] your aunt Bettie Goodloe has another daughter. I reckon y that is as much as you can bear this time, so I must go and hunt Laura some more dewberries so goodbye for the present. Affectionately. Lizzie
07-034-P02 [[separate block: different hand, note to Joda]] Dear Joda. I am expecting you home by the 18th of May and consequently will not write you a long letter this week but for fear you dont come I will put a word in Lizzie's letter to you. Yours per George gave me great hopes of seeing you soon. My only fear is that you may ere this have been ordered to Alexandria and if so I wont look for you till the war is over for I know you would come if you could. My health continues very good though Emmie has been puny ever since she had that colic of which I wrote you. I suppose Lizzie has told every thing in the way of news and this will have to suffice this time. if I get a letter that you are not coming I will write immediately. Hoping to see you soon I remain your devoted wife. Susanna Bell.

Editorial note. Final page of the May 7–8 letter. Lizzie signs the main letter; Susanna Bell signs the added note. Livinia is the spelling read here. The place name Alexandria is divided across lines. Local marriage and property news is introduced as report or gossip. The unsigned later attribution at 07-020 should not override these signatures.

07-035 · Later identification of Lizzie’s April 2 letter

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 35

07-035-P01 To Geo. Douglas from Lizzie. Brushy, Tex. Apr. 2, 1863

07-036 · Flooded roads delay the mail and spoil a church gathering

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 36

07-036-P01 Letter No. 9. Brushy Texas April 2nd 1863. Dear Brother: It has now been near two weeks since we received a letter from you; and you may imagine how anxious we are to hear from you, your whereabouts & C. as your last letter stated you would leave Galveston in a few days. I cannot tell, why it is, we have not got letters lately unless it is the fault of the mails, as there has been a great deal of high water lately. Last Saturday and Saturday night it rained very hard harder at some places than it did the other big rain on the 25th Feb. but not so hard on Brushy as then: but it disappointed a great many people, about going to the quarterly meeting. Uncle Joes folks had been fixing for it for three weeks and Prudence was also making grand preparations for the reception of company, and allmost every body was “fixing up” to go to the quarterly meeting; but on Saturday morning the clouds, which had been hanging Sullenly around for the past few days, began to let fall their “garnered fullness” which soon made many a face, I have no doubt, look as gloomy as they. The consequence of it all was, the “magnificent meeting” as Mrs [[Thos.?]] Hillin would have it, was a “Sublime failure”. I would have [[deleted: went]] [[inserted: gone]] Sunday any how despite the mud and water if it had not been, the horses, on that particular morning took care to keep themselves, clear out of sight: none up but Jenny, our new nag and you know I could not go by myself. Mary Orr had been nearly all week making a new dress to wear, so she was highly disappointed. Ann Kelly had all of her ribbons in a box ready to start down here, so you may be sure there was a “tempest in the teapot;” there. The miss Bransons of [[four?]] mile got to uncle Joes before the rain commenced so y[[lost: edge]] see there were a few strangers there. The miss [[Farrars?]] of Chambers Creek were also up, also Mr Duate, who has re[[lost: end of word at edge]] his health, and intends returning to the army soon I must continue

Editorial note. First leaf of the April 2–3 letter, continuing 07-037–039. A few letters are clipped at the right edge. Letter No. 9 is written here as well as on the February letter; the source’s numbering is retained, not silently renumbered.

07-037 · Warren’s brief visit and four long months of separation

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 37

07-037-P01 We were highly gratified, on tuesday evening last, by the arrival of Warren and Beck. Warren has about recovered from his sickness though he has not entirely regained his strength. They cannot stay long with us, on account of Warrens wanting to start back to the army about the first of next week. They will have to start home on Sunday next. We are very sorry of this, as we thought they would stay at least three or four weeks when they did come. But “to arms! to arms!” is the cry, and every man that can drag one foot after another must go. We have no late news from any where, every thing [[deleted: seems to be]] is a stand still in this way of news, but the war keeps going on there is no stop to that; and whatever raised such a hope of peace by the “first of March” and the “first of June” and the “first of July”; is more than I can tell. I have got out of all hopes of peace, soon. If Old Lincoln had ever meditated peace, he would not be enrolling his men from twenty to forty; and the South is not going to give it up, as long as they [[deleted: can]] muster a thousand men in my opinion. Three O Clock P.M. Not feeling very well to day I have been trying to “snooze” a little and as I feel somewhat refreshed I will try to write some more, although I feel like I can't write any thing that would interest you. The ballance of the family are well and the health of the neighbourhood I believe is generally good, with the exception of Mrs Payne, who is now very low: it is feared she will not recover. Some of us will have to go over there to sit up to night. Sis Bell staid with us last night, the first time she has visited us since you left; which by the by is just four months ago to day. Four long months it seems to me more like a year. Lizzie Bell and Jennie have neither been here on a visit since you left They say they can't get time to come but they manage to get time to go every where else

Editorial note. Continues 07-036, followed by 07-038. Statements about conscription, Lincoln’s intentions and prospects for peace are the writer’s contemporary understanding and opinion.

07-038 · A verbal map of the farm and spring wildlife

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 38

07-038-P01 I will not quarrel with them about it, of course; for if they do not want to come I will not want them to: but it pains me to think, that people whom I have always considered as friends, to appear so distant: not so distant either when we meet, for the always appear friendly and ask nay, beg me to come to see them, but I cannot think people sincere when every thing is in word, and nothing in action. But “with these few remarks” we will drop the subject and wander on, and perhaps we will strike something more interesting. Father finished planting his six acres of corn [[deleted: just]] last week, or rather [[deleted: he]] Walker did: and this fine rain on it, I think it will do well, if we can just get it worked. Perhaps you would like to hear how the ground is divided off. We will begin at the west end of the field. Mr Graves takes the ground worked last year by Penee Nave and Walker; then Mr Dawkins comes in he has fourteen acres which includes the dewberry patch then Uncle Alf takes a few acres I don't know the exact number about four or five though, I think: this brings us down to the wheat. Father has left some ground just west of your wheat where he intends sowing the hungarian grass, then comes the corn and from the corn to the house and from the house to the Graves ground is left uncultivated I think there is about ten acres left for the weeds. This has been a beautifully clear day. The wind is from the South plenty warm this evening to have both doors open. The cotton wood trees have leafed out enough to give considerable shade. And just let me inform you the varmints are getting pretty thick. I went out to milk the other morning looked down in the bottom right south of the calf pen and saw some kind of an animal I could not tell whether a fox or wild cat and I did not follow it, to make out its particular title.
07-038-P02 [[separate block: inverted upper margin]] Mother staid with Mrs Payne last night she is no better

Editorial note. Continues 07-037, followed by 07-039. Land allocations are described as cultivation arrangements; this page alone does not establish legal ownership. Penee is the name as read and may be a short form.

07-039 · Deer, conscription and a bitter observation about slavery

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 39

07-039-P01 Friday 3rd. I got so sick yesterday evening, I had to drop my pen and quit writing. I feel right smartly better this morning and I think I will be well now. I wasnt very sick at first, but the medicine I took made me very sick. The ballance are all well. Ellen has just come up to me and says tell Uncle George “just one more letter”. I commenced telling you about the game yesterday evening. The deer have become allmost gentle; as I was going to the office the other day, I saw three, they circled around me about fifty yards off, held up their heads and looked at me as saucy as you please, while they trotted gently along. The turkeys appear to be very scarce this Spring; I have only heard one or two gobble yet: I saw a gang of six over the creek the other day, the only ones I have seen; directly afterwards Rob and his brotherinlaw Parks passed on down the creek after them, a gun awakened the echoes that evening, the first sound that had aroused them, for many a day. I am very glad indeed, that the conscript let Rob off; for I consider him a good man, and very useful to the neighbourhood, besides, he never had any thing to do, in bringing on the present troubles; but alas many a poor fellow as innocent as he has to bear the trials and hardships in common with those that brought it on. But it is no use to talk about who brought it on, and did not now, for we are all into it: but a person cant help thinking about things: here is Graves and all of his family at home, and you off fighting for his negroes, a person can deny it looks hard: but let me not be ungrateful to Mr Graves, for he is the only one that interested himself about tending our ground, I should not have said the only one either, for Rob would have taken some I expect if Mr Graves had not. I reckon I had better not ask you any more questions, as you were taken so heavily on account of my questions before. I think they were all put to it for something to talk about, to go to joking you about that. I wish you could get a good joke on that Capt. You can tell him old Mrs Partington heaved a sigh when she read he carried all of his wounded men out of the fray him self, and thought, “no [[deleted: doubt]] wonder the poor little delicate man fell down in the water, when that [[counchie?]] shoulder exclaimed Oh! my Susters [[separate block: side margin, continuing quotation]] if you dont take us away from here we will all be killed!!”
07-039-P02 [[separate block: inverted upper margin]] You must excuse this letter if it partakes some of my sickness, for I do feel pretty bad this morning you need'nt tell Evans what Old Mrs Partington said unless you can run a good joke on him by it. With my love to you and Joda I remain Affectionately Lizzie

Editorial note. Final leaf of April 2–3 letter. In the sentence about Graves, “can deny” is retained as read although “cannot deny” might be expected. The joke uses a difficult phrase read tentatively as counchie shoulder; no exact meaning or corrected wording is supplied. The next sentence names Evans in connection with the joke. The quotation runs along the lower and side margins.

07-041 · Laura’s January letter: rain, anxious mail visits and war rumors

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 41

07-041-P01 In Little Room Jan 28th 1863 Dear Brothers Warren & George I received your letter of the 18th yesterday at noon we ar so anxious to hear from you all some of us go to the Office Twice a week & ar most all ways there the day your letters come as they arive most invariable on Tuesday or Friday, rain or shine some one is there. It has been very rainy for the last 3 weeks it rained all day for 2 Sundays Then in the middle of the week besides. Though it has not affected the well at all I think the old well is beyond cure. Every body else's wells ar full. The creek is runing briskly. Wheat looks tolerable well considering the dry fall, the ground is very soft since so much rain & the little Snow. We had more rain than we have had since last Spring the hog-wallows are all full it looks as if the drouth was over. if it is I look for better times for War & famine go together, now if the famine is over wont the war be soon Oh! I hope so. I heard to day Lincoln has been killed Shot while in his carriage. now I cant give credit to this but Then it may be so. I wish it may be if it would in any way bring the war to a close probable if another were in power Thing would take a turn for the better. better or worse I suppose we must put up with it. We have no late news from Ark. All well last account. [[Darnells?]] Reg. has started east of this River to Vicksburg whether they get across or not is uncertain the River being full of gunboats. Nashville is not retaken. Memphis is. [[Hamman?]] [[Brinn?]] & Loyd were killed in that fight several more wounded I have not learned their names. Thus falls one by one of our acquaintances. [[3?]] of the Lancaster Co. have been killed several others died, will half get back. I got a letter from Beck the other day of the 10th they were all well getting finely she had not got any letters relative to the fight up to that time. Mr Evins has not been down yet after the corn [[lost: lower edge; overlapping view continues at 07-042]]

Editorial note. Beginning of Laura’s letter (signature at 07-047), physically inverted in scan. The lower portion is repeated and extended at 07-042. Reports about Lincoln and military movements are explicitly contemporary hearsay; the supposed killing of Lincoln in this January 1863 letter is a false rumor, not the later assassination. Names and the small numeral before Lancaster remain uncertain.

Nashville is not retaken. Memphis is. [[Hamman?]] [[Brinn?]] & Loyd were killed in that fight several more wounded I have not learned their names. Thus falls one by one of our acquaintances. [[3?]] of the Lancaster Co. have been killed several others died, will half get back. 07-043 · Laura’s pony, neighborhood parties and fears about conscription

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 43

07-043-P01 some better allso I am independent about rideing now a Pony at my [[deleted: command]] [[inserted: command]] at any time convenience to consult but my own he is regularly drilled Cavalry Service. Poney know how to jump ditches & goles Right left wheel Charge & c & c There has been several tow life Partys lately one at George [[Hoatters?]] one at Hursts. [[Magg?]] Lemmon attended (against her Mothers will) danced both places. Hursts was last Friday night next day they heard of Hammans death. The old man was in Lancaster when the news came he got drunk cursed & swore a round right [[deleted: swear]] afterward. how strange man will put no restraint on their passions even some girls ([[inserted: it is said]] [[Lemley?]]) got drunk that night at [[Hoatters?]] Party. Jim Jeffries has returned from the Salt Works he could not get on big enough scale to keep him out the Army he took sick & had to come home I dont know what he intends doing. They have enrolled Dallas conscripts To forty all that would be enrolled. I dont know what will be done about those that would not be Nave & Bill [[B. Hill?]] ar the only ones I know of though I heard there was several others. nothing has been done or said as yet about them. Ellis is not being enrolled nor do I know when is enrolling day. [[deleted: There]] There is I understand a call session & the Represintive from here say he is going to urge the conscript Law To Sixty instead of forty. We are in a glorious place ant we. Let them extend to sixty then what who will attend to things at home. The prospects are gloomy there is now scarcely men enough to provide for Things what is the army to do. I am afraid There is suffering in the future. There is scarcely enough provisions in this part of the country to last till harvest Some of what is here has been [[lost: lower edge; overlapping view continues at 07-044]]

Editorial note. Continues 07-042, with lower section repeated and extended at 07-044. Names at the parties and of one conscription resister are uncertain. The source reads tow life, likely intended as low life, but is preserved. Statements about enrollment and a proposed age limit are the writer’s reports, not a checked account of law.

07-044-P01 [[lost: clipped upper line]] a call session & the Represintive from here say he is going to urge the conscript Law To Sixty instead of forty. We are in a glorious place ant we. 07-045 · Orr family losses, shared carding tools and resentment over substitutes

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 45

07-045-P01 The country whether it is any better in The Northern Counties I can not tell I fear not. but we must hope for the best we have never come near starving yet & I trust never will. Sqr Orr has lost his son David he has only one left John & he does not know whether is is alive or not he was among the Donellson Prisoners.
07-045-P02 [[deleted: Thursday 30]] [[inserted: Friday 30th]] I have just returned from Aunt Cynthia's she & Mother have [[inserted: gone]] to see Mrs Crum. Aunt C. loaned me her cards for a few day & Sam. is going to the Office Therefore I must hurry & finish this letter & & get to work I have to spin when ever I get a chance as I want a carpet & nothing way to get it. Ma & Lizzie keep my cards busy Spining our dresses. I started Mr [[Goslings?]] this morning after some turnips but as Mary could not till tomorrow I will wait. Mary has grown very fast she is higher than I am. Lizzie & Jennie have finished their cotton dresses we have ours ready for the loom, have commenced others. Father has not rented any more ground he is talking of getting Alfred Oats To tend some. It is getting cloudy I fear we will have another rainy Sunday. but no preaching next Sunday. Ned & Stewart have been up at Uncle Alf's [[deleted: illegible]] for several day. They with Uncle Alf are here now getting some Corn for Their horses Uncle Alf is in the second Army been to Yorks I suppose. York has sent a substitute so he is still to make his poison as usual. I do wish all such were obliged to go but all mean & moneyed men can stay at home in Security while Poor men go & fight. “Mother sends her love to you both and says She wants you to consider all letters equaly addressed to you both” as you are [[inserted: one]] as much as the other to us & we think you are interested a like about home. I suppose Joda shares your [[lost: lower edge; overlapping view continues at 07-046]]

Editorial note. Continues 07-044. Lower section repeated and extended at 07-046. Friday 30 replaces Thursday 30 in the date. The phrase “nothing way to get it” is retained as read; likely omitted wording is not supplied. Statements about Squire Orr’s sons are contemporary reports. “Cards” here are tools for preparing fibers for spinning.

07-046 · Overlapping view: Mother’s equal love for both brothers

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 46

07-046-P01 [[lost: opening clipped]] Uncle Alf are here now getting some Corn for Their horses Uncle Alf is in the second Army been to Yorks I suppose. York has sent a substitute so he is still to make his poison as usual. I do wish all such were obliged to go but all mean & moneyed men can stay at home in Security while Poor men go & fight. “Mother sends her love to you both and says She wants you to consider all letters equaly addressed to you both” as you are [[inserted: one]] as much as the other to us & we think you are interested a like about home. I suppose Joda shares your letters too, for the present I beg to be excused excuse my form too for I just write things as I think of them.

07-047 · Letters, reused envelopes and a request for seashells

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 47

07-047-P01 Both write as often as convenient for [[deleted: Nothing]] Nothing gives us more satisfaction than letters from you. affectionately your sister Laura Douglas
07-047-P02 I have not yet got any envelops I have to turn or make them I hope I will get some when [[Carrol?]] goes To Cedar Hill [[L. D.?]]
07-047-P03 [[separate block: note signed Sue]] Dear George Take good care of yourself and and go to hear preaching if it is not exactly the substantial gospel perhaps there is some good even in the fine spun discourses which you have to listen to. When you get home I know you wont have to go to meeting if you are not inclined to do so. Go down on the Beach and gather me some sea shells if you get time You can put a few in Warrens trunk for safe keeping. Your Sister Sue.
07-047-P04 [[separate block: note continued on 07-048]] Well George: I went over and staid all night with Phony last night: the first time I have been over since I went to Johnson. I keep so busy spinning I hardly ever go any where. Phrony has come to the conclusion, she dont want any body else to go to the war, because Granville has gone. You know she used to think every body ought to go because Granville was gone. Gran writes quite hopefully: he says [[deleted: illegible]] he thinks the war will be over in six months any how. He thinks prospects appear brighter [[lost: bottom edge; see overlapping view 07-048]]
07-047-P05 [[separate block: margins continuing the end of 07-048, left to top to right]] round as big as ever. She is delighted because [[deleted: Aunt]] Cynthia gave her Jim and can talk about old Branson till you would get sick I havn't seen any of the Red Oak girls lately but as Tom Roberson says there is great probability of Ellen Petty and Higgins G. Marrying No more at present from Lizzie Yours No 4

07-050 · Joda sends cloth home despite scarce food and limited money

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 50

07-050-P01 Dear Sue, I have been at work all day [[obscured: verb]] Cotton — consequently am very tired and feel but little like writing to night. I have been so buisy lately that I have neglected to write as often as I ought. I get Letters from you Tolerabley regular the last I got come in four days. I received a letter from Lizzie the other day She says she is well pleased with her new home She invites up to see her & to get something good to eat. If I can get off I will except the invitation if I cant get a leave of absence to go up and see her I will call on them as I go home. We are getting on about as usual plenty to do and but little to eat. it is hard to have to live as we do when we are in sight of such a bountiful supply of Flour Bacon and every [[inserted: thing]] & c. So it is I hope such a state of things will not last always. I & George send by Dr. Lawrence two bolts calico [[54?]] yds in each bolt. I bought it at auction and owing to its being slightly damaged I got it at 26½ cts per yd; I think the stain will wash out if she ready if it dont an you have to tear it off it will be a good deal

Editorial note. First leaf of Joda’s note, signed on 07-051, accompanying George’s January 26, 1863 letter. The cotton-work verb is faded. Yardage is read tentatively as 54 per bolt; compare George’s statement of over 100 yards of each material at 07-053. The sentence concerning washing out the stain is awkward and retained rather than repaired in the direct transcript.

07-051 · Cloth prices and Joda’s instructions for dividing the purchase

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 51

07-051-P01 Cheaper than any I could have got by the retail; for Callico of that width is selling at 50 cts. we also send 2 bolts domestic upwards of Sixty yds. we paid for the wide 45 cts the narrow 35 it is of an inferior quality but is the best we could get at the prices. in fact nearly all the goods in market are of an inferior quality. I have saw one good lot of domestics [[inserted: sold]] them at 45 cts by the large lot. but little now in market. Me & George are equal Shares in the Stock the half of each piece is yours however you all can divide or [[deleted: illegible]] [[inserted: distribute]] to suit your [[deleted: illegible]] [[inserted: fancy]] the dark will make nice dresses I think. I would have sent you some thread if I had the money but it took all we could raise to get what we did if I have good luck I will soon be in funds again and if I can get off home I will try to get some more goods. I will write again soon So for the present good night Joda

Editorial note. Continuation and signature of 07-050. “Upwards of Sixty yds” does not explicitly say per bolt here; it is left as written. Prices are cents in the source, without specifying currency. “Stock” refers to the jointly purchased cloth in this context.

07-052 · George writes from Houston about cold weather and short rations

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 52

07-052-P01 Houston Jan 26th 1863 In reply to yours of 14th I will begin by saying that I am in a hurry and have but a little time to spare at the present as it is Sundown and after night I will not have an opportunity to write and I want to put this in the office so it will go up tomorrow. For several days we have had some very cold weather in this latitude and it has not yet run out yet no rain or Sleet however to incommode us this time. Our stove we enjoyed finely also the Society of our friends who called on us frequently. Rations are about as [[deleted: usual]] usual this time of year we get plenty of Meal not quite of beef and nothing else. Soap Sugar Molasses Vinegar and such like articles are “played out.” We Still have some of “that” on hand yet but when the supply is exhausted we will have to fall back on No. one for supplies. This Evening Chas G went to [[Fox's?]] Soap factory to buy soap He enquired if we were soldiers and to what

Editorial note. First leaf of George’s companion letter, signed on 07-053. “That” and “No. one” are the writer’s expressions and not identified here. The soap factory name is uncertain.

07-053 · Free soap and a shared shipment of cloth for home

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 53

07-053-P01 Co[[lost: faded letters]] and we belonged to & c, when he h[[lost: faded letters]] gave us a bar and refused pay. Ordinary Soap is worth 15 cts the Pound. Plenty every where but in the Q.M. and C.S. Depts. Still plenty of flour in the city but Jeff has none for issue. Goods are slightly on the mend Domestic at retail from 40 to 60 cts per yard. Other things in proportion. Dr Lawrence Warrens old Marion friend is here, he lives at Wax on [[Moon?]], he has agreed to carry what Jody & I intend sending, namely, two bolts calico & two bolts Domestic in all over 100 yards of each. The qualities of the goods are all different. We will arrange the cost between us and let you know how to divide. I have delivered the goods to Dr Lawrence four bolts, mark'd N. L. D. on each with agreed price he will carry them with his own, if I mistake not to the Widow Dennis's below Waxahachie. We will be able to pay for the goods without troubling you any on that score. It is too dark to write, so I will close excuse bad writing for once, [[Goodby?]] George

Editorial note. Concludes 07-052. Opening is faded and continues the question about military unit. The short phrase after Wax is uncertain. The text says over 100 yards of each material, while Joda’s account at 07-050–051 gives details whose exact quantities are uncertain; these are preserved separately. N. L. D. is a shipping mark, not expanded to an ownership claim.

07-055 · An unexpected homecoming at Brushy Creek, April 1864

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 55

07-055-P01 Brushy Creek Apr. 2nd 64 Dear George I got home on last Sunday Evening. I found all well I tell you I was glad to see them all. I took them on surprise for they had just got my letter of Mar. 15 telling them not to look for me, so my appearance was very unexpected. I found but little change in the looks of the home folks none of them appeared to look much older. I was glad to find them all looking so well. Ellen & Emmie have grown smartly. Little Mary is an interesting child & I think very pretty. I must tell you something about my homeward trip. I was eleven days on the way I had to lay over one day at [[Bren.?]] & one at Houston at Beaumont I heard that our Batt was ordered to La. & that [[illegible: name or word]] were to go [[deleted: illegible]] Sabine P. to relieve

07-056-P01 our Batt. When I heard this news it caused me to be uneasy for fear that I would be stopped, [[deleted: to]] particularly when I kept seeing marching orders all through & detailed men on extra duty. I was very uneasy until I got away from Houston. But I had luck & broke Satan's [[jaws?]] once more in this day of desperate [[suits?]] & troubles. I have been enjoying my self finely the past week. Every time I sit down to the Table I think of you & the other Boys & how I wish you had some of the good things to eat. I tell you Biscuit Ham & many good things look inviting when I get to meals. 07-058 · Father’s sixty-second birthday and Sue’s affectionate advice

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 58

07-058-P01 [[separate block: upper corner annotation]] 1863
07-058-P02 Sunday morning: the wind is in the north it got there yesterday morning so I suppose by this time it has reached you. It is quite cloudy, but I do not think we will have rain to day. This is Fathers birth day: he is sixty two years old and enjoys better health than he has for years past, I suppose, on account of exercise. I will quit as I might run this into a “sister Jane of thousand words”. Affectionately Lizzie
07-058-P03 George you must excuse me for finishing my letter to Joda on your paper but as we presume that each of you see the others letters we think it dont make much difference. Our paper and envelops are getting quite scarce as Warrall failed to go to Cedar hill to get us more at the stated time so we have to do the best we can. Lizzie has written so much that I dont know what else to offer. I think you are pretty severe in your criticism of her letters, but perhaps it will be an advantage to her in the end as it may serve to spur her mental capacities which would otherwise have remained dormant. Take good care of yourself keep company with the intelligent and [[separate block: right margin, continuing sentence]] well disposed kiss little white Lily for me and don't forget [[deleted: illegible]] your Emmie and little Ted. Yours Sue

Editorial note. Contains the end of Lizzie’s note and an added note signed Sue. The date February 15 is supplied by the identifying slip; the year 1863 appears as a corner annotation, and the connected receipt at 07-059 reads February 26, 1863. The statement that Father is sixty-two could support a February 15, 1801 birth date if this dating and the father’s identity are confirmed. It does not by itself identify his father or birthplace. The quoted sister Jane phrase is retained as read.

07-059 · Reassurance from home and an offer to send more clothes

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 59

07-059-P01 Page 7th You must be sure to write to us when your clothes give out, socks as well as your other clothes, so that we can send you more. I have counted it up and to night you are standing guard if if you are not sick. I expect you think of home right often when you get off in the cold with no one to talk to; but don't get homesick the time may be nearer than we anticipate, when we will have peace and you will all get to come home again. I do not recollect what Laura wrote, but I suppose from your letter, she must have presented rather a gloomy picture. If so I will just attribute it to the state of her mind on that occasion for you know, we all feel more gloomy at times than others. I will now present my picture We are all getting along finely have good health, consumption only
07-059-P02 [[separate block: inverted upper margin]] Rec'd 26 Feb — 63

07-060 · Good wheat at home and a reported death at a bridge

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 60

07-060-P01 only at meal time, or any other part of the day when we feel hungry; we have plenty to eat now and expect we will have, all this year. The wheat you sowed, looks as well if not better than any I have seen. We have plenty to wear, and will have as long as we have health to make cloth: so you need have no uneasiness about us, we are getting along very well. Mr Crum has received a letter from Charly giving an account of Harmans death they were making an infantry charge across a bridge. Harmon was struck directly he crossed the bridge, either in the head or breast Charly did not know which, as he did not see him after he was killed. They say he did not utter a word when he was shot, but threw out both arms and fell upon his face. He had a hundred and eighty dollars and a journal which he had kept since going into the service, on his person, which were [[deleted: illegible]] not recovered [[separate block: bottom margin continuing sentence]] at that time So I was informed

07-062 · George questions hopes for peace and describes wartime controls

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 62

07-062-P01 Sister Lizzie Sabine March [[30th?]] /64. No 64 As the month is almost out I thought I had as well finish it off by writing a day or two sooner than usual, not that there is any thing interesting going on but to pass off time. Bad colds were [[illegible]] in this [[illegible]] for I have quite a [[severe?]] bad cold. Somehow go [[ill?]] with me in this latitude than they did in Ellis, the only reason I can assign for the difference is, the cold in this section is damper. Don't yell too fast on the Peace question, everybody is perfectly cool in this country; don't look for peace until one side or the other is completely exhausted, and it will take some time to do that. Report came here yesterday to the effect that the Yankees had taken Sabine Town and a battery with equipment at that place. (cant vouch for the truth of it, though I think it is generally credited). Sabinetown is 125 miles above here on the Sabine river, and about 100 miles due West from Alex. Taylors Cavalry have been ordered to La and have gone. All is quiet here and the Weather very good; We did have a cool norther but that has blown over. Four men deserted from Bickleys Co night before last and went to the blockade. Somehow some of the rebs still have hankering for Sea life. This last act continuing in the service for the war in their present organizations all between the ages of 18 & 45 is an “eye opener” and rather gives the lie to the universal reenlistment of the troops on the other side. Well every thing has been done that can be done and that is some satisfaction. Firstly. Every able bodied white male citizen of the Confederacy between the ages of 17–50 is hereby declared to be in the Military Service of the Confed. for the War! & c Secondly. Persons owning 15 able bodied field hands on the 1st Jany 1864 are hereby exempt, provided such persons sell all surplus provisions raised Year to Year to the Govt at fixed prices, & bind themselves to furnish [[100?]] lbs Meat [[illegible]] hand

Editorial note. Letter No. 64, continued on 07-063. The autograph date appears to be March 30, while later slip 07-061 says March 20; the reading remains tentative. The opening cold-related sentences are faded. Military reports and the digest of Confederate measures are George’s account, not independently verified legal text. The phrase field hands refers here to enslaved laborers counted for an owner’s exemption. The final quantity and wording are uncertain.

07-063 · Civil liberties, prisoners and blockade-running news

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 63

07-063-P01 Thirdly. Impressing officers will take whatever is necessary for the use of the Army wherever found at Govt prices, provided it is not all a fellow has and give some kind of paper pay for it, (no matter what, is the spirit). Fourthly. All Confederate money West of the Miss will be taxed [[33⅓?]] per cent after the first of July (Now [[illegible phrase]]) Fifthly. The Writ of Habeas Corpus is hereby suspended in certain cases. So at last all is gone step by step little by little of our public liberty to [[illegible word]] personal affairs, all is in the hands of the Govt. This is something like [[illegible]] might have been anticipated from the beginning. The way things commenced and the way they have ended are in splendid keeping. The fuss was made about nothing, consequently had to or has to end in something. Wind blows higher from South, pretty apt to blow up a war shortly. Griffin has gone to Galveston, don't know what for, to be absent Six days. Only two Howards have to wear the large balls, instead of three as before stated. Jackson & Doggett are only under guard for 90 days. I would write to W. J. C. again if I knew where to direct to, tis reported here that they are ordered to La. tis a very hard matter to catch a cavalry man with a letter when he is always on a march or Scout. I directed to him always according to his instructions couldn't do any better of course. Ask Hefner what rank he held on Howells staff. The Steamer [[deleted: Isabel]] Isabella ran the blockade at Galveston, brought in a large quantity of ammunition arms & c, a few boxes wine for old Mag, also several Schooners have run in there recently. Confederate money [[illegible: remaining bottom line]]

07-065 · George to his sisters: cold weather and desertion, January 11, 1864

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 65

07-065-P01 No 51 Dear Sisters, Sabine Jany 11th 64 Another week has passed quite disagreably, considerable sleet fell the other night, the ground froze tolerably hard, the wind damp and chilly and all together disagreable. Today is cloudy and threatening rain, mud is abundant. It is all a joke about this Latitude being warm in the winter time it is not as cold as it is in Ellis but then the cold is damp thus making it more disagreable than it would be if it was dry. After all things considered we are faring very well for soldiers and should not complain. It is much more pleasant to be quartered in houses than it is to lie out without tents as they have to do out about Lavaca. Of beef and bread we get enough to live on tolerably well, fare we [[illegible]] a great deal better than some others.
07-065-P02 Late advices from the east are discouraging, the yankees are jubilant and the rebels downcast, everything looks dark for the Confederacy, our armies are in bad condition and the enemy Vice Versa, our men all want to go home, the yankees say they intend to reenlist (See Tel, 8th Jany). The militia are very home sick and intend going home as soon as their six months is out, go where it leads. 50 desertions have occurred from our batt since the last big scout in Dec, it is reported that some of them have been taken but I am inclined to disbelieve the report, it came in rather a crooked way. The Davis Guards have continued to desert some eight or ten having gone to the yankees. As a Co they were moved by harsh treatment, for some slight offence one of them has been balled and chained and they say Magruder promised them that they should never be punished in so degrading a manner. They petitioned him to remit the sentence of this man, and he [[illegible: faded bottom line]]

Editorial note. Letter continues on 07-066–068. The final line is too faded to recover. “Tel” is the writer’s abbreviated newspaper reference. Military news and reported promises are his account, not independently verified facts.

07-066 · Resistance to punishment in Griffin’s battalion

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 66

07-066-P01 Since the first, one or three more have been balled and chained and they threaten if they are not treated better they will give up the fort to the yankees the next time they come along. So much for so much, what the foregoing is worth remains to be seen, if the “Paddies” carry out their threat it will be a serious affair.
07-066-P02 Great dissatisfaction exists in the Batt which threatens serious results, and if somebody dont back out some one will get hurt. About three months ago two men (not in Co C) missed roll call. The roll was called some fifteen minutes earlier than usual and before the drum beat. The orderly sergeant ordered them to carry some guns as a punishment for their absence, this they refused to do because the roll was called before the proper time. They were arrested and tried for disobedience of orders and sentenced to wear a barrel shirt [[20 Dy?]] [[inserted: twenty two hours each day]] and then ten days solitary confinement on bread and water alone. On the barrels was marked their names and the words “disobedience of orders and fatigue duty”. Yesterday the attempt was made to put the barrels on them when some of their Co came out with their guns to resist the enforcement of the order. The barrels proved to be too small and larger ones were procured by this morning. In the mean time however Col Griffin ordered the mutineers to be put in the guardhouse, this they resisted and a great many of the Batt promised to sustain them. This morning they left camps and went out in the country, thus abandoning their arms and cause. Col Griffin made a speech to the Batt and told them that if they resisted the decree of the court martial he would arrest all concerned for mutiny, and if he could not do it with what men were here he would report the fact to Magruder who would use every means in his power to arrest and punish them to the extent of the law. [[Shriver?]] as it would be mutiny to resist the order

Editorial note. Continuation of 07-065; sentence continues on 07-067. The first phrase appears to read “one or three”; it is not regularized to “two or three.” Duration of the barrel punishment and the final word/name are uncertain. “Paddies” is the writer’s derogatory term for Irish soldiers. All incidents are narrated from his perspective.

07-067 · George criticizes discipline and doubts the Confederacy’s future

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 67

07-067-P01 and the original parties having [[carried?]] it all quietly knocked under and allowed them to wear the barrels. Co C showed more disposition to mutiny than any of the others. Of the others or the men that came out with their guns to resist the order yesterday the Col declared it his intention to arrest if possible and punish. I suppose however they have abandoned the post a thing I would do if I were in similar circumstances, but I hope the time may never come when I will have to mutiny. Such rigorous punishments for such slight offences is having a very demoralizing effect on the army, it has caused directly near twenty desertions and it will cause a great many more. Griffin stands at least forty degrees below zero in the estimation of his command, he is despised for being so precise and military in his conduct, he governs men by the force of military law and not by anything like mildness: he treats them pretty much in the same manner an overseer treats his negroes, never has any thing to say to them only when he wants something done, this is the character of the man and I suppose he cant help it; but one thing I have learned never to get in a regt again commanded by a military man. All has quietly flowed over and it is to be hoped we will have peace in the command for the future.
07-067-P02 I received your letter of Dec 19 the other day, and in answer to your query about Warren I can only say he is as big a fool as ever, he is like an old hard shell Baptist you cant convince [[inserted: him]] of any thing he dont want to be convinced of. Nearly everybody else is disgusted, and in my opinion the Confederacy cant last much longer unless some great change takes somewhere, something must [[deleted: turn out]] turn up that will change the whole aspect of affairs and that shortly or its “up” or “out”. Besides what I have already said I believe there is nothing new or interesting.

Editorial note. Continuation of 07-066. Opening syntax and the reading “carried” are uncertain; the family version flags this rather than silently repairing it. The comparison with an overseer explicitly invokes slavery. “Hard shell Baptist” is the writer’s religious comparison; no denominational identity is inferred for Warren.

07-068 · Impressment, defeat, and a faint hope of peace

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 68

07-068-P01 From the reading of late official documents I learn that the impressment act is not working up to their expectations, apparently more dissatisfaction is expressed than was expected. Maybe Congress will repeal it, it would be a good plan I expect for taking things from private individuals by main force is a bad plan, if the people are not willing to support a government it is bound to fall inspite of all efforts made by a few to the contrary. If the people dont think enough of the country to save it themselves the policy is a poor one to try to force them to it.
07-068-P02 The defeat at Chattanooga you will see will turn out pretty much as I predicted, it will cost the Confederacy Thirty Thousand men, and three fourths of them will be lost by prestige; look at the admissions made by the Houston Tel. Abe’s last proclamation is a [[tall news?]] document. As fast as the yankees get possession of the country the people will take the oath as prescribed by the proclamation. ’Tis a tempting bait to have security of persons and property guaranteed simply by taking an oath, which can be broke in two minutes after an opportunity is offered.
07-068-P03 Morgans escape was a pretty “cute” thing and no doubt John will trouble the yankees a sight now yet. Dont you think that “[[View-au-Sie?]]” colors his pieces pretty highly, Somehow or other sensation pieces dont rate as high as they used to. &c &c.
07-068-P04 With the slightest imaginable hope for peace this summer I remain affectionately George.

Editorial note. Conclusion of January 11, 1864 letter, 07-065–068. Criticism of impressment, military losses, oaths, and newspaper reporting are George’s opinions. The name or pseudonym near the end and the phrase describing the proclamation remain uncertain. The letter does not establish the predicted casualty total as historical fact.

07-070 · George describes the march toward the gunboats, May 10, 1864

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 70

07-070-P01 Sister Lizzie, Manhassett May 10th 64 [[illegible: letter number]] The time since our last writing has been [[replete?]] with events of interest, and I suppose that before this reaches you you will have obtained the outlines of the news, so I will fill at once with the details. Last Wednesday night we got marching orders for Calcasieu, at sundown we struck and went as far as town, there we were supplied with three days rations of Crackers and bacon, each ones outfit then consisted of one blanket canteen three days rations musket and sixty rounds of ammunition. We were then ordered to go to sleep and in the long reeds [[illegible: several words crossed by show-through]] and commenced cursing the [[illegible]]. At daylight all arose and took up the line of march.
07-070-P02 The first six miles lay across a bog marsh over which [[scores?]] of Stock had passed when wet and the walking was rendered more difficult by the rank grass. Here a great blunder was made by marching too far and fast without rest, several gave out to lie down in the first six miles. Our road now lay along a sandy ridge through a thin settlement where refreshment &c water could be obtained in abundance. At the end of the point 20 miles we stopped for the artillery to come up. At four oclock the [[round?]] was resumed and about a half an hour by sun we passed the last house on the peninsula, yet to go was some 18 miles; the Sgts we thought it [[knew?]] and for some 6 miles the Capt and [[illegible]] were moving constantly. About midnight we reached [[Oyster?]] Bay which led to the [[illegible]], we snatched an hours sleep while the Sappers and [[illegible]] built the bridge. It was six miles yet to the gunboats, and three to water every canteen was empty [[cursing?]] was [[dry?]] and very grainy too. When we reached the well there was nothing to bring water with. So we had to march on with no prospect

Editorial note. Main letter continues through 07-073. Heavy reversed show-through crosses the writing; several clauses remain unreadable even in enlarged native scan crops. Place name of the bay, some marching details, and letter number are uncertain. The letter is dated at Manhassett but describes a march to Calcasieu and a subsequent engagement; it does not place the whole battle at Manhassett.

07-071 · The advance under fire

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 71

07-071-P01 of getting any until the fight was over. This was rather a dry reflection in case of being wounded, on we went however and at daylight were in half mile of the boat. The force consisted of about three hundred of all kinds including [[Creuzbaur’s?]] artillery, the battery was planted and we moved off at double quick to the charge. The Infantry had been divided in to two divisions, three companies of [[Spaight’s?]] Batt with Co [[F?]] of Griffins under command of Capt OBrien were to attack the upper or lefthand boat. Co’s [[A?]], C, D, & E Griffins Batt were to attack the lower or righthand boat under command of Major McReynolds. Moving at double quick the four Co’s soon got mixed up together and rushed forward more like a drove of beeves than disciplined men. We had advanced about 200 yards when the batteries opened fire.
07-071-P02 Seeing the confused state of the men the officers tried to get them in line, but no sooner had the command “Guide Right” been given than all [[deleted: illegible]] crowded over against the right guide and were getting directly between the battery and boat (the boat had not yet opened fire, we afterward learned the first intimation they had of our approach was the battery playing on them). The officers then commanded “Guide left” the crowd surged off to the left in a bunch. Seeing every man was pretty much his own commander, and every one had lost his place in ranks I concluded I would be my own general, I let the crowd go but continued forward in ranging from behind and before, for I knew the crowd would draw the grape and the shot and shell passed a few feet over me. I kept my eyes on the muzzles of the cannon in front and whenever one flashed I would fall a little quicker than I had ever performed the maneuver before. I kept on this way

Editorial note. Continuation of 07-070. Artillery commander’s spelling and some company designations are tentative. The tactical division and strength are reported by the writer. “Beeves” means cattle; “grape” means grapeshot.

07-072 · Thirst, exposed positions, and breakfast under fire

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 72

07-072-P01 until I was near the boat then I was in danger both of falling shells and minny balls, and as the grape began to go low and plentiful I [[obliqued?]] to the left and got out of range though in [[the?]] range. We were all in a hundred and fifty yards of the boat though not directly in range, the grape whistled pretty close. At last our fire was poured in from port holes from the minies and rifles until along the sides the feds could scarcely man their guns they kept up no steam and could not move the boat, the pilot wheel was so exposed no man could [[deleted: illegible]] live at it a minute, and the minnie balls went through the sheet iron around the port holes. Such was the condition of affairs half an hour after the fight commenced. I was so dry I could scarcely swallow and with dozens of others I lay down on the ground almost exhausted and rested. After I was some what rested we were ordered to save our ammunition and not shoot unless we saw some one whenever any one in the boat showed himself and the most quiet place.
07-072-P02 In the position I was there was more danger from behind than from before for they were scattered some distance back in the grass and weeds firing. I had a great curiosity to see how things were going but this could not overpower the sense of danger. I had been in this place about an hour when the boat swung round broad side to us and we were ordered to fall back out of range. I kept close to the boat and [[illegible: route or movement described]] between the boat and battery and got out of range below her [[illegible]]. Feeling very hungry I called to Henry Collins who was close to come up and take a snack with me. We pitched in to a haversack of bacon and crackers in full view of the gunboats and made a pretty hearty breakfast. While eating a cannon ball cut down a weed
07-072-P03 [[separate block: inverted upper-margin continuation, following 07-073 margin]] Three were killed on the Wave I do not know how many wounded. They threw their dead overboard. I cannot now give a precise [[illegible]] 10 or 11 were killed on our side and about as many wounded. Next week I will give you the balance of the detail. All well, affectionately your brother George.

Editorial note. Continuation of 07-071; main text continues on 07-073. Several phrases are awkward or obscured; they are not silently reconstructed. “Minny,” “minnie,” and “minies” refer here to rifle ammunition. Inverted upper-margin text concludes the letter after the inverted margin on 07-073. Casualty numbers are the writer’s provisional figures, not independently established totals.

07-073 · The aftermath of the capture of the gunboats

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 73

07-073-P01 in ten feet of us but we eat on thankful that it came no closer. After we were through we started toward the bank of the river to get out of the range of the upper boat when I noticed the [[deleted: illegible]] lower one had surrendered. We stopped to look at it a minute when another ball from the upper boat came whizzing along clipping the tops of the weeds about three feet above the ground. We dropped before it got to us, it missed me six or eight feet and him about two feet.
07-073-P02 We then went back to the boat that had surrendered and found Sergt Jones dead, he had both legs broken and a grape shot through his breast. In twenty yards of him lay young [[Sprinkle?]], the top of his head had been cut off by a grape and his brains were lying on the ground near him; his left arm shoulder and side had been terribly mutilated by a shell which exploded near him. I think this was done after the grape had killed him. In ten feet of him lay a man belonging to Daly’s Batt with his head shot off by a cannon ball, and a little off to one side was a Sergt in Daly’s Batt shot through the thigh by a grape, calling for water. A short distance to the rear was Lieut [[Iglehart?]] badly wounded in the thigh by a grape. Further back still was a man by the name of [[Burrell?]] of Co [[C?]] mortally wounded by a grape, no one had a drop of water and I had none to give. Such was the melancholy sight that greeted me after the battle was won. The friends of the wounded were around them and I could be of no assistance so I [[deleted: illegible]] turned from the melancholy sight. They were supplied in a few minutes from the boat with water and carried on [[litters?]] to the hospital. On the field there was not a particle of shelter from the balls nothing but grass and weeds the ground was as [[deleted: illegible]] level as a [[deleted: illegible]] floor.
07-073-P03 [[separate block: inverted upper margin]] We attacked the Granite City, Spaight the Wave. The Granite had eight guns aboard the Wave six. They only used three guns on us nearly, the prisoners numbered about 140 including officers, 14 were wounded on the Granite 2 of which have died.

07-075 · Food, gardens, and artillery drill, July 10, 1864

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 75

07-075-P01 Dear Sister, Manhassett July 10th/64 — No [[77?]] Your letter of June 26th came to hand last friday; and found us all hearty. Times are dry though we had a good rain the other day. We contrive to live pretty well for the times, had roasting ears and tomato soup for dinner dont you think that will do very well for a Reb? especially when it is obtained twice or thrice a week, we could live a good deal better if somebody would run in a load of garden seeds from some foreign port. Vegetables degenerate so rapidly here that in the course of two or three years they run out. I have been told beets will not go to seed here, and cabbage will only head the first year. There is no kind of vegetable here that is the same to be the natural production of the soil. Melons and grapes grow finely, I have seen tolerably good corn cotton and tobacco, potatoes sweet and Irish grow finely. Irish are about extinct, the people depended on getting seed from the north but the blockade shut down on that dependence and left them without. If I owned a place here I would have a vineyard. I think the soil here is well adapted to the growth of all kinds of grapes, mustang grapes grow spontaneously, the “French” grow pretty well in gardens. This is a fine country barring the musquitoes.
07-075-P02 For the last three or four weeks we have loafed around camps and done nothing but this week a few more lessons will have to be taken at the big guns. Artillery drill is easier learned than infantry, but I dont like the way they rattle in a fight, they are what draw the balls bombs and Shrapnel. The latter is a spherical case filled with musket balls one side of the case is very thick the other quite thin, the thick side is put in the gun next the powder, the thin as a matter of course goes in front. When they explode the entire charge of balls is thrown forward scattering like an old blunderbuss and properly directed will kill and cripple all the men at a gun. [[illegible: concluding phrase; words “our cannon and” and “at Calcasieu” visible]]

Editorial note. Letter continues on 07-076. Letter number appears to be 77, matching the slip 07-074, but the final digit is not fully clear. The awkward sentence about vegetables and the writer’s technical description are preserved as read; neither is independently verified. Bottom line remains difficult.

07-076 · Compulsory service and an unpopular inspection

George Douglas Papers Folder 4- Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 76

07-076-P01 For [[lawing?]] for angry Rebs [[Morrow?]] received some compensation but to what extent, according to the nature of the cases, I do not know. Almost every kind of cases came before him as to him another, some Lo Co [[gians?]] had themselves proved legally dead to avoid conscription. Everything between this and desertion came into his line of business. If men did not have to stay into and come into the service but very few would be in the ranks now. I confidently believe that if every man were discharged that would come in, in two months the yankees would be in every hamlet and village of the South. It is strange how men can be made do anything but they can be driven about by the leaders just like an ox driver drives his team about. News from Va is to the effect that Grant has been checked in his onward movements and that he has gone to fortifying and that he will have to take Richmond by siege. Nothing but from [[Johnson?]] and Sherman.
07-076-P02 The other day we were inspected by an officer of Magruders staff a Capt with more conceit than brains and sense of both. There was so much grease on the guns he got his hands dirty which no doubt caused him a good deal of trouble, he presented quite a Dirty appearance and after inspection was over the boys began discussing his merits loud enough for him to hear. Some said he was [[illegible]] others Dutch others something else finally deciding however that he was Dutch and did not understand his business. He wanted to know of Evans if he allowed his men to talk that way. Evans who had not been paying attention to what was being said replied “yes he generally allowed them to say what they pleased”. He replied that would have to report us well armed and drilled and presenting a fine military appearance but in a very bad state of discipline. That chap wont want to inspect this Comp again shortly. A great many inspecting officers come around to see what we have on hand in the way of clothing &c and make reports to Hd Qrs but I never could see as it ever done us any good. Fayette is inclined to poke fun at me in the “Belle Lettres” department, However I think I keep ahead of “Websters Unabridged”. Affectionately George.

The two vessels that were captured there have been disarmed and I learn one of them is Loaded with cotton and will try to run out. I havnt got a letter now for a long time the last was Aug 6 it came in georges what is the matter have you quit writing or not. I think it must be the fault of our mails. I hope I will get a letter tomorrow morning. George says all he wants is a pair of drawers. you must excuse this Scroll for I have had but a few minutes to fix it up in the Boat is now about ready to Start & I must close. I will write again in a few days [[illegible]] my love to all. Your true & devoted Husband J M Bell.

07-102-P01 Sunday Dec. 11th ’64 Brother George I suppose you have become domiciled again in camps by this time and perhaps the monotony of some lonely hours may be relieved by a line from me. We are all tolerably well my own health is not very good but now that winter has set in I hope to improve. It has been pretty cold here since last wednesday and people are busy killing hogs as it happens though my chance for hog meat is pretty slim owing doubtless to the absence of the only one who was competent to take care of them. He has four teams now on the road or I suppose at Brownsville now hauling thirty bales at nine cents per lb from San Antonio He will go into winter quarters about christmas. 08-096 · A land warrant sold and news of cholera, June 5, 1854

George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf · Scan page 96

08-096-P01 Murfreesboro Rutherford County Tenn June 5th 1854 Mr N. L. Douglass my old and tried friend your letter dated April the 25th [[inserted: came to hand on the 27th of May]] enclosing an eighty acre land warrant regularly transferred, with the request that I would dispose of it to the best advantage and pay the proceeds to Mr G. A. Sublett, which request was attended to with as much punctuality as the nature of the case would admit of. which you will learn from his receipt which you will find herein enclosed. I sent the warrant to Nashville, and ninety dollars is the highest price that can be commanded in that market, the speculators commanding ninety three in New York. I have reserved a copy of the receipt to guard against miscarriage or other accidents
08-096-P02 By the by our old friend Sublett continues in bad health I think his constitution is perfectly prostrate and that he never will regain any thing like general health again. I would here remark that the Cholera made its debut upon the City of Nashville on or about the 26th of last month, and also at several places in this County, more especially the west end of this County adjoining Davidson. There have been fifteen or twenty died in Nashville in two or three days when it first broke out, and also about the same number in this County, but it has some what abated (the weather having become more favorable to health) still there is a spirit of apprehension resting upon the bosom of the community

Editorial note. Continues on 08-097 and 08-098, signed Hicks. Insertion is placed after the letter date. Reports of health, deaths and prices are the writer’s contemporary claims, not independently verified statistics.

08-097 · News of the Ott family, an inheritance dispute and a criminal trial

George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf · Scan page 97

08-097-P01 Anderson Ott has sold out his little farm near this place, and has bought a farm of about 150 acres ten miles South-east of Town on the Manchester turnpike. He and his family are all well. Nat. Ott is carrying on a shop, but his health is very delicate, last Spring twelve months he had a dangerous attack of Hemorage of the lungs, and a slight recurrence of it this Spring my opinion is that he is bleeding internally working at his trade. His family are all well at present
08-097-P02 The old gentleman John Ott died sometime in the last of January or the first of February last. Nat at the request of the children adms on his estate. There is a suit now pending in the Chancery court between the heirs relative to the distribution of the negroes and their increase that the old gentleman set apart to them some years since to be divided with their increase at his death, and Abate having some thus his proportion in his possession at his death refuses to give them up for division. Mr [[Wm Harrison?]] & family are well and doing as well as a Heart can or ought to desire
08-097-P03 Many of our good old citizens have died since you left this County, such as Major Gannaway, Jack Ransom, R Halliburten to gether with many others
08-097-P04 you have no doubt heard the whole history of Col. Sam Richardson killing Dr. W. Smith. It was a most cold blooded murder as ever was committed in his first trial he was sentenced to the Penitentiary for ten years, but got a new trial, which has not has not come off since

08-098-P01 He then is lying in jail. Your Kind folks on the river and Mr Nance below this from my best information are all well. Murfreesboro has improved much both in appearance and population since you left here besides the Male College we now have two fine female colleges. The Methodist female college is considered one of the finest buildings in the west cost about twenty thousand dollars. This the second Session will close with about 160 Scholars.

08-100 · Illness, a baby raised by hand, and grief for Mary, October 16, 1849

George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf · Scan page 100

08-100-P01 Readyville Oct 16th 1849— Dear Sir after considerable delay in consequence of others writing to you I did not wish to give a repetition of the news— in the first place my own family has been sick all summer and fall with the flux with the exception [[illegible: crossed or abraded words]] our son Robert but by the blessing of heaven we are all on foot again. Rebecas health is now tolerbly good she is as fleshy as [[inserted: she]] ever was— our baby to be raised by hand has growed very well— all the ballance of the friends are well— Newtons family has been with us ever since June they will leave for home in a few days I answered your last epistal I learn through your letter that you had not [[received?]]
08-100-P02 My wife wrote a lengthy letter in answer to Rebecas address giving a history of the death of our beloved daughters and her trials on that occasion—and the Christian fortitude was all that saved her own life. My own heart was almost Broken but I concealed it from my wife and acted as a philosopher in consoling her that we had others to live for and let the will of the Lord be done— but to mention that beloved name Mary will yet make the tears flow freely May we all remember that a similar fate awaits us too—

Editorial note. Continues on 08-101 and 08-102. Wrapper 08-099 may identify the writer, but signature remains provisional. A damaged exception clause is marked. Rebeca is the writer’s spelling. “Daughters” is plural as read; Mary is named later.

08-101-P01 Sam has ritten from alabama but was very unfortunate before he started for home he had a difficulty with parson Drew and struck him with a piece of pailing and killed him— sam says he acted in self defence—I saw in a news paper that Drew was the aggressor sam speaks of going Back and give himself up to [[inserted: the]] authority and stand a trial if not he will go to Callifornia he remain two weeks and was not taken he has been at home four weeks and has [[inserted: not]] heard from thare since Fletcher is to write shortly then he will no how to act. Sam thinks himself entirely Justifiable—
08-101-P02 [[J Orr?]] is still for Texas but cant go this fall in consequence of Cynthia increasing the family a few days ago it is a son unless he goes by water Theodosia Nance is looking for an heir every day of course he will not move this fall family sicity Mrs Gresham and Betsy is getting along badly and quite unhappy hostility still exist between Julia and Orr J. 08-104-P01 Readyville Jan 26th 1854— Dear Sir I again appear before you [[inserted: in form of a letter]] in the first place I wish to kno why you have [[inserted: been]] silent so long I had almost come to the conclusion that you were no more—or had become offended—I seen a pair of letters the other day from your diggens from Sam & cousin John L—which I was very thankful—I did not find your name in either document

H. Wood he has been in greater fever ever since about Texas he wants me to go with him he says [[inserted: he]] wants a thousand acre field—he wants to take four Jacks with him in a two horse waggon and to ride in it he wants Chs Lowe to go with us me & Joe would be some in a waggon at least 500 lb—so you will see us when we get to your house
