08-105 · Lewis Jetton: the boys’ work, family jokes and an account settlement

George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf · Scan page 105

08-105-P01 I want you to see our boys to putt in seek [[inserted: business]] while they are young they are qualified they have nothing do but start after they get started business will come to them—I must tell about Rebeca she seems to be increasing in flesh daily she is getting so far along she has quit making fun of me she is making a figure pretty much like cousin [[Lucy Pay?]] she weighs about 160 lbs—I think—the ballance of the family are all well—Say to the boys that John has gone back to college to get his Sheep Skin Granville gone to East Tennessee joining North Carolina to do business for young D. McFerrin—White is making arrangements to go to Statesville to Teach School

08-124-P01 a bad chance to start in this world he was put in the army when he ought to have been at school I was opposed to him going to Texas—he was doing verry well here but thought he could do better in your country so he put out so if he does well and becomes satisfied with the country I will endeaver to help him start in lifes rugged road—now we are wandering about in the dark of this political Chang of our government we cant surmise or even guess what the future may be—& its even hard to tell the past in fact I cant I just know that I past through greate trouble Just immagine the greate Chang that is made to see the negroes march out Election days to vote Congressmen Legislators and all officers & all the white men stay at home how degrading though I have the right to vote hardly ever do so because the ballance of my race is deprived of this priviledg—now you know that we are both geting old its not expected that we can labor & make a support I am now warned of the fact while writing this epistle my eyes refuse to see almost still I am trying to carry on my farm it cost me one half of the proceeds to do so—then time the stealing comes their is but little left for me so a support is all I can expect

08-127-P01 Readyville Sept 1st [[1860?]] Dear Sir I take the present opportunity to drop you few lines believing that you have never received a letter that was addressed to you some time ago in relation to Julia Lows Death if you had—you certainly would have answered it so I take it for granted that you have not received it—Julia Died suddenly on the 23d of June she was attacked at [[illegible: line at dark fold]] in 24 h she could never speake so as to be understood—we gave the particulars in a former letter to you & to Granville we recd a letter from Granville since he never said a word about his aunt he may have never got his—yours and his were mail together—I again state to you that it is nesesary for some person to administer upon her estate I have written to all the legatees they have all answered me agreeing for me to administer—so I am waiting to hear from the relations in Texas—if I have any thing to do with the matter I wish it to be agreeable with all I went to Murfreesboro on yesterday to see Capt Sam Davis I had a conversation with him in relation to Julias lands in Texas he knows all about it he says he saw it and inquired about it for Julias satisfaction at her request the day that Davis got home from Texas she died—Mr J L [[Dyer?]] who Julia employed to get up the case would never give her any satisfaction about the matter

Editorial note. Continues on 08-128 and following. Year, surname Low, and attorney’s surname remain provisional; a heavy fold obscures part of the illness description. June 23 is clear, but the year is uncertain. The letter explicitly calls Julia Granville’s aunt without specifying the exact line of kinship. Reading the entire letter, including the reference to Bell and Everett on 08-130 and the continuing enslavement of a boy on 08-129, supports 1860 for the uncertain year; the date remains marked pending further checking.

08-128 · A proposal to recover, occupy and eventually sell Julia’s Texas land

George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf · Scan page 128

08-128-P01 Tharefore she lost confidence in him for that reason she got Mr Davis to examin into the whole matter—So Mr Davis Reports to me that the land is worth some $3[[obscured: digit]]00—that it is improved and has one hundred acres under fence and that it ought to be taken possession of imediately by Consent or a writ of possession to be run against those that have it in possession he further states that thair is about five hundred Dollars expens attach to it Lawyers fees &c now I propose to [[obscured: word at fold]] the land into Market Sell it pay Expences & all Attorneys fees and let the residue be divided amongst the heirs—I think Alfred might go down & see it if you should not be able—I guess you are like my self not always able to go about—Alfred could live a year upon it before it would be advisable to sell it probable—as I understand that the abolition and the drouth has reduced the price of Texas lands verry much perhaps it would be best to delay the sale of the lands till the excitement pass off—I shall write to the ballance of the legatees for them to write to you to use thier names in a petition to Court for a Decree to sell [[inserted: the]] land—when ever you and Texas kin think it advisable—Capt Sam Davis sets out for Texas this day he will call on you—you can advise with him about the lands—he attending business of that [[inserted: kind]] an Attorney I think he is a Gentleman and a reliable man [[lost: bottom continuation]]

Editorial note. Continuation of 08-127. A blot obscures part of the reported valuation: $3?00, not a confidently read $3,000. Abolition and drought are the writer’s explanation of lower land prices. Legal proposals are not evidence of completed court proceedings or sale. “Abolition” is the writer’s word and is not modernized as completed emancipation; the letter’s likely date is 1860.

08-129 · Julia’s estate, an unnamed enslaved boy, and disputed fees

08-129-P01 you and the kin will take interest in the matter and look into the case Mr [[Horril?]] was the Attorney in the case he lives in Palestine he should be consulted and perhaps continued you must be the Judge of the matter if none of you will act I [[obscured: word]] no chance for an agent unless we get Mr Davis to attend to it—I will have to administer at the 1st monday in Oct as that is Court day as longer delay will be injurious to the [[obscured: word]] the property here consist in a negro boy worth some $1200—she has some beds & beding—some three or four hundred Dollars in notes—she owes some money I do not know how much—my wife thinks she ought in Justice to have the house stuff for taking care of Julia—her and the kin for that—I am fearful Mr [[Dyer?]] will try to press his claim upon the Estate here for [[inserted: his]] services in the Texas matter—when I know he was to take it [[inserted: out]] of the lands—he may have the advantage in absence of a contract the boy is hired out and has been for the last seven years I cant get possession of him till Christmas of course I cant sell him till that time
08-129-P02 I have wrote a rough [[word?]] if you can understand me—I would have yesterday wrote by Mr Davis—but it was a big day Murfreesboro—& I am so nervous at times particular when warm I cant write so you see I have to take advantage of my nervous system when I write while they [[inserted: are]] quiet—(I am a Sober man too

Editorial note. Continuation of 08-127–128. Torn edges, folds and stains obscure several words. The page treats an unnamed enslaved boy as estate property and records seven years of hiring him out; those statements are preserved without endorsing them. The first attorney’s surname is uncertain.

08-130 · Crop failure, an Arkansas journey and Uncle Jake at eighty-two

George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf · Scan page 130

08-130-P01 this letter leaves us all well Rebeca health is much better than usual she spent some five weeks at the [[Christal?]] Springs July and part of aug which improve her great deal uncle Jake is down & confined to his bed I fear never to get up again he is verry old & feeble 82 years—like a child knows nothing hardly—politic verry high Bell & everet will carry the state beyond a doubt Mr Davis will tell you all about it you have heard of our short Crop the like was never been known in Tenn before we are sending our hogs to Illinois & indiana to be fatten several thousand already gone by Rail Road—and others will go—we will make from two to three barrels of corn pr acre some places hardly any they are asking five Dollars from the heap—which is mighty hard for Tennesseans—my son White & [[Hotell?]] starts for Arkansas in a few days if they like the Country they will locate—or return—tell Granville that John wont make one barrel of corn to the acre this year—I will make two on an average you will Show this letter to all that are concerned I would write to all separately—it is uneasary and I have so much of it to do—excuse me if you please tell Alfred to write if pleases—for he never will git a letter from Tenn till he writes—answer this imediately we send our love & respects to all of the kin N L Douglass Lewis Jetton

Editorial note. Concludes 08-127–129. The political reference to Bell and Everett helps assess the uncertain date as 1860. Resort name and companion’s surname are uncertain. Crop yields and political prediction are reported by Jetton. Uncle Jake’s age is stated as 82; no surname or exact birth date is supplied.

08-131-P01 Readyville March 7th 1854 Dear Sir after longer delay than I expected in consequence of failing to make collection I enclose you a twenty Dollar Bill = in my next I will enclose a five on the reception of the last you will please to forward a receipt for the whole you polly both sign it = we are all well at present = the spring verry unfavorable for farming—but little news some little excitement about provisions for the turky & Rucia war but [[inserted: small]] a advance in prices as yet—you will please write to me & let me kno how the boys are doing and their prospects and say something about your self I remain most obedient friend N L Douglass Lewis Jetton

08-133-P01 Readyville Jan 4th 1859 Brother N L Douglass Dear Sir after a long silence I have taken my seat with two candles and my [[deleted: and]] glasses on—to drop you a few lines to let you kno that we are still in the land of the living and enjoying the blessings of health hopeing these lines will finde you & family enjoying the like blessing—it has been so long since I have written to you I hardly [[lost: word at tear]] what will interest you to give you a history of your old acquaintance would be a repetition of that I heretofore written to you—for all that I will say there is but few of the old settlers alive thats living about here Esq Martin & lady is no more—several more has past away Esq Ready & uncle Jake are almost gone they are in thier dotage in a maner kno nothing—so old men are growing scarce—so they the people call me one of the old men [[inserted: the]] of neighborhood—our country has undergone a greate Chang since you left the country old man Ready and myself are the only men that resides in the same place from Woodbury to Murfreesboro—this is remarkable

Editorial note. Continues on 08-134 and following. The salutation is rendered as written but not treated alone as proof of a biological relationship. The author’s description of older people’s mental condition is historical language, not a diagnosis.

08-134 · Henry travels to marry in Kentucky; Granville heads toward Texas

George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf · Scan page 134

08-134-P01 I was happy so was all the family to think that Henry thought so much of us as to under go the expense & time to visit us on his arrival we were all happy to have his society once more—we were sorry when he left because he could not stay longer we only excuse him because his appointment [[inserted: was]] out to get married tharefore I felt my duty to send White with him to Ky—so they mounted in the Buggy & set [[inserted: out]] with all our good wishes so White return in fifteen days & saw some [[obscured: word at tear]] world—so we will ever be grateful to Henry for his visit—I wish it was so that we all could see each other again in the flesh—Granville and his father & law with families [[deleted: move]] to Arkansas they set [[inserted: out]] the 13th of last Sept they landed in Washington County we have never recd but one letter from him—his sister & law has written a letter to her cousin I learn from it that his father & law has bought land & settled Granville did not like the country and is on his way to your country the letter states that he left Washington County the 16th of Decr—I suppose he will go to your house or where Henrys lives if he should come to your house I will take it as a greate favor from you to sho[[lost: page edge]]

Editorial note. Continuation of 08-133. The writer’s “White” is a personal name. “Father & law” and “sister & law” mean in-laws. December is abbreviated Decr. Information about Granville’s journey comes from a relative’s letter; arrival in Texas is not confirmed.

08-138 · Historical notes on managing community property after a spouse’s death

George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf · Scan page 138

08-138-P01 Sec 33. Where the wife dies, her husband surviving, administration [[inserted: is unnecessary]] except as to any separate estate which may have belonged to her. The husband continues to have the same power of disposition over the community property which he possessed during the continuance of marriage. But he shall be required to return an inventory and appraisement of all such property; and to file a bond, signed [[deleted: Signed]] by one or more sureties, to be approved by and payable to the district clerk of the county; in an amount equal to the value of the whole of the community property; to the effect that he will faithfully administer the same, and pay over one half of the surplus after the payment of the debts with which the whole is properly chargeable, to such person or persons as shall be entitled to receive it.
08-138-P02 Sec 34 The husband is liable to be called to account at any time after one year from the date of the bond.
08-138-P03 Sec 35. Such bond is suable, recoverable, and in every other respect the same as the bond of an administrator.
08-138-P04 Sec [[deleted: illegible number]] 36 The surviving wife may retain the exclusive management and control of the community property of herself and her deceased husband in the same manner, and subject to the same rights, rules and regulations as provided in the three preceding sections until she marry again; but upon a second marriage she shall cease to have

Editorial note. Continues on 08-139, which identifies the excerpt as general laws of the 12th legislature. This is a transcription of the historical copy, not verification of its legal accuracy, applicability or current effect. An insertion completes the otherwise interrupted opening sentence.

08-152-P01 Austin Texas April 10/69 N L Douglass Esq Waco Texas Sir The Draft was received by the Comptroller this morning. It came yesterday but when we called for it the mail had not been distributed, hence we did not get it. I have endorsed the draft in accordance with the authority you gave me and the draft will be sent to Houston for collection. As soon as we hear from it I will send you the Comptrollers receipt for the amount. You need not give yourself any uneasiness about it. I will attend to it and you shall be troubled no further. With the best wishes for your safe return to your home & family I remain Your Friend Joseph Spence

08-167 · N. L. Douglas’s oath of allegiance and office

George Douglas Papers Folder 5 - Daybook of N.L. Douglas.pdf · Scan page 167

08-167-P01 Oath of Office. I N L Douglas do solemnly swear that I have never voluntarily borne arms against the United States since I have been a citizen thereof; that I have voluntarily given no aid countenance council or encouragement to persons engaged in armed hostility thereto; that I have neither sought nor accepted nor attempted to exercise the functions of any office whatever under [[deleted: the]] any authority or pretended authority in hostility to the United States; that I have not yielded a voluntary support to any pretended government authority power or constitution within the United States hostile or inimical thereto; And I do further swear that to the best of my knowledge and ability I will support and defend the constitution of the United States against all enemies foreign and domestic, that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same, that I take this obligation freely without any mental reservation or purpose of evasion and that I will well and faithfully discharge the duties of the office on which I am about to enter So help me God.

Editorial note. The reverse is labelled January 1868 (08-166). The oath names N. L. Douglas in its opening, but this scan shows no separate signature, witness, attestation or specific office. It cannot by itself prove that an official administered or accepted the oath. Original council retained.

09-002 · Rebecca Goodloe to her daughter Mary, April 18, 1852

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 2

09-002-P01 Rutherford Co Tennessee April 18th 1852 Dear dauhter I received your Letter with Rebeccas dated October 18 1851 it come to hand in due time I would have answered it but I thought I would get another as soon as Mr Andrews got there—and I have bin waiting all this time and has got none You wish me to [[deleted: illegible]] write often as I know by myself how glad I am to get one yes I am glad from my very hart to hear from you all—I am glad to hear that Susana wes Baptized I hope she will do good that she be rich in good works ready to distribute willing to Communicate laying up in store for herself a good foundation against the time to Come that she may lay hold [[deleted: illegible]] on eternal life My sister Betsey is no more she died the 26 of january she suffered greatly she was [[tapt?]] 7 times she Lived 9 days on a little snow and snow water it was all she wanted she was very willing to die there [[inserted: fe]] ll a big snow on the 18 of january I visited her all I could while she was sick I was there by her when she died—I heard from you all by john Cock he said you was all well but Mr Douglass I am sorry to hear of his affliction I wish he could take care of himself and get well—I do not know how you can do there where every thing is so scearce and so dear—I [[deleted: illegible]] would like to hear whether the few things I sent you by Mr Andrews was damaged or not in cashing if the peafowl feathers went safe [[separate block: margin]] Quoted from Timothy [[1st?]] [[6?]]. 18 verse

Editorial note. Letter continues through 09-004, signed Rebecca Goodloe to Mary Douglass. An uncertain word before “7 times” may read “tapt”; the treatment is not identified confidently. Biblical passage and marginal reference are retained; it echoes 1 Timothy 6:18–19. “Cashing” is the source’s spelling, context uncertain.

09-003 · Weaving, gardening, household work, and neighborhood news

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 3

09-003-P01 You must give my sincere Respects to Mr and Mrs Andrew for their kindness and generosity I would be glad to hear that they was well pleased with that Country I wish them all prosperity in this World and happiness in the next Rebecca wants to hear where all the girls is that married since she left here It is more than I can tell I think some of them had better lived single Isabela Hill has moved to the western District she had a daughter name Rhoda Louisa her health was very delicate when she went away as I heard Well now I must write something about myself and my own afairs—with the grate blessing of almighty God my health is reasonable good I can stir about and see to buisiness as usual nit and sew and card and spin some on the little wheel I have bought me a Loom and Mary has wove me 2 [[10?]] webs of cloth this winter I find it is better than to have my weaving I have bin gardening I peas come up and stuck Irish potato coming up onions a growing Beans an Oker [[deleted: illegible]] planted & Beats cucumbers pepper & cabbage plants a grown we have planted some corn & will plant cotton this week Mary works out this crop with garden & Sam Judy has a boy Baby name Jim Says three mounths old and she doe the cooking and washing & Amanda is at Betsey Grahams & I dont know wether [[deleted: illegible]] I can spare her out of the crop or not Alfred let Wm Arbuckil take Tom this year for his victuals and clothes & to learn how to work and be smart Bill is here he carrys watter and mind the children enough of this

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-002. An unclear number after “2” is marked instead of silently resolving it. Names of workers and children are preserved. The passage does not itself specify everyone’s legal status; it should be read alongside the collection’s evidence of enslavement rather than assuming all were relatives or paid employees.

09-004 · Family marriages and moves; signed Mother Rebecca Goodloe

09-004-P01 Cousin Betsey [[deleted: Ad]] Adams Billy Adams widow has moved here and rented the [[Gonnatya?]] house from Mr Hall I have let her have some land for her boys to work her son Billy attends the saw [[inserted: & grist]] Mills Brother Jacob has Bought the mills from Ned Adam & is carrying on good buisness Brother Jacob is as [[inserted: busy as]] a bee he is building a Bridge [[deleted: there]] at home they are all well Rebecca and Anda Alexander is well. Granville Jetton is married to Miss Elizabeth [[Conn?]] Dick Jones has married the third wife mis Mary Daughter of Eldar McHenry Mary Waight to Sam Rucker Mary Goodloe [[illegible]] still remains helpless and was worse the last time I heard from her William Goodloe has moved to the western District gibson County trenton & Henry Goodloes two daughter [[inserted: altamira & emly]] went with them on a vissit to spend the summer with their relations James Goodloe is married to Mis Ann Neal of gibson County—and lives in Trenton Rebecca wished to hear how Ned Adams and cousin Betsey was they are well and doing better than they did at first they have lost one of the twins the little girl is dead O I can not think of half the news that Rebecca would like to hear Cousin Livve Posey is well and all my family except Hannah she is very weakly and has some very bad spells Betsey has Bought a house and lot with her own money and has got a deed in her own name [[inserted: in woodbury]] Well Poly rite here Alfred come home & brought your long looked for and welcome letter which I have just read with grate satisfaction I [[deleted: commenced]] commenced this letter [[deleted: illegible]] Sunday I wrote some yesterday this is tuesday I was just about coming to a close when Alfred come Julie is at Betsey in woodbury I remain your loving Mother Rebecca Goodloe Mary Douglass [[separate block: margin]] in woodbury

Editorial note. Conclusion of 09-002–003. A horizontal dark line crosses the marriage news, apparently a crease rather than a cancellation. House name and Elizabeth’s surname are uncertain. The repeated “in woodbury” note is preserved. The address and signature directly connect Mary Douglass with her mother Rebecca Goodloe.

09-005 · Rebecca Goodloe to her granddaughter Susannah, April 21, 1852

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 5

09-005-P01 Wednesday 21 Dear Susannah I was nearly done writeing when your grateful letter came to hand I read it with pleasure and I do [[deleted: illegible]] assure you it was a grate consolation to me I thank you my dear grand daughter for your gratitude and I hope you will always Remember me as your grandmother it is a very good letter I did not think you could write so good—I am very sorry for your Father I would allmost persuade him to try the water practice it might cure him if he know how to apply it he must be the best judge of himself for the cramp colick hot [[inserted: watter]] dip a blanket in it and ring it out and wrap the person in as warm as posible put on warm blankets or a big feather bed put warm rocks or boiled corn to the feet and shoulders so as to sweat them quick I write this for the benefit of your mother as she use to be subject to the colick—dear susannah you must write again and tell me what you are all doing give my love to Rebeca & tell her to rite to me as soon as [[deleted: illegible]] this comes tell the boys to rite to me I send my love to all the Family I expect I will try to write again The rest of this Family must write for them selves this is all I can do now no more from your affectionate grandmother Rebecca Goodloe Susannah Douglass Hannah was mighty glad to hear from you all

Editorial note. The date reads Wednesday 21, following the April 18 letter. Descriptions of “water practice” and treatment for colic are historical remedies, transcribed as evidence, not recommended medical instructions.

09-006 · S. J. Goodloe reports his mother’s death, June 18, 1852

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 6

09-006-P01 Woodbury Cannon County Tenn June 18th 1852. Mr N L Douglas. Dear Sir, I understand that Lewis Jetton wrote to you concerning the Death of Mother, though he did not state to you the particular incidents connected with that solemn unexpected and lamentable event, My dear Mother is no more; She departed this life on the 6th of May last; After having lived to the age of nearly Three Score and Ten years, and passing through the trials and vissicitudes of life with that patience, exercise and Christian deportment that characterize and distinguish her to a hight that many do not reach, in the paths of rectitude Morality and religion, She at last goes down in peace and quietude to the silent Tomb of the grave ready and prepared to take her Flight to the Mansions of Heaven in the Eternal Kingdom of God on the Morning of the resurrection.

Editorial note. Letter continues on 09-007–009, signed S. J. Goodloe and addressed to N. L. Douglas. Wrapper 09-010 expands the writer to Sam J. Goodloe and explicitly identifies the deceased mother as Rebecca Goodloe. “Nearly three score and ten” means nearly seventy.

09-007 · The sudden collapse on May 6

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 7

09-007-P01 She arose from her bed on the Morning of the 6th of May last apparently well as usual and Seemed to administer her domestic affairs with ordinary diligence and ease, until late in the Evening while Sewing upon a pair of pantaloons, She fell Suddenly from her Chair, as if Having received a general Shock of paralysis, [[Jena?]] a negro girl being the only person in the Room ran to her assistance and aided her to the bed, Mother called Julia at the time She fell from her chair, though Julia did not go thinking nothing Serious the matter and being engaged at Something in another Room of the House, however Julia got to her about the time She reached the Bed, and on interrogating her Mother observed that She was very Sick and Seemed to be very Stupid, and from every Symptom She Seemed to have had a Stroke of the Apolexy, However She immediately appeared to feel better, [[deleted: illegible]] though manifesting by her expressions a loss of Memory at times. I being

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-006. The girl’s name is uncertain. The source uses a racial label; family reading uses “Black girl.” “Paralysis” and “Apolexy” are the writer’s impressions, not modern diagnoses. The phrase “Mother observed” is retained though its grammar is awkward.

09-008 · Her final half-hour and those present

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 8

09-008-P01 gone from Home all day came in, and Julia told [[inserted: me]] Mother was Sick, that being just before Sundown, I went to her Bed Side and asked her what was the Matter, She replied that She was Sick at the Stomach and also had a pain in her eyes and head, Though She told me She felt better; I then dropped out of the Room, and in Some ten Minutes after Julia called me and said that Mother was dying, I Hastened to her and Saw that death had fastened itself upon her and in about Thirty minutes She was gone forever, She died almost without a Struggle and would clasp my hand as if to bid me farewell, not having Spoken Since She told me that She was better as above mentioned, None of the family were present at her death but [[Jena?]] Hannah and Myself. Some of the nearest neighbors were present. Hannah grieves very much and She is in very delicate Health. Julia Hannah and Alfred will Stay on the farm

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-007. The sentence about who was present names “Jena” tentatively; it does not explicitly list Julia there, despite Julia’s preceding actions. Preserve the wording and inconsistency. No cause of death is independently established.

09-011 · Rebecca sends cloth and clothing to Polly, October 6, 1851

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 11

09-011-P01 October the 6th 1851 Dear Polly I hope this will find you all well with the Blessing of god I am as well as usual Hannah is still complaining she can walk about and smoke the pipe & that all she doe I have just heard from the [[deleted: illegible]] western District Mr Nance has the fever and Lucy and four of the children has the chills and fever Cynthia an all her family has bin sick Your Brother Sam is in Lebanon going to the Law school we have not heard from Mobile since last spring my sister Betsey woods is very sick & low with the Dropsy she was tapt last thursday & 4 gallons of water was taken from her which relieved her misery some I have no hopes of her ever recovering Mr Andrews family will give you all the news Well Polly I send you some cloth by Mr Andrews for you to dispose of as you think best I [[inserted: wish]] Mr Douglas and Warren to have Coats if they chose—there is 22 yards of jeans in trunk I allowed the green for George Cote and breaches I could not get them all dyed the weaver Martha ann [[goad?]] Adams was in a hurry to get the cloth out of the loome as John wanted to move to Arkansas you must have some walnut bark and a little coppres and dye his breaches black as the last end is not all of a coler there is 13 yards of dark brown and 5 pale brown I send some [[deleted: illegible]] summer cloth for Jessee and [[deleted: illegible]] Warren pantaloons and eight and a half yards of plad for the little girls winter dreses I send a pair of yarn socks for Mr Douglass and a pair of Cotton Stockins for yourself and a pair for Laura a pair for Mary little blue ones & some yarn to nit the

Editorial note. Continues on 09-012. “Jeans” means the cloth, not a pair of modern denim trousers. The weaver’s intervening name is unclear. “Dropsy” and drainage are the writer’s historical descriptions of illness. Dye ingredients are retained as historical household practice.

09-012 · Seeds, quills, baptisms, and a marriage rumor

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 12

09-012-P01 the rest of the children some Stockings I send 8 yards of Calico to Rebecca and if it is not enough to make her a dres she must give it to Susana I send Susana and Laura Cotton dreses there is three and a half yards blue Check [[inserted: calico]] for little mary if it will make her a dres if not take it for something else I send some pea feathers and goose quills I send some sage and some garden comfry seed I raised myself and a little starch I am sorry to pester Mr Andrew so much but he is very willing to do any thing in his power to oblige Mr Douglass he says Mr Douglass has bin a grate friend to him—Remember my love to Jessee and Henry and all the rest of the family and except the same yourself from your Mother Rebecca Goodloe
09-012-P02 We had 4 [[inserted: &]] 5 days meeting at Riplecreek Meetinghouse Brothers Trot and Corlee preached and [[Sanda?]] Jones and Baptised 14 John [[deleted: illegible]] Smith Eveart & Houghs two of Nathan Hales Daughters [[Polenna?]] Jones) Emily Goodloe and Altamira was Baptised before [[deleted: illegible]] it seems like I cant rite nomore now you must write to me as often as you can Rebecca and Susana to rite by the mail every opportunity O I like to forgot I heard Sarah Barr a going to get married To Mary Douglass
09-012-P03 the braid is to trim susanas green sack put two rows round

Editorial note. Conclusion of 09-011. Names in the baptism list are partly uncertain; original punctuation does not clearly separate all names. “Sack” refers to a garment in this context. Sarah Barr’s engagement is reported hearsay, not a marriage record. Meetinghouse spelling retained.

09-013 · The Pleasures of Memory: an unsigned essay

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 13

09-013-P01 The Pleasures of Memory.
09-013-P02 How often our minds revert [[inserted: pleasures]] to by gone days. Pleasures that were impressed upon our minds before we knew the cares of this world, never to be effaced by the corrosive hand of Time. It is true, our minds are often burdened with the cares and perplexities of life, and we feel there is nothing bright to look upon; when all at once some familiar sound, a silvery voice, breaks the stillness of our hearts, and calls us back to some cherished scene of the past. We think of the dear ones at home, whose loving hands were ever ministering to our wants, and whose guardian influence [[deleted: was]] ever directing our footsteps through the uneven scenes of life.

Editorial note. Continues through 09-015. Opening insertion “pleasures” has an awkward position; preserved rather than silently reconstructing the sentence. No signature or date appears on these three pages, and authorship is not established by the wrapper describing Emily’s separate song.

09-014 · Memories of home, prairie flowers, and streams

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 14

09-014-P01 We think of Home, that sacred spot where have been passed the happiest hours of life. It matters not how drear the spot How proud or poor the home Love still retains some deathless chains That bind the heart to home.
09-014-P02 We think of the surroundings of this home; the many happy hours spent in roaming over the broad prairies gathering the many colored flowers which was then the hith of our ambition. And again how much delight we would take in wandering along the mosscovered banks of the beautiful streams which were nearest us forgetful of Times rapid flight.

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-013. The four verse lines are set apart in the manuscript. “Hith” is retained as written, evidently meaning height in context.

09-015 · Sunday-school memories and the comfort of remembrance

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 15

09-015-P01 Let us think for a moment of the pleasures realized in after time, when we are old enough to attend Sunday school; how happy is each heart on entering the school room, as they crowd round their teacher in eagerness to learn sacred lessons from the holy Scriptures. With what implicit confidence they look into their teachers face, and how indellibly his instructions are impressed upon their minds, These scenes are permanently impressed upon my mind and I can imagine after our earthly race is almost run, we can truly say There are moments in life [[inserted: that]] we never forget, Which brighten and brighten, as time steals away; They give a new charm to the happiest lot, And shine on the gloom of the lonliest day.

Editorial note. Conclusion of the unsigned essay 09-013–014. Quoted or verse-form concluding lines retained as part of the manuscript; no external authorship attribution has been imposed.

09-018 · Miriam Stevenson reconnects with Polly from Columbus, October 24, 1855

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 18

09-018-P01 Columbus Oct. 24. 1855 Mrs Douglas My Dear old friend This evening I have determined to do what I have long wished to do, but not knowing your address (untill recently), I hope you will excuse me. I have just returned from Tennessee our old native place, There I learned your whereabouts. While there I saw Mrs Sam Davis who delivered a message sent by her husband I was more than happy to hear of your wellfare and future prospects, May you live long and be happy is the wish of my heart, and believe me my dear friend, there is none that feels more deeply interested for you and yours, than your humble servant. Well Polly (for so I am wont to speak) we both have had many troubles and trials to contend with since we parted, but it is all for our good if we love the Lord, I have long since learned that all things earthly are transitory and that this is not my abiding place, but look for a city whose maker and builder is God, My heart and Treasure is There, I have no cause to murmur, My health is fine, weigh 144. When I was in Tennessee I saw your sisters Mrs Jones and Mrs Nance, Doca was on a visit looks very thin, so does Julia, I did not see

Editorial note. Continues on 09-019–020, signed Miriam Stevenson. She calls Tennessee their old native place; this refers to writer and addressee, not independently to N. L. Douglas’s birthplace. Weight reproduced without supplying a unit not explicitly written. Doca/Dora name spellings vary across pages.

09-019 · Changes in Tennessee and Miriam’s life after her husband’s death

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 19

09-019-P01 Rebecca nor Betsey, as it was not convenient for me to visit them. I heard that they were well, saw a great many of our old neighbors, and some new ones that I never saw before. Mary Weather[[s?]] for instance, has seven daughters. just to think but no, I must stop, The very country appears strange I saw few persons or things that looked natural, Rebecca Alexander looks very well, Andy looks badly, Uncle Jacob and Aunt Polly are very much broken, though as anxious about the things of this world as ever, There are so many changes that I can not speak of them all, I received a letter from sister Louisa this morning stating that Virginia McKnight, (Johnson that was) is dead, went to her mothers on Sunday and was taken that night, died on Thursday, Sister Lou lives very comfortably, makes plenty of every thing to supply on I stoped a few minutes in Murfreesboro, saw Aunt Brown Amanda Mosby Dora Brown, and Dora Nance all together, could not stay long enough to learn any thing particular Now I must tell you something of myself I am still teaching and trying to make my self useful. I kept house two and a half years the happiest time of my life, After I lost my husband I kept house no more. He had 4 children, his relations took 3, I kept one, a sweet little girl now nearly ten years old her name is Virginia

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-018. Mary’s surname uncertain at the right edge. “He had 4 children” is retained: the passage does not identify Miriam as their birth mother. The reported death of Virginia McKnight is distinguished from the child Virginia described at the end.

09-020 · Teaching, raising Virginia, and maintaining old friendships

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 20

09-020-P01 The only care of my life is to raise and educate this child, She is pretty well advanced for her age. I am happy to tell you that my means are sufficient, without my labor to support us, but I prefer employment, I know it is conducive to health and happiness, I have been boarding at the hotel for several years, consequently have not much to do but go to school and Church. We have a very nice house of worship meet every Lords day and worship according to Bible. Mr Darnall Elizabeth an Eveline have all had the chills lately, They are living near by and doing very well. Thomas Sherrill is also living here and is one of the best Artists [[obscured]] I will send you a specimen of his work for a remembrance in my next, if this should be so fortunate as to reach you, I hope you will favor me with a long letter very soon. Remember me to all the family who have any recollection of me, Mr Douglass has not forgotten me no never, say to him I would be delighted to rec. a letter from him, Ann [[illegible]] Farewell my kind farewell Yours sincerely Miriam Stevenson

Editorial note. Conclusion of 09-018–019. A seal or stain obscures words after “Artists”; the art medium is not specified. A fragment before the farewell is unclear. The means of Miriam’s financial support is not identified in this letter.

09-021 · Miriam sends her portrait, March 29, 1856

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 21

09-021-P01 Columbus March 29th. 1856 Dearest Mrs Douglass After so long a delay It is with much pleasure that I acknowledge the receipt of your truly welcome letter. We have had a very cold and disagreeable winter, consequently great irregularity in our mails. but now the weather is pleasant I will venture to send my type, not because I thought it of much importance to any one, but I wish to live in your memory, and may be so you have forgotten my exact contour. If so, it will recall by gone days. yes this is me in my 48th year, weighing 145 and as youthful as when 19 (that is in my feelings and disposition My health is fine except a slight touch of that fashionable disease, Neuralgia which knots me up a little at times. I am still teaching but think now that this is my last session, I am getting tired of confinement, I should like very much to travel if I were not a coward, but I must confess that water and steam affect my nerves so as to produce very unpleasant feelings.

Editorial note. Continues on 09-022. “Type” refers to the likeness being sent; the specific photographic process is not stated. Age and weight are retained as written. This letter describes a portrait but does not prove that the image survives among the supplied scans.

09-022 · An enduring friendship and news from Sister Lou

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 22

09-022-P01 I am truly rejoiced to learn of [[inserted: your]] wellfare and also of your childrens, they are all dear to me, because they are yours. & I would be happy to see you all but cannot now promise my self the pleasure of ever doing so But time nor absence can ever efface from memory the pleasant recollections of youthful days. No they are as green spots in my recollection that time nor distance will ever obliterate. I received a letter from Sister Lou not long since, she says that your Cousin Tompson Wright was married to Miss [[Bowen?]] and that Virginia McKnight, (Williams wife) was dead. My friends here are all well, and desire to be remembered to your family. Say to Mr. D. I appreciate his good wishes, and kind regards and return them four fold. My love to my dear Cousins James and Cynthie I do remember [[inserted: them]] fondly, and desire to be remembered by them. Please let me hear from you soon. My best wishes attend all that relates to you and yours, now farewell my dear kind friend farewell. May the Lord bless and protect you through life comfort you in death, and receive you in Heaven is the prayer of your friend. Miriam Stevenson.

Editorial note. Conclusion of 09-021. Bride’s surname tentative. “Your Cousin Tompson Wright” is an explicit relationship statement, but degree of cousinship is not supplied. Virginia McKnight is identified as William’s wife here.

09-024 · Miriam describes the portrait’s dress and hairstyle, July 6, 1856

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 24

09-024-P01 Columbus July 6th 1856 My Dear kind friend Mrs Douglas Your favor of May the 26 came safe to hand and found a warm reception, I was amused at the idea of your thinking that there had been a mistake perhaps in the picture. I do assure you that it is my own dear self, I had a head dress on of mohair with 3 curls on each side, My dress is of rich brocade, blue and brown, but the colors did not Take, I rejoice to learn of your [[deleted: illegible]] health and prospects. I pray that your life may be long useful and happy and that I may be permitted to see your face again in the flesh, O how pleasant the thought, but we must [[inserted: not]] presume upon the future, the present only is ours. When I call to mind the many pleasant hours we have spent together it spreads a gloom over my feelings to know that [[inserted: they]] can never be recalled. But we must not permit the recollections of the past cast a shadow upon the future. My health is pretty good, I shall leave for the country soon and remain 2 months, the warm season is not pleasant here

Editorial note. Continues through 09-027. The writer explicitly identifies the picture as herself and describes mohair headwear, curls, and blue-and-brown brocade. “The colors did not Take” describes the result in the image; do not infer a particular photographic process.

09-025 · Country air and religious fellowship

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 25

09-025-P01 It is very pleasant to get out and breathe the pure country atmosphere O I long to be off. I have been closely confined for 10 months but now I am free once more. Well, having just returned from Church I will finish my letter. We had no preaching to day as our preacher is sick, but it is our practice to attend to the ordinances of the Lords house preacher or not, this we never neglect, and Oh that all could see and Appreciate their liberties as they ought, Then we should [[inserted: see]] Christians meeting together to sing, praise, and give thanks, rejoicing in the commandments of our Lord and Saviour. My dear friend this to me is the greatest pleasure of my life, I feel under many obligations to my Heavenly Father for his goodness to me particularly since I have been living in the South, circumstances have been peculiarly favourable to Christianity. You know that I was persecuted and shuned and sneered at on account of my faith and practice in my early career, but I always did and do now rejoice that I am counted worthy to be made partaker of his sufferings, who suffered so much for me.

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-024. Statements about past persecution and the South’s religious climate are Miriam’s personal testimony. No specific denomination or persecutor is named here.

09-026 · Miriam responds to Mary’s discouragement

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 26

09-026-P01 My dear friend you speak despondingly in your last. I fear that you attach too much importance to earthly matters, You say few and evil has been the days of my pilgrimage Now dear friend do not let such thoughts [[inserted: intrude]] themselves, Surely you have one of the kindest of husbands (at least I think so) and a circle of children that have never disgraced you, Think again my dear, and you will find ten thousand things to give thanks for instead of repining, I fear that you have never submitted wholly and solely to the government of High Heaven. If not you must not expect peace, There is no peace to the wicked, You must [[not?]] infer from this that I consider you a great sinner no, no, but I mean that you must be a member of his body, or else you are none of his, Look to it my friend and make your title good to mansions in the skies. I hope to hear from you soon again for indeed it is a source of great pleasure to me. I intend to send you a present if an opportunity offers. Do present my [[double breasted?]] affection to Mr Douglass, he shares largely in my respect and esteem, also to your children those of them who remember me

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-025. A possibly omitted or faint “not” before “infer” is marked rather than silently inserted; the following “no, no” supports the intended sense. Unusual phrase modifying “affection” remains tentative. The theological advice expresses the correspondent’s beliefs.

09-028 · W. Douglas to his sister Rebecca, June 3, 1856

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 28

09-028-P01 Wardville June 3d 1856 Dear Sister I have recd. and read with much pleasure your kind favor of the 20th Ult. I was surprised a little at first, but upon a thought I was surprised that I was surprised at all. For what is more to be expected than that we should often think of & write to each other. It is surprising that we never have before. As for me to forget you or to love you less, with the lapse of Time, & the change of circumstances the thing is simply impossible! for all my recollections of the past are inseperably connected with you. Back to the extreme limit to which my memory stretches; you were the constant and almost only playmate of my early childhood and still onward through boyhood and youth and up to full Maturity you were my companion how then can or could we cease to cherish a warm and steady affection for each other No, other ties may be formed—other friendships decay—but ours is part and parcel of our very lives, an affection [[inserted: that]] [[roots not low?]] in the clay. I am well, and that is about all that I have to write about myself for nothing occurs to me that would interest you

Editorial note. Continues on 09-029–030, where the writer signs W. Douglas and names the recipient Rebecca Winnifrid. Metaphorical phrase near the bottom remains tentative. The initial is not expanded to a forename.

09-029 · Why he wants to leave Texas for California

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 29

09-029-P01 these hard times. We had a greatdeal of wet weather this spring but it has been quite dry for some 3 weeks and rain is much needed. The prospect for corn is pretty good wheat is nowhere in this country I have recd. a letter from Henry by the same Mail that brought yours, he was well but times are dull with him too, & like me I think he is a little unsettled in his mind about his future course. You seem a little horrified at the idea of my going to California; you need not be I think—for men, & better than yours, are & are going there. Every man of intelligence that I have ever conversed with who has seen California speaks highly of it as a Country. Many advise me to go & some are going the second time, with their families I find it impossible to rise above a mere hand-to-mouth living in Texas, without the practice of the most stringent dealings & economy. Things that find place neither in my nature, nor my philosophy. Why then should I be so closely bound to Texas when I am already separated effectually, and hopelessly from you and all others, who love me. If there is a better place why not find it Why not enjoy the best of a little world like this, when even that best, is bad enough I do not think of any sudden acquirement

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-028. “Men, & better than yours” is retained as read. This passage states a proposed migration and its economic motivation; it does not establish that the journey occurred.

09-030 · Preparations for California and a proposed visit

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 30

09-030-P01 of wealth by the move, but I think I can do better there than here, at any rate I have had it in my head for a long time, and it is worth my while going there if even it is only to correct the mistake if it should turn out a mistake.—You may put it up as pretty Certain, that I will go to Cal. in the spring if life is Spared me; for to that end I have already begun to make my arrangements District Court begins here on monday and I have to attend as a witness in a land case, If nothing happens I will come down immediately after, but it is uncertain as I do not know what business may come up for me. Indeed I can think of nothing more, at present, Uncle Lewis &c were well last accounts. My Respects to Norvell & all enquiring friends. I Remain Truly Your Brother W. Douglas Rebecca Winnifrid
09-030-P02 Write often, your letters will always afford me new pleasure W. D.

Editorial note. Conclusion of 09-028–029. Signature read W. Douglas; recipient’s surname retained in its manuscript spelling. The prospective spring follows the letter’s June 1856 date. Uncle Lewis is named but no surname or exact genealogical identification is supplied.

09-031-P01 Corinth Miss July 9 [[1874?]] [[deleted: illegible]] Cousin George I have just Rec your letter of June 23d Bringing the sad news of the death of your Father we were Sorry indeed to hear it. tho acording to the natural corse of things we could expect nothing else for he lived to a good old age. we are all well and doing very well those of us that is living Sister Marthah died last August [[Ma?]] has had better health this year than She has had for several years— as far the [[illegible]] is concerned I never intended that any of you should Sufer any uneasiness about them I thought that I had written to that effect several times so you can give the amount to Aunt Polly and cousin Lizzie & if that do not settle it you can write to me again we have a good crop and I have been hoeing cotton to day so feel very little like writing so that will account for short letter and bad writing I would like you to write me a long letter and give me a history of the country the changes how the Rail Roads Runs and the price of Land &c Give my love to all. Yours &c E. M. Hyneman

09-043-P01 Quincy Tenn Dec the 16th 1860 My Dear niece I received your letter in due time but neglected to answer it I hope you will pardon me for my negligence we were very glad to hear from all the family through you. we were very sorry to hear of the death of Georges wife through Henry Orr. Mr Nance wrote to your Father soon after her death [[deleted: illegible]] she departed this life on the 29th day of August 1856 with Typhus Fever. [[deleted: illegible]] in the 17th year of her age [[deleted: She was a]] kind and affectionate child and devoted Christian. Wite and Robert Jetton have gone to Arkansas and bought land they came by here and spent a day and night with us they are very intelligent and fine looking young men. White favors his Mother and Robert his Father. we regret that Henry did not visit us when he was in Kentucky we would have been happy to have seen him and his Lady. give my love to all the family Tell them to write to me accept my love and sincere regards for your future happiness. write soon. T B Nance to Lizzy Douglas My Dear Sister Through the kindness of our heavenly Father we are blest with health food and raiment. for which we are very thankful to the great giver of all good. my health is some better than when I wrote last. I am much obliged

Sister Betsey is living with sister Nancy She writes that She is much pleased there I have written for her to come and stay with me. 09-047 · W. W. Nance on the war and a sick son, April 20, probably 1862

09-047-P01 [[obscured: county name]] Co, Tenn 20th Apl [[1862?]] Mr [[J.?]] D Orr Dear Sir Your very welcome letter of 28d March Came to hand yesterday,—found all in usual health. wife rather feeble, health generally good. We were very sorry to hear of James Sickness and hope he has before this time, So far recovered as to be able to come home,—We know Something of parents anxiety for a Sick Son away from home, and can truly Simpathize with you— I am much pleased with the Spirit of your letter, and have in It expressed my Sentiments in refference to this unholy war waged against people who have never wronged a Yankey in no matter whatever while they cannot Say the Same of us. So Im In for everlastingly Separating from Such people. we now only [[obscured]] them to return to their homes and let us alone, thats all, and If they fail to do so many of their vile bodies will find a Southern home & by & by—Altho we have met with several disasters on the waters yet I feel encouraged, all seem to be satisfied that when they leave the waters we will make them bite the dust— The roar of heavy ordinance is so common now as to attract but little attention, altho thers been none nearer than the Mis river. The enemy have possession of that river as far down as to Fort Pillow. that fortifycation is at Randolph opposite Covington the County cite of Tipton Co. I am told Its a strong place, but I dont know whether we will be able to hold It or not but I recon they will have a pretty lively time passing that point with their Gun boats I hear very heavy guns in that direction ever few [[obscured]] but cant learn any results [[obscured]] to get news as

09-048 · Reports from Shiloh and news of wounded relatives

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 48

09-048-P01 [[lost: left edge]] re not permitted [[obscured]] Camp. On 6th & 7th (Sunday and Monday one week ago) [[obscured]] before this reaches you. There was [[obscured]] splendid battle [[obscured]] Shiloh, (a church house), near Corinth Miss, [[lost: left edge]] our boys done Some [[obscured]] fighting on those days. William went through both days without receiving a Scratch, but, 2 of his Company fell, and Several wounded, one of our near neighbour boys was killed and another wounded, the wounded one came home, I met him on [[inserted: my]] way to Corinth, I was not allowed to proceed, and came back. The great wonder is that our whole Regiment was not nearly all killed, for they made 7 charges and took a battery every charge. Strange to tell they lost only 25 or 30 men out of their Regiment. We live about 80 ms from Corinth or Shilo, quite a number of our wounded have come into this region of country. among them one of my Sisters Sons (Shelton) who was Shot through the breast, he is not thought to be dangerously wounded. I had no knowledge of his being in the army untill day before yesterday evening, when I went to Gadsden Station on the M. & oh RR, at which place I understood that he was in that neighbourhood, I went to him Immediately, and Saw him. Charly, he enlisted at or near Nashville. The yankies have possession of Union City (at the crossing of the Mobile & oh & North Western RR, in Obion county) They have Pensacola—You may not be Surprised to hear a Stampede of yankies from Tenn. Price & Van dorn are at Memphis, encamped there with their commands. this has been reported for several days but I have not been Satisfied of the fact untill Since I commenced writing this letter— You write that Its probable that your boys may come to Tenn, and [[obscured]] may be they are at Memphis with Price. If So, and I learn the fact I will hunt them out, when permitted

09-058 · Mock battle, winter clothing, and better food

09-058-P01 Drill is over and I resume my pen. we had general review and inspection yesterday morning and Big Drill in the evening with our Regt and capt Pratt Battery the Boys would charge the Battery and they would fire blank cartridges At them it went like A fight sure enough. Col Burford Pitched About like A hog in high rye with [[Hayberg?]] after him—There was A great many Spectators and old Persons tried to show off to an advantage fortunately I was not in the Drill. Our Regiment drew A fine lot of clothing the other day Henry was lucky enough to get A fine overcoat which he was very much in need of. I drew A pair of Pants and A Shirt we have drawn A Plenty we are living better in the way of eatables at this camp than we ever have Since we have been in the Service. col Burford Says he thinks we will Stay here all winter. You must excuse this Short letter and bad writing as my pen is very bad Tell Mary to write me and give All the news and Maybe I will answer Nothing More At Present only I Remain Your Obedient Son R C Orr P S Gran Jetton and all of your friends are well [[R.C.O.?]]

I can [[illegible]] and [[illegible]] I defy [[illegible]] them anywhere. It has rained several times during the last week and musquitoes are increasing rapidly if we can [[illegible]] week we will have to have bars or else be hard times. Major Mann [[illegible]] says he has written four times to Houston for musquitoe bars whether he has or not I dont know. Somehow nobody likes to believe him whether he tells the truth or not.

09-061 · George contrasts strict camp rules with guard duty at Galveston

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 61

09-061-P01 The entire batt. is prejudiced against him from the manner in which he has treated them, in enforcing the regulations so strictly. He has issued an order for every man in the Batt to have an uniform the men did not like to take them but were forced to. He is out in another order for every man to wear a uniform cap. And there has to be a dress parade every evening. He wont allow the guard to sit down while on guard he has to walk his post continually and not let his gun out of his hands. Now this looks well enough on paper but it is mighty hard to practice. When the guard is relieved instead of marching direct to the guard house he has to go around with the relief untill all are relieved. We never done this way before while at Galveston (and we were looking to be attacked every day about the 1st of Jany) when relieved we always went directly to the guard house and went to sleep. While on post we set down lay down and walked as we pleased if we got tired of our gun we would set it down by the side of a house and wrap up in our blanket about two or three times the relief while the Corporal was relieving the first sentinel, would go on ahead and relieve the balance of the Guard before the Corp—could catch up. All this was known to the head officers at Galveston and they never grumbled nary time.

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-059–060. “batt.” expanded as battalion in family reading. The clause beginning “about two or three times the relief” concerns the relief party going ahead of its corporal; it is not a claim that George fell asleep while on post.

09-063-P01 Saturday Aug. 8th 1863. Letter 31 To All at Home. Writing time has come again but [[illegible]] nothing from home the fault is in the [[illegible]] gap between Beaumont and [[illegible]] every day almost they run off the track or some [[illegible]] they would let us go [[illegible]] any but to waste time. Capt [[Odlum?]] has been absent several days at Beaumont, and returned at night on the [[Dime?]] says he is a little lower in the mouth than any one I have heard express himself yet. This grand scheme of Rio Grand speculation is leaked out and been established fully by circumstantial evidence and there is no longer disguising the facts. Only twenty five bales of Gov. cotton has ever reached Brownsville and no body but Gov. friends have had the control of the transportation. The Mexican breakers were employed by the [[illegible]] of superior officers to take Gov cotton to the Rio and are there yet. It is plain who has made a pile and this is what has disheartened our Capt. It is enough to dishearten any man that has a honest feeling for the Gov. A man by the name of [[Chisham?]] belonging to our Batt has been wagoning to the Rio grande since we left Galveston he is now with us, says that when [[Magruder?]] was at Brownsville he sent three of his staff to Havanna, yet gave it as his opinion that [[Magruder?]] was acting himself as a private citizen. 09-064 · Guard duty and a proposed return to Galveston

09-064-P01 I do not know but what I would as soon go to Galveston as to stay here, yet we are not as apt to get as good quarters there again as we did have, but we can see more hear more and have a livelier time generally, if they dont put us to digging dirt and such like [[illegible]]. Some say that Cooks artillery are to take our place, but to make this place defensible it will require both artillery and pickets and plenty of them. That [[illegible]] how my [[train?]] of ideas is getting shorter than a sheet of paper here lately as I find it difficult to manufacture something without material. To day is my guard day somehow I get my share of the Sunday for guard in this little difficulty of ours. I am to go down the river to night to keep watch in that direction, we have watched in that direction for a long time never to have discovered any thing dangerous. We go after dark and come away before it is light enough to be seen by the enemy. There is seven prisoners in the guard house now for petty offences, it is quite an easy place so [[illegible]] it and some had rather be in than out there ought to be a lock up for these little petty officers who have not self respect enough to keep themselves out of such places, and put better innocent men by imprisoning them. Rogers who done the stealing at Dallas and was guarded by us to Houston and there left in charge of the Provost Marshal and there tried and sentenced to work on the fortifications three months was returned the other day to his company for duty, and in about three days was put in the guard house for getting drunk [[illegible]] on guard.

There was a case of insubordination here the other day, Capt [[Odlums?]] Co. or rather the principal part of them refused to drill one morning, giving as a reason for so doing that they had not any soap to wash with and had not had for a long time and that they were out of money and wanted the pay that was due them five months pay is now due. The spirit of insubordination is abroad and despondency with it, about one half of this Batt. is whipped and ready to give it up as a bad job. 09-068 · Letter 32: summer heat, food, and canceled transfer orders

09-068-P01 The weather is getting hot down here sure enough, I dont think I ever saw it so hot in Ellis as it is here, there is scarce ever any breeze stirring, hot cloudy and calm. An abundance of watermelons have been brought here from Sabine Bayou in two little lighters and [[schooners?]] which they sell at tolerably fair prices, they are very good as are our water pumpkins can be had tolerably cheap and are pretty good with bread and beef a change, anyhow. The Zehorlda brought a couple of Co's to relieve us last night. But the order for us to go to Galveston had been previously countermanded so we will stay here for an indefinite length of time yet. I prefer this place to Gal. until the yellow fever season is over, for here we have a chance to skedaddle while at Gal. we would not have. If there is any yellow fever at Houston I have never heard of it I guess it is all a mistake, such reports are apt to get out at this time of year anywhere. I have heard that a great many men are going home from La on short furloughs, but most generally “they have left their certificates of disability behind.” We are all in good health at present, [[Jeems?]] has been complaining for a few days but there is not much the matter with him. I suppose that there is no healthy man here for we are all well so far as I know. Tell [[Essie?]] that I will write to her yet awhile, but I never was born a poet and shall never be as well. I believe I have told all the news My love to all Your Brother George

09-070 · Letter 21: soldiers take the staff’s confiscated liquor, May 14, 1863

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 70

09-070-P01 Sabine Pass May 14th 63 Number 21, Sister Lizzie I received your dates of 29th and 30th ult yesterday, they were mailed May 2 and only eleven days on the road, I dont see why my letters dont reach you, for I have not failed to write weekly. Since writing before we have had a jolly night, or rather the boys had, for I did not “pitch in.” It seems that the “Staff” are quite fond of rum and they leave no stone unturned to get it, First they took a demijohn from a boat man, next they found a barrel of whisky out in the country, and they took that. Next they took a half barrel of rum from a frenchman. This they reported on their returns as destroyed to keep the soldiers from getting drunk, but they were destroying it by a slow process. At last the boys got tired at the way the “Staff” was doing and determined to finish the whiskey. So one night after tattoo had been beat the cavalry marched up to headquarters and rolled out the whiskey, and called for all hands to come up and drink for it was a free thing. The barrels were carried out in the prairie and every [[inserted: one]] pitched in with cups canteens coffee pots and buckets and near every body got drunk. The staff done all they could to save the whiskey but to no purpose, they could not get a guard in time. C company was only a little behind others that is the cavalry and boat hands. They C were organizing a squad to take the whisky when the others came along. Directly after the [[deleted: boys]] fuss commenced the long roll was beat and Lanier said every man [[lost: left edge]] did not answer to his name had to go in the

09-071 · Letter 21: the aftermath and daily rations

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 71

09-071-P01 guard house. Some of the boys came up and told the Capt about it, and asked him if they must fall into line. he told to fall in or not just as they pleased and that none of his men should go in the guardhouse. So I lay still and did not get up. The whiskey was all drank and two empty barrels only showed where it had been. Since then the Staff has been quite dry, no doubt, but maybe it will learn them not to take whisky that dont belong to them. It was the privates that broke up the Showman business here, they broke up the whisky business. Wherever they hear of a bad thing, pitch in [[illegible]] They have been cutting up so I expect we will be trotted to La and put us to active service. The federals have been quiet for a good while here, their last freak was to halt our pickets below here who wouldnt halt but kept going when they fired at them but without effect. The lighthouse guard has been discontinued so we have but little to do but cook and eat, the latter we do to perfection. We get a pound and a half of [[deleted: meat]] beef and full rations of meal a day, Every ten days we get about three pounds of sugar a pint of peas a little over half pint of vinegar and [[deleted: to that]] about a pint of molasses sometimes more generally less. We dont get more than a fourth part as much soap as we need and that very indifferent. I was mistaken about the molasses only a pint to three men for ten days but generally more. Excepting the staples beef and bread you might say we get nothing at all. we have been issued peas twice since we left Galveston and vinegar only occasionally.

09-074 · Letter 28: the lighthouse expedition, July 22, 1863

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 74

09-074-P01 Wednesday Evening, July 22 Letter, Number, 28th, 1863 Sister Lizzie, I have delayed writing longer this time than usual on account of a three days residence at the lighthouse. Col Griffin set a trap to catch some Yankees at the lighthouse. Some body imagined that they saw one or two Yankees there, so last Wednesday night a detachment of 60 or 70 men under Bickley [[invested?]] and took possession of the place without opposition. Warren with a squad of 20 men were left to take in such yankees as might come along. Saturday night they were relieved by Lieut Deen and 20 men, of the latter I was one. We went down as near the L H as we could get in a boat. We got the boat in about thirty feet of the shore, the interval was knee deep mud. One man took a sack of provisions and started ashore he got about half way and stuck fast, Warren and his squad soon arrived with some plank which was laid down to walk on and the rest of us got safe ashore without sticking. Then commenced the battle in real earnest—but not with the mosquitoes instead of Yankees

Editorial note. Reading order of this letter is 09-074, 09-076 (marked Page 2nd), 09-075 (marked page 3rd), 09-077. A possibly superfluous “not” before “with the mosquitoes” is retained as written; sense is clear from the continuation. 09-075 · Letter 28, page 3: conflicting war news

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 75

09-075-P01 page 3rd Col Griffin returned yesterday having only gone as far as Beaumont. Some Lieut Col came with him I expect he is the inspecting officer of this district. There is no news of importance in this country, the militia are to be drafted next Saturday. Rumors from the east are still contradictory. Some say that Vicksbg has been taken others say not, though it is pretty generally believed that it has fallen and Port Hudson also. Rosecrans has flanked Bragg back to the Tennessee river, compelled him to abandon his stronghold at Tulahoma. One report says that Grant and Johnson have had a fight the latter taking 8000 prisoners why did he not do that before Vicks surrendered [[inserted: illegible]] Lee is about to take Pennsylvania, and whip out Hooker in toto, it must all be true I reckon for he never was whipt. It is to be expected that he will clean up the northeast as Grant does the southwest. I wish they would quit their playing and go home, and let every body do the same. Our prospects of getting away from here are decidedly dull, though we may be called to northern Texas this fall to meet the yankees in that quarter. If Vicksburg has fallen I look for active operations in La this fall, unless they take a notion to work on the other side of the water first.

Editorial note. Read after 09-076, before 09-077. Reports about Vicksburg, Port Hudson, Grant, “Johnson,” Lee, and Hooker are not reconciled or silently corrected to later historical knowledge. The 8,000-prisoner claim is explicitly a report; the remarks about Lee read as skeptical irony. “in toto” means altogether.

09-076 · Letter 28, page 2: officers under arrest and deaths in the company

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 76

09-076-P01 Page 2nd We fought them manfully until day light when we brought a battery of smoke to bear on them and succeeded to drive them pretty effectually from one room. After waiting & watching for neds last night we came back having caught nothing. No one is there now. Having arrived in camps, I found our Capt under arrest for refusing to salute Maj Hammer on dress parade, and for giving him a cursing to boot. Maj Hammer is under arrest for drawing a six shooter on Capt Payne. Col Griffin has gone to Houston and Hammer with him. I understand that Hammer is very anxious to resign and go home, he will have opportunities enough after this little affair is cleared up. Capt Odlum now commands this post and Capt [[Mc R?]] the Batt. Thursday, 23rd The boat came in late yesterday evening but brought no letter to me, I have not received later dates from home than Lauras of the 24th and 25th of June, what is the reason of this I cannot have any idea for letters have come from Tarrant Co as late as July 6th. Two more deaths have occurred in our Comp, Mark Evans died monday evening and Wm. K. [[Joyn?]] last friday, both were at Beaumont. William [[Joyn?]] had the measles. The sick at this place are doing well,

Editorial note. Read after 09-074, before 09-075. “neds” retained without an uncertain expansion. The captain’s reported arrest, Hammer’s alleged action, and his intentions are George’s account. 09-077 · Letter 28: inspection, fort construction, and fading hopes of peace

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 77

09-077-P01 Well as the steamer leaves this evening I will close. Lieut Col Mc Neil inspected us this morning in grand style, he first reviewed us and then had us to pass in review before him, he then inspected our arms in regular military style, next we had to manœuvre in Batt drill till he got tired of that, and then company drill awhile, then the manual of arms and then we quit, after having been on the parade ground from half past eight until eleven. So much for so much we were glad to get rid of his presence I assure you, Men like to show their authority “mighty well” in this latitude. Capt Evans has been released from arrest and I think from all that I can learn Major Hammer has been also. Col Griffin assured him so that his resignation would be accepted he has a certificate of disability from the Drs, and this will insure its acceptance. We are glad to get rid of him on any terms, and hope next time we will get a better one. The Fort is progressing slowly. More darkies have been sent for to work on it when it will be finished it is impossible to say. It is estimated that it will cost the Government $100,000. I wish you would write to me who all were drafted in our county for I have a curiosity to know how many will be or are left. All hope of a speedy end of the war is abandoned in this part of the country, pretty much everybody believes that Vicksburg has fallen, and the pet notion of foreign intervention has died. The weather still continues rainy though the last few days have been tolerably pleasant. My paper is about full, so for the present Goodbye, George

Editorial note. Conclusion of the letter beginning 09-074; reading order 074, 076, 075, 077. Source uses a racial term for the Black people sought for fort construction. Their legal status and whether/how they were compelled are not specified in this passage. Cost is a reported estimate, not an audited expenditure. The name Evans here supplies the captain’s name absent from the arrest statement on 09-076.

09-079-P01 indulged in of the kind. Some thirty five different scenes were represented, and it was quite late before they got through. I think they must have intruded on Sunday a little. 09-080 · Letter 23: food and soap at Sabine Pass, May 28, 1863

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 80

09-080-P01 Number 23 Sabine Pass May 28th 63 As I said I got yours of 7 the other day and now I will answer the more in full. I was sorry to hear that Samm was sick, for sickness is such a disagreeable thing anyhow. I have been quite puny for some time but am about well again. Sabine beef and bread is dog living compared to what I have seen it is true we get a few other articles but no vegetables except what we buy and it has been so dry here this spring that the people made but little more than they have use for, as they live by gardening mostly anyhow they have no farms and all they have to eat is vegetables and beef, besides what they buy. Most of them have large stocks of cattle, but some how this year they failed to make much milk & butter for sale. Some wont sell anything to us but give, all such as these men will go to for anything, others that do sell are soon bought out entirely, and so they have nothing to sell. It is almost impossible to get washing done at present, the Government dont furnish soap enough to wash socks, and the citizens are out generally. The country for 3 or 4 miles around has been ransacked, to get washing done but the universal cry is “no soap!” I am very thankful for the socks you sent me, but would much rather had woolen ones. The pills also came to hand by warren and the fine comb, the latter I am happy say I have not needed since I left home and hope I shall not [[lost: bottom line partly cut off in the source image]]

They had been gone one day when the order was again countermanded whether they will go on home without getting [[deleted: getting]] [[inserted: Sammy]] angered or not I do not know.
