Let me know when the Telegraph will stop and I will try to [[inserted: send]] the news to you for a while as the Tel has doubled its rates your subscription must be nearly out. A very pleasant shower has fallen this evening the first for about a month, the worst of it was it didnt rain half enough as water is getting scarce in the cisterns. Sunday May 31st No boat has yet arrived though the Sunflower is confidently looked for to day. The cause of her long delay lies in the fact that she has been carrying troops to Nibletts bluff for several days past. how many are being sent across I have no idea There must be some danger in that direction of late.

09-083-P01 Galveston Jan [[22th?]] [[1862?]] Dear Sister Time passes off in quite a monotonous manner. Galveston is a much prettier place than Houston. there is less mud and the streets can be better drained. The shell for paving purposes are more convenient than at Houston and I think it is a much healthier place. The monotony was somewhat relieved yesterday by the Federals shelling the town and ft point which is about two miles east from here They commenced about three oclock I reckon and fired 107 shots which did no further damage than the wounding of four men at Ft Point one of whom has since died. A good many of the citizens had returned to their homes these fled to the west of town with their families; some negroes who were at work at the east end of town went through to the west at quick time, some mischevous soldiers threw a barrel head among them and hollered “Theres a bomb” the affrighted blacks fell flat of their faces on the hard pavement. During most of the engagement I was on top of our quarters in a lookout and [[inserted: could]] see every shot that was fired or rather the smoke from the guns and I could hear the report also. The most of the firing was done from the Sciota a gunboat whether ironclad or not I do not know it came up in about a mile of what is called the south battery and fired at the town and surrounding country in order I suppose to find out if there was any batteries about, the Brooklyn fired at ft point all the

09-084 · Galveston letter: shells, a flag of truce, and captured ships

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 84

09-084-P01 time and almost every shell after the first few rounds struck its mark. The Brooklyn shot about four miles and [[deleted: and]] would drop a shell among the tents or in the batteries every time. They shot sufficiently close to cut the [[flagstaff at R R pier?]]. While I was in the lookout a shell from the Sciota came singing its peculiar song directly towards me so Direct it seemed to come that I involuntarily dodged. This was the only one that came near me. This morning I saw three shells that were fired at us that did not burst, two of them were round and would weigh about 130 pounds the other was an oblong shell fired from a rifle gun it was steel pointed and about five inches thick by fifteen long. There are now five vessels in sight but I do not think they will attack us until reinforcements come up; a flag of truce went out day before yesterday on official business not made public, which learned [[deleted: that]] from the Federals that they intend attacking this place shortly, how much truth and how much bombast there is in this I cannot tell. They say they can whip us here and that they intend doing it but what Mr Yankee intends to do is very uncertain. All the rigging has been taken off the two barques captured here and is stored away. They cannot get them out for the blockade and the water is too shallow to move them up to Houston and consequently they have to stay here. They have repaired the Harriet Lane and I understand she is now ready for sea but she cant get out either, steamboats run from here to Houston but little travel is going on.

09-091 · Practical surveying: triangles, traverse tables, and closing a boundary

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 91

09-091-P01 dividers & sometimes the protractor also which I think I left at home. A Traverse table is indispensable in making surveys that are irregular in their Shape. I never to be sure did nor understand how to Calculate Latitude & departure which are the base & perpendicular of a triangle of which the distance is the hypothenuse and degree for angle of departure known. In practice the degree being known either line of the triangle may be measured & the table gives the other two. All irregularities in surveys can & must be reduced to triangles in calculating area The base & perpendicular multiplied together & product divided by 2 gives the area. In practice where you hold a survey upon another you consider the lines of the first as the base & in diverging from their direction you consider the divergence the departure & the last lines your latitude irrespectively of the cardinal points. Field notes must balance the traverse table is the simplest & easiest means of [[rectifying?]] or determining the length of unknown lines in irregular surveys. In practice the measurements seldom close either less than a chain or two where the ground is [[uneven?]]. You consequently [[choose?]] the most favorable side of a survey & leave it so long to be run measured. For the same reason in so work establish your beginning corner until you run all round & then establish it where

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-090, ending mid-sentence before 09-092. Some phrasing is irregular as written, including “I never to be sure did nor understand” and “in so work establish.” The family reading explains the evident caution about fixing a starting corner but does not present this historical letter as a modern surveying manual. “Latitude” and “departure” are technical surveying terms, not ordinary geographic latitude and a journey’s departure.

09-092 · Surveying advice: boundaries, field notes, and compass variation

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 92

09-092-P01 ever the closing line intersects the beginning line. A few varas more or less is a trifling & common error with most chainmen but for a line to vary from the true course is disproportionate. [[inserted: Yet errors must balance; figures and final words illegible]] Surveys not to one should as nearly as possible be square—fractions of less than 80 acres not to be left between surveys. [[Avoiding?]] [[illegible]] boundaries unless it be entirely Surrounded vacant. When it is necessary to have a [[line?]] of a new Survey upon an old one it is desirable to point the corners or line trees in a new direction. You must then in your field notes adhere to the direction first taken. For instance if you begin on a line running N.60°E. you may trace that N but you must turn E S & W & North to the boundary line & then close down by that; & in this line in order to come as near to a square as possible [[deleted: your]] the mean between your N. & S lines should equal your E. or W. lines. In practice it is best always to adapt the variation of the needle first to correspond to the old lines. 10° is the most common but they vary from 9° to 12° & sometimes even more. It is the custom lately to state at the bottom of field notes the var. used.

Editorial note. Conclusion of the surviving September 22 letter (09-089–092); no signature. Several short instructions in the middle remain uncertain and are not made more definite by paraphrase. 09-099 · May 31: a flag of truce and a Northern newspaper

09-099-P01 May 31st The boat is just in sight some ten or fifteen miles off so I will try to finish by the time it [[deleted: got]] gets here. Tis rather a welcome sight to see one again, as they are the connecting link between here and white folks. The other [[inserted: day]] a flag of truce went out to the blockade, to learn the fate of one Taylor, who from bad treatment by the Secesh went to the yankees and was wounded in the light house fight. The boat was sent out at the request of his wife who lives about twenty five miles above here. If his fate was ascertained it has not been made public. The boat brought back several late northern papers, one of which I read yesterday the New York Times. The spirit of the paper is firm for the Union as it was, and the constitution as it is. It offered no peace to the rebels but calls on all patriotic men everywhere to stand [[lost: left edge]] in the say combating until the rebellion [[deleted: was]] put [[lost: left edge]] down. If it cant be done in two more years perhaps it says the next administration will [[lost: left edge]] prosecute it with renewed vigor. Of the late battle between Hooker and Lee [[lost: left edge]] supposes that their total loss will not exceed [[lost: left edge and casualty figure]] while that of the rebels is from 20 [[lost: left edge]] 25,000. They claim to have taken 2500 prisoners [[lost: left edge]] 17 pieces of artillery. Their communication [[lost: left edge]] cut off [[deleted: for]] with the rear for twelve [[lost: left edge]] by a sudden rise in the Rappahannack [[lost: left edge]] destroyed the Rail Road, in their retreat [[lost: left edge]] were not molested by our Troops. [[lost: left edge]] It contained Commodore Porters official dispatches of the capture of Grand Gulf which was effected [[lost: damage]] May [[lost: continuation]]

09-100-P01 Porter says he has the door to vicksburg. He said in his dispatches that if the fortifications had been complete he never could have taken the place as it is a stronger natural defense than vicksburg. The paper says that a great many of the prisoners nearly one half will take the oath of allegiance. It also contained an account of Gen Stonemans raid in Virginia with his cavalry. They claim to have passed in the rear of Lees army destroying his railroad communication with Richmond also destroying all the bridges [[deleted: of]] over the Chickahominy, and went within two miles of Richmond and captured one aid on Gen Winders staff. It also gives a secure & northern account [[lost: left edge]] troops are in high spirits and sanguine of final success. The boat brought me Lauras letter of 15–16th Laura complains of my reserve in writing about myself. I dont think I am reserved at all, I write every thing about myself, or every thing I do. The temptations of camp life I had supposed you were familiar with, so there is my particular writing. Nothing to do is the greatest drawback aside from the regular form of military life so there is no [[lost: left edge]] for grumbling and discontent there. If anything dont go to my notion it is none of my fault. I have not the management of things there is no use of getting mad about it. If I dont [[deleted: of]] like it I think very contemptibly to myself and dont trouble any body with it. I have not the control of things nothing turns [[lost: left edge]] to vex and disquiet me, no responsibility rests on me beyond the regular routine of soldiering and it is but little difficulty to act a part I have got used to it. Affectionately George [[separate block: preprinted stationery, three repeated unused forms]] T. H. McMAHAN & GILBERT. GALVESTON, __________ 18__ __________ T. H. McMAHAN & GILBERT.

09-101 · George in Houston: uncertainty about orders, March 19, 1865

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 101

09-101-P01 Houston March 19th/65 Sister Lizzie Again I will write you from this place with but little idea how long we will be permitted to remain. Nothing have we heard yet in a reliable shape connected with our future movements though tis the general opinion that we will go east of the Miss sometime this Spring. But very few have any inclination to travel in that direction I assure you, though if ordered twill be very few who will refuse to go. I have heard no late news of any importance lately. A few days ago a rumor was afloat that a battle had occurred between Sherman & Beauregard in which the former was routed and the latter killed. The papers however say nothing about it. Last authentic accounts from there said Sherman and Hardee were racing for Charlotte and Sherman was about to get there first. Evidently there will be active times there this spring and if some Yankees dont come this way Somebody from this Dept will have to go East of the Mississippi sure. One of two things is evident. Either an attack is feared at Galveston or the troops on the Coast are to be relieved and sent to the field. All the old troops from La & Ark are coming this way

Editorial note. Continues on 09-102. March 19, 1865 is written in the heading. Reports of troop movements and the supposed death of Beauregard are the writer’s contemporary information; he explicitly says the newspapers do not confirm the rumor. “Miss” expands to Mississippi in the family reading.

09-102 · Troop movements, coffee, and a sermon without politics

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 102

09-102-P01 I got a letter from Henry Orr dated 13th inst in which he [[deleted: said]] said he expected they would move to the Brazos Country in a few days as the forage was exhausted about Waverly, and said for me to answer him at Hempstead. De Brays Regt is at Hempstead now. Tom wrote from Tyler under date 10th and says his old Regt is on the march for Hempstead. Walkers old Division is ordered I understand also [[deleted: the]] Greens old Brigade. This I think is indicative of apprehensions of an attack on the coast or Starvation in La & Ark. We still have good health and live pretty well all things considered. We joined funds the other day and bought a Sack of flour & thirty pounds of Coffee. So we have Coffee & Biscuit at our house. This makes about 45 pound Coffee which we have bought since we came here. Confed money has fallen to 27 again and not very current. Specie is also Scarcer than it was, goods generally a lower owing to the Scarcity of money. Blockade Running Still continues at Galveston by which means goods plentiful in the Market. Cotton Cards brought 1.60 per pair by the dozen pair at auction. Today I went to hear the old presbyterian, had an excellent Discourse in which no allusion was made to the present War any way, the Confed, Jeff, [[deleted: Abe]] Abe or any other political Dignitary. As ever your brother Geo.

Editorial note. Conclusion of 09-101. “27” is recorded without a stated conversion basis; it should not be presented as a verified exchange rate to a specific currency. “Cotton Cards” are tools for preparing cotton fiber, not playing cards. Initial deletion before the repeated Abe is retained.

09-108 · George mourns his sister, March 10, 1865

09-108-P01 To all at Home. Houston Texas March 10th/65 It was with the deepest Sorrow that I heard of the death of my Sister through Capt Evans who came down a few days ago. Little did I expect to hear of so sad an event, it came unexpectedly but ah! too true, and we can but weep over the departed with unavailing Sorrow, for they cannot be recalled, but the evidences of the Higher Hope of immortality which they have left, gives comfort to the sorrowing hearts that are left behind. To me it is a greater Source of happiness to know that She died in [[full?]] hope of Heaven and everlasting bliss, than to have been crowned [[the?]] richest Queen of the Earth. and while we mourn her loss [[illegible: fold obscures part of line]] her gain. It looks hard for her to be called [[away?]] from her young family, but the ways of Providence are [[always?]] the best and tis but meet that we yield without a murmur to its decrees. Sad indeed it is to the children to be thus early deprived of their protector, deprived of her care and love [[such?]] as only a mother can bestow and thrown almost upon the World for awhile. Sympathy for them increases our sorrow for [[our?]] loss, but we must do all that lies in our power in their [[behalf?]], Seperated by fate or fortune from their only parent. More than ever I feel that I am needed at home but less [[and?]] less the Chances appear to me for returning any time shortly, the future grows darker and darker as we advance and [[not one?]] ray of light appears ahead.

Editorial note. Continues on 09-109, signed Geo. Douglas. The deceased sister is not named on these two pages. Dark folds and a clipped left edge obscure several words; bracketed reconstructions are not certain readings. The phrase about the children’s “only parent” is preserved without inferring the other parent’s fate.

09-109 · “Any way almost would suit me now”: George longs for the war to end

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 109

09-109-P01 Rumors are plentiful about being ordered across the Miss river and to La and I am pretty confident that that we will start Somewhere east by the first of next month. We may be sent east of the river and if so the Chances for a single individual to remain on this side are very Slim, for under Such circumstances no transfers would be given. The men are almost unanimously opposed to such a move but you all know what orders are. It is reported that Lee has ordered 30,000 troops east of the Miss and if this be true I look for the worst. However I will not trouble myself about it any more than I can help, only wish my term of service was out. No news reaches us except what comes through the blockade. Sherman is occupying the coast cities almost [[without?]] opposition and [[Lee?]] is concentrating. Indicating I think a field Campaign this year almost altogether; Perhaps twill hasten the war to a close, by subjugation if no other way, any way almost would suit me now. To day has been fast day and all has been quiet. I do not attend their war meetings and preachings. The Country is ready to receive anything in the Shape of Govt now, will submit to anything, their Spirit is broken. It is late and cold so I will close. With best love to all I remain as ever affectionately Geo. Douglas.

Editorial note. Conclusion of 09-108, dated March 10, 1865. “Lee” and “without” are obscured by a dark fold. The asserted troop order is explicitly a report, and the statements about the country’s spirit are the writer’s opinions. “Fast day” refers to a day of fasting, not speed.

09-111 · George to Laura: dry weather and the stranded Clifton, March 11, 1864

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 111

09-111-P01 Sabine Pass, March 11th/64 — No 60 Sister Laura This weeks mail brought me your letter of the 21st ult, and found us all on the Square. I see you have had some cold weather as [[inserted: well]] as us, from what I have been able to learn the past winter has been tolerably severe in every place. The weather still continues very dry and unless we have rain soon all the cistern water will be gone, and the well water is quite indifferent. In and around the precinct of Sabine Pass everything moves on in the usual way, but little arises to excite attention, and the general pleasantness of the weather tends to increase that disease commonly known as laziness, and which always prevails in a garrison to a considerable extent. There is two of our Co sick at this time, one at Beaumont and one here; both pneumonia one caused by the measles the other an ordinary attack, neither from what I can learn very dangerous. The Clifton has not yet departed, made an unsuccessful attempt to go about two weeks ago, grounded on an oyster reef at high tide and lay out of plum a day and night which sprung a leak somewhere in the bottom though not bad enough to keep her in port, she will try again the first favorable time.

Editorial note. Letter No. 60. Continues on 09-112–114. “Ult” means the preceding month. “Out of plum” is retained as written; the family reading interprets it as lying out of upright alignment. Medical descriptions are the writer’s report, not a modern diagnosis.

09-112 · George questions newspaper victories and growing rumors

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 112

09-112-P01 Our foreign news is quite meagre, merely what we get from the papers and of course we get the best side of the tale if it is not always to be relied on. Lying has got to be so fashionable that almost every source of intelligence is filled with it, somebody, or some people rather are getting so well up to, and used to it, that they can lie without knowing it, it seems. Twice has Sherman been badly whipt in Miss! The first time he ran pretty fast no doubt, but unfortunately for the South the Rebs walked in the lead. If his last Skedaddling was like the first, where now is Polk? The farther a tale travels the bigger it gets, this rule works everywhere and now Since the fall of Vicksburg tales have to come a roundabout way, consequently they assume large proportions. No reliance can now be placed in the details of affairs east of the Miss, only the general items can be credited and the general features of the case are rather dark. Some Strange ideas have worked themselves into the upper country, I see by the tone of your letters. Yanks and Rebs are on better terms Westward than here if they allow Schooners to run in and out at will, only fire a few blanks at them, here they always Shoot to hurt. When no better amusement presents itself the Yankees Shell our Pickets on the beach.

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-111. “Foreign news” here is the writer’s label for news beyond his immediate area, including east of the Mississippi. His claim that Sherman was twice defeated is ironic: the following sentences question the reports. The family reading keeps that irony explicit.

09-113 · War weariness and teasing Laura about marriage

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 113

09-113-P01 Several came ashore the other evening about dark but the cavalry failed to take them in, couldnt find them in the night. Evidently the people of your section are badly whipt, even worse than the Soldiers, or express themselves more freely. Maybe we are bold and maybe not, who knows. Fewer remarks are made about military affairs now than formerly, all somehow seem to be careless about it any way. To brag about Confederates and run down Yankees is an old song worn out long ago, and tis scarcely ever hummed nowadays. No one pretends to say how the Women and children will live after the supply now on hand is gone nor do they seem to take any lively interest about it. However the present stillness may not last beyond a few weeks, and then, all may be storm and commotion again. And still they marry! I was Surprised to hear of Mary [[Pattons?]] union for I Supposed She was too young to leave her mamma. Em Chapman I only know by character and hardly by that. She is cousin to Lizzie I believe, wonder if Lizzie will do likewise. White folks are very uncertain, so are the Women. Dont marry yourself off to Some gentleman of the “Bush” merely because you get a chance, better call back “[[Bowle?]]” first, though he is aged, and rather “red” headed,

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-111–112. Mary’s surname and the quoted nickname at the end remain uncertain. The statement that Em Chapman is Lizzie’s cousin is qualified by “I believe” in the source. “Gentleman of the Bush” is left as the writer’s phrase, without identifying a particular man.

09-114 · Jayhawkers, writing paper, and beef buried with military honors

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 114

09-114-P01 A raid of Jayhawkers towards Nibletts from some of the La Swamps has excited some little attention. I understand Greens Brigade has been ordered to that region for their benefit. There is quite a a nest of them beyond Calcasieu lake from here and have been doing some mischief in that region. It is reported that they are sustained by Banks, but every species of rascality now days is attributed to Yankee credit. I have a sufficiency of paper to last Six months so you need not trouble yourselves on my account. I am very much obliged to Sister for her present, but will not need it for some time to come. In the varying scenes of war I hope I may have a chance to be at home and get [[inserted: it]] by the time I have use for it. Tell her I will try to write to her during this month. I received Marys letter the other day, and will have to send her word that She is Still very modest; She had better outgrow that. One of our co has been released from the guard house; Gilbert the man that left [[Millican?]] sick and went home last fall. We still get plenty to eat such as it is, but the quality is rather poor. Some of the troops on Galveston Island have not had beef for a week. The last the got was so poor they buried it with the honors of War, and have refused to take any more because it was no better. Affectionately, George

Editorial note. Conclusion of the March 11, 1864 letter, 09-111–114. Banks’s supposed support of Jayhawkers is explicitly reported hearsay; George questions the tendency to blame every offense on Yankees. The place/name after “left” is uncertain. The present from “Sister” is not identified beyond the surrounding discussion of paper.

09-115 · George travels down the Brazos, April 11, 1865

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 115

09-115-P01 Sister Laura Houston April 11th 1865 I promised last week to write a larger letter this week so I suppose I will have to comply with Said promise. Wednesday morning I Started for Velasco, twas dry though cloudy, arrived at Columbia on the Brazos River at four oclock in the evening. Columbia is a Small place noted only for being the terminus of the [[H.T. & B.R.R.?]] The Country traversed by this road is low and flat, mostly prairie and very fertile. Tis thinly Settled, though a few rich planters live along the route. The Brazos is the prettiest river that I have Seen in this latitude, tis about one hundred yards wide and very deep, the banks are lined with Cottonwood and willow, and covered with quick Sand. Left Columbia thursday morning on the Steamboat “Era No. 3” for Velasco distant about fifty miles by the river route. The weather still continued cloudy wind blowing [[lost: start of line]] and from the east. Eight miles below Columbia is Brazoria [[also?]] a Small place on the river bank in the woods. This [[is?]] the only town below Columbia. The boat Stopped [[frequently?]] along to take in men belonging to Bates Regt [[who?]] had been in the bottoms hunting and cutting poles to [[build?]] cook houses with at the mouth of the river. [[lost: fragments of another line at bottom edge]]

Editorial note. Continues on 09-116–118. Left edge and bottom of the reproduction clip parts of words and a following line. The railroad initials are tentative and have not been silently expanded. The boat name reads Era No. 3. This is the writer’s travel description; distances and assessments of settlement are his own.

09-116 · Delivering a prisoner and finding Dock at Velasco

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 116

09-116-P01 Some four or five miles above Velasco the timber [[deleted: gave]] [[inserted: gives]] out and the river emerges into the open prairie. Like Sabine the Country is low and flat, the banks of the river Scarcely eighteen inches high. Near the lower edge of the timber was Some of Magruders ground hoggery in the Shape of a Small field fortification with two embrasures for guns. About two miles above the mouth is another earthwork mounting one gun. Arrived at Velasco at near three oclock, wind very hard from east and pretty cold, hunted up Hd Qrs [[G.C.M.?]] & turned over my prisoner according to orders and then began looking about for Dock. I Soon met with him but would not have known him, His beard has not heard of a razor for years and besides he is tolerably gray as much so as father. He was in good health but very sick of the war and anxious to hear from home as he had not heard Since the battle of Shiloh. Velasco is on the east Side of the river and Quintana on the west. The principal portion of the troops are at Quintana Hd Qrs are at Quintana. Velasco Contains five or Six dwellings only, Quintana about twice that No. The two Cities are exactly opposite each other, the river between is about three hundred yards wide. There is no bay at the mouth. There is a fort on each side immediately on the beach, each commanding the Channel

09-117-P01 During the night it rained considerably and the [[wind?]] continued high from North East; two Schooners [[were?]] loaded ready for going out, one [[deleted: started]] [[inserted: started]] and [[ran?]] her bow into Steamboat, Smashed down the [[bow?]] a foot or two and damaged one Chimney [[considerably?]]. 09-118 · Men stranded in the rigging; George returns to Houston

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 118

09-118-P01 There was no life boat nearer than the wreck of the Acacia ten miles off on the beach to windward, and no boat could be launched on the open Sea in [[deleted: illegible]] Such a gale. Up to the time the boat left nothing had been done for the relief [[deleted: of]] of the poor fellows who were left clinging in the ropes and nothing could be done without a life boat and that was not obtainable. I never Saw so rough a Sea in my life before and hope never to see again when a vessel is in distress. There was no Chance to get the men off untill the Sea calmed. Saturday morning the wind was from the north and if they had not fallen from the rigging from exhaustion they were doubtless relieved. But two nights and a day was a long time to hang on to ropes and the Vessel rocking like a cradle in the Sand with every Swell of the Sea, and threatning to part. Friday I returned to Columbia, it rained a good portion the day and was disagreeably cold it continued raining friday night & Saturday, Saturday I came on to Houston, arrived in the night and found the mud very deep & thin. Everything had been in an uproar on account of Whartons death but all was [[deleted: illegible]] quiet. [[separate block: inverted writing above main text]] All well here at present. We are not ordered away yet tis rumored that transportation has been ordered for 30,000 men — George [[Dou... ?]]

Editorial note. Conclusion of 09-115–117, April 11, 1865. Inverted closing read separately after rotation. The final surname is clipped. George says the men were “doubtless relieved” only if they had survived until the sea calmed; this is his supposition, not a witnessed rescue. “Acacia” is the reading of the earlier wreck’s name.

09-119 · Sabine Pass, April 25: a burst cannon and uncertain battle reports

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 119

09-119-P01 Sabine Pass Apr 25th Number 18 I received yours of number 9 I wrote to you the other day, [[Lauras?]] at the Same time No 8. Yours was mailed the 4th of this month 21 days ago a long time for a letter to be on the way inside of the State. Henry [[Mundwell?]] got in day before yesterday, and says that Warren will not start for camps before the first of May. I wrote all about the skirmish in my last; since that time there has been no hostile manoeuvres. Five feds come a Shore the other night, and run our cavalry picketts in to town, or rather the pickets they got scared and came of their own accord. H R A serious [[deleted: accident]] accident has occurred here thursday. The cannon on the Bell a 64 pound rifle gun burst while they were practicing with it, killing two men and wounding two. It was a mate to the one that burst on the Bayou City the morning of the Gal fight. The defeat of Sibley at new Iberia is confirmed by report but as yet I have seen no published acct of it. It is said that he lost 250 killed, and is now himself under arrest for being drunk on the day of the fight. There is also another report current the Yankees have Taken Alexandria, La,

Editorial note. Two columns, read left then right. Year and addressee are not stated in the surviving heading. Continues on 09-120; the ending may be missing. The reported loss, arrest and intoxication of Sibley remain claims in a letter, explicitly unsupported by a published account. Standalone “H R” and a printed H at the right edge are not expanded as personal names.

09-120 · Orders for western Louisiana and beef too lean for gravy

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 120

09-120-P01 and are thirty thousand Strong. I do not know how much of this is true; but there is one thing I do know and that is this. Col Griffin got an order yesterday from Gen Scurry to hold all of his disposable force ready to march at a moments warning to western La. This was read on dress parade yesterday evening. Today they are taking a list of all the guns and cartridge boxes in the company. I would guess by this that they are getting so [[anxious?]] to start. I had about as Soon go to western La as to Stay here, for all the difference in the [[inserted: world]]. If they would keep us on the Island all the time I think we would have better health. There is no sickness in camps now worth naming except the mumps: and generally that is in a light form. Our staple of fare is cornbread and blue beef. I have seen beef so poor and plenty of it that after boiling a kettle full well done there would not be a drop of grease to be seen on top of the water. However now it is improving considerably: we sometimes make a little gravy now which is a great improvement. [[separate block: names and marks above right column, not a letter signature]] [[A B Henry?]] [[P. Cox?]] [[J. Shackleford?]] [[tally marks]]

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-119. Names at the top of the second column are separate from the continuous letter and are tentative; they do not establish authorship. No closing or signature to the letter is visible. The reading “anxious” is tentative.

09-121 · George returns to Galveston, May 4, 1865

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 121

09-121-P01 Sister Lizzie. Galveston May 4th 1865 Since I last wrote you we have changed base to this city. We came down yesterday on a Special train, quitted our old quarters after breakfast and got into our new ones time enough to get Supper. The weather was fine and altogether twas the most pleasant move we ever made. On the Second we were reviewed by Col Spaight, marched about over the principal part of Houston in column of platoons, owing to the absence of O Briens Co our position was on the left wing of the regt (“the tail” as tis called) and had to pad along behind a Co of Creoles who could neither keep a line or time or distance. In Consequence we Showed only at a moderate advantage. Several of the Ladies were out to to See us though no excitement at all was displayed. Scarcely ever a kerchief waved and “never a yell.” One little “[[Husky?]]” in her teens looked So much like She wanted to do Something I lifted my hat to her and She acknowledged the Same by a polite bow, I did not excite further notice afterwards. Many were the regrets [[deleted: that]] of the Citizens at our departure, Some of the most prominent did their best to persuade Magruder to let us remain but he would not hear to them. They (the citizens) gave the regt a box of Tobacco and 620 pounds of Coffee on the morning of our leaving, and Some Said they would be willing to pay “C” Co $10.00 per month Specie per man to let us Stay. That Shows how we Stand in Houston after a residence of five months. Our being moved is explained in few words. Magruder wants Ashbel Smith to command Galveston island [[El... ?]]

Editorial note. Continues on 09-122. Final line is partly clipped. The word George places in quotation marks for a teenage onlooker is uncertain and is not replaced by a more familiar epithet. His description of the other company and local opinion is retained as his perspective. “Specie” means coin.

09-122 · Schoolhouse quarters, a sea bath, and reports of surrender

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 122

09-122-P01 on the island but Elmore was Senior Col to Smith and must be removed and Spaight was the only junior Col in the Sub district to Smith, so we came for Smiths accommodation. We are quartered in the Robb Schoolhouse, room plenty for the Co and no other with us quartered with us and none nearer than a block distant. The location is pleasant, in the Southern part of the city a little over half mile from the South battery and about a half from our old quarters on Strand Street. On the east Side of the Street running from Smiths garden to the Custom house and Market, three blocks if I am not mistaken from the custom house, Jody will know the location. To day I luxuriated in a “roll in the brine” and “Shipped” a little Sea water in the operation. A blockader was off, not very far, I could See the men walking about the decks and the black ports frowned darkly, but they did not interrupt us; [[deleted: uncertain number]] [[inserted: Twelve]] vessels in the fleet. They had a flag of truce to day, have not heard from it yet. The “Wren” came in night before last loaded with cannon and ammunition brought N. Y. dates to 22d ult, they report that Johnson and Beauregard Surrendered on the Same terms as Lee. There must be Something of it as the blockade fired a Salute the other day. I heard to day that Some news had come in which the authorities [[deleted: were]] would not allow published. I got a letter from [[Doc H?]] this evening, he was not well, he wrote on the [[28th?]] ult. When we get a little better settled I will write again. Supper is about ready so I will quit. Excuse Haste Affectionately George All well in Camps,

Editorial note. Conclusion of 09-121. George’s information about surrender and withheld news is expressly reported, not witnessed. “Johnson” is retained as written. Inserted fleet total reads Twelve. Correspondent’s abbreviated name and date remain tentative. No identification of that correspondent has been inferred.

09-123 · A damaged and deserted Galveston, May 7, 1865

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 123

09-123-P01 Sister Lizzie, Galveston Texas May 7th 1865 Yours of 22d ult came to hand last evening, one must evidently be lost as there Seems to be a lack of connection. As to what I promised to tell you when I got back from Velasco I can Say I believe I forgot it, however twas only Jody going home which was then only prospective. The Capt says tell Jody to not hurry back, get what he went for if possible, no one has come in Consequently cant give an extension of time, Jody will not be looked for before the 1st of June nohow and not a great deal then unless transportation can be had conveniently. Galveston is badly Shattered by hard treatment, marks of abuse are everywhere visible, tis not near as pretty a city as it was two years ago, though tis ahead of Houston yet in beauty. Business has Stagnated, nothing is doing, the city looks deserted. Most of the wealthier Classes have gone, the poor are still here but there is no employment for them and how the get along is more than I can tell, no money in circulation that I have yet observed, all the business is done at Houston and Galveston is neglected and forgotten. There are Several regts here I do not know how many. They are quartered in every part of the city, and everywhere They have been they have Succeeded in ruining the houses. The Tremont house and Island City hotel are worthless. Every fence and old house has been burned for wood that any pretext could be found to commence on. Magruder has ditched and dug this end of the island full of holes thus ruining the landscape. An unbroken breastwork extends from the South Battery to Ft [[Scurry?]] and I dont know how much further. All the Sand hills between the S Battery and Ft S. have been leveled by order of Bankhead Lt Col, but under the influence of the wind they are rapidly reforming. [[illegible: clipped final line, includes “Street back near the Court house”]]

Editorial note. Continues on 09-124. The reference to the fort is tentative; the final line is clipped. The captain’s message about Jody is not a surviving formal extension of leave. Descriptions of poverty, housing damage and military earthworks are the writer’s observations and judgments.

09-124 · Rumors that the war is over—and George’s explicit caution

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 124

09-124-P01 Well now for News! Great and multiform are the rumors afloat but from them all this much can be deduced without peeping behind the Scenes. Johnston has either Surrendered or in Such a fair way too that he cant avoid it, but of the details you can [[know?]] as much as I. Now for behind the curtain. It has been rumored for Sometime that there was Some unpublished news on hand in fact this was definitely known, Flake of the Bulletin said as much. Of this news I have got an inkling. Col Wilkes has just arrived from New O. paroled, and Says Sherman and Johnston have come to the agreement that Johnston Surrender the Confederate Army everywhere, turn over all the arms [[deleted: illegible]] to the several State arsenals, disband the troops and Send them home. The Several State governments to continue in their present organizations, only renounce the Confed and renew their allegiance to the U.S. local laws and officers to continue as they are and all return to the Union. And an armistice of forty days agreed on to consult the Washington Cabinet. The Cabinet rejected the propositions as they recognized State Govts. Grant says he will sustain Shermans course with his army as it is a Military Surrender; made with the approval of Breckenridge and Davis. So matters stand if my inkling is correct. Warren is my informant and he is not likely to jump at a conclusion of this kind, he thinks the war over and that this news is only Suppressed untill it come officially for this Dept to give up and go home, and let the Change be effected as quietly as possible. If this is not premature a couple of months will wind up the Drama. Very likely a good deal of it is ahead of the hounds, yet the air of mystery around the published accounts warrant some surmises. Stoneman has made a raid in rear of Johnson and destroyed an immense amount of Supplies, Railroads and R.R. bridges, this is unpublished news, came by Wilkes. The foregoing you can take for what tis worth I cant vouch [[for its correctness?]] [[lost: rest of final line]]

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-123. No clear signature survives at the clipped bottom. This is a chain of reported information through Wilkes and Warren, expressly qualified by George. The described terms and claimed forty-day armistice have not been presented as verified historical facts. Johnston/Johnson spellings are retained as they occur.

09-125 · February 26, 1865: sore eyes, spring weather, and Confederate money

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 125

09-125-P01 Sister Lizzie Houston Feby 26th 1865 Your last of 11th inst came to hand a day or two ago. Glad to hear that you were well of the Sore eyes [[for?]] the little experience which I have had with them has abundantly proved to me that they are unpleasant in the highest degree, fortunately however I have been but very little bothered with them so far. The past week has been very fair and very foul, Some days it rained and [[some?]] it never though all in all quite a quantity has [[fallen?]] during the past week. Friday and friday night it rained [[very?]] hard. Though Saturday was a pretty day and to day the [[mud?]] has dried very fast. Spring has opened I think [[in?]] this latitude, Some few cold days will come yet but [[none?]] to do any harm I predict. Prices current this [[week?]] a little higher than last. Confederate Money has [[risen?]] to 25, and not a great deal in circulation. There Seems to be a determination to reduce the circulation [[of?]] it Somehow though Something extraordinary will be [[accomplished?]] if it ever becomes good again, and I think [[nothing?]] will ever make it good but an uncompromising [[tyranny?]] carried on under the immediate Supervision of [[the?]] Military, and plenty of that will be Served up during [[the?]] ensuing year in all kinds of Style to Suit Vendors,

Editorial note. Continues on 09-126–128. The supplied reproduction clips many line beginnings; reconstructed words are bracketed. The currency figure “25” has no explicit exchange basis. No modern medical diagnosis is assigned to “Sore eyes.”

09-126 · George mocks appeals to “military necessity” and unlimited sacrifice

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 126

09-126-P01 War news this week is very meagre. No fighting going on which has amounted to anything of importance reported, Since peace prospects were broken off. But very little truth ever escapes these latter days I opine owing to the precarious condition of Confed affairs east of the Mississippi. There is a good deal of “Freedom of Conscience” and “Speech” and “Press” I presume [[under?]] the present regime of Military [[Despotism?]], I presume [[it?]] is under and a long ways under, So far under that it will never get out. “So mote it be.” There is always a way to patch up broken places and tis really amusing to see the manner in which States rights are patched, & all other Strongholds [[of?]] Liberty. All are justified under the plea of “Military Necessity” and he is not a “patriot” who growls at anything done by the Government when the ultimate object is Laudable. All means are expedient just and proper and even Laudable [[when?]] one iota of good can be accomplished. It is nothing [[more?]] than the part of a “Good Patriot” to Surrender all he [[has?]] in property produce and Personal Liberty to the Govt [[for?]] “the time being” to accomplish the “Glorious End” of “[[Southern?]] Independence.” It is better to Sacrifice the “Last [[woman?]] & Child” on the “Altar of Liberty” than to Submit [[to?]] Yankee rule! Anihilation is preferable to “Such Slavery.” [[And?]] he is a coward and a knave who will not do all for his [[country?]]. Such is the Spirit of the Fire Eating press of to day

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-125. The left edge clips several words. This passage is sustained sarcasm criticizing the “Fire Eating press”; the extreme demands are not George’s recommendations. Tentative “Despotism” is partly overwritten. Quotation marks in the source are retained.

09-127 · The loudest war advocates—and an unkind assessment of city fashions

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 127

09-127-P01 Brave Editors behind desks, and brave legislators in Congress brave old men in chimney corners Smoking pipes and brave boys under the Conscript age can talk about what “Well do” with the Yankees how long “Well fight” and all this Sort of thing. Men who never smelled burnt powder and never will, will fight longer than any body else, and those who talks most of fighting are the very ones that never do any of it. Some of the Stump Speaking, fire eating, patriots, who at the beginning of this war Said that they would Spill the “last drop of blood” told an unconscious truth, they will be the last to Spill a drop of “blood.” I went to the M. E. Church to day, house was full of Soldiers Citizens and Ladies. There Seems to me to be more ugly Women in this City than any place I was ever at. As long as I have been here I do not remember of having Seen a handsome one yet. They always Spoil their looks with Superfluous clothing Some fancy touch Somewhere or everywhere reveals a [[soft?]] place in the “Phrenological Regions.” There is [[too?]] much of the Spirit of Novelty among them to Suit me, [[Vanity?]] in other words, a morbid desire to display Something [[new?]] that will attract attention, reminding of Burns “O wad Some power the giftie gie us” “To See oursels as ithers See us” “’Twad from many a blunder free us, An foolish notion”

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-125–126. Left edge clips a few words in the lower passage. The disparaging statements about women are preserved as the writer’s opinion. His quotation attributed to Burns is transcribed in the wording visible here, not corrected from an outside edition. “M. E.” is expanded as Methodist Episcopal in the family reading.

09-128 · Children playing bring George’s childhood to mind

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 128

09-128-P01 6h P.M. This Evening I took a Stroll through the western part of the city which presented quite an interesting picture when compared with the business portion. Everything was quiet and in Sunday attire. Some were Strolling the Streets enjoying the balmy Spring air and pleasant Sunshine but by far the greater portion were grouped in their handsome parlors passing the time, apparently, pleasantly enough. Pleasant Cottages and their homelike associations are pleasant to look at even if they cannot be [[deleted: illegible]] enjoyed at the present by me. Groups of merry children playing on sunny slopes and in grassy yards reminded me of days past but fondly recollected. Scenes which cannot recur but can always be held freshly in the Memory when types of them are presented to the view, and nothing can bring back to mind the Scenes of the past as quick as groups of gay children. The Church bell is ringing and I will attend So will close this and mail as it will go up tomorrow. I do not remember Miss Luna or Kate [[Denny?]] but Miss Lizzie K. I do. Tell the girls to “go it while they are young” for when they get old may be they Cant. With Best love to all I am as ever your Brother George

Editorial note. Conclusion of 09-125–128, February 26, 1865. The surname after Kate is tentative. “Gay” has its period sense of cheerful. No childhood location is identified in this recollection.

09-129 · Houston, December 11, 1864: yellow fever and church music

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 129

09-129-P01 Sister Lizzie Houston Dec 11th 1864 Your letter of 19th ult has been Recd. Found all present well in body and mind So far as I am capable of judging. During the past week we have had plenty of cool and Some cold weather. Sufficient I think unless the weather turns [[illegible: fold]] again to clear the city of yellow fever. There has been a good deal of it here lately but confined exclusively to citizens houses. No cases have occurred among those who have returned Since the freeze of 20th Nov except Such as occupied houses where it had been during the Summer. I feel no apprehensions of it breaking out among the troops as we are quartered in houses where none has been this Season. I attended church this morning at the Methodist Church, Speaker and Sermon were neither extra and congregation Small for a city. Up in one corner was an Organ from which music was pumped for the occasion. A big Negro worked the handle, while a Lady fingered the keys Scientifically.

Editorial note. Letter continues through 09-134. Dark fold obscures words about a change in the weather. George’s belief that cold weather and prior house occupancy governed yellow fever risk is recorded as a historical belief, not a medical explanation. The organ attendant’s race is stated; his name and legal status are not.

09-130 · George compares Methodist and Episcopal worship

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 130

09-130-P01 Music is as much out of place in church as a dog in a parlor, I felt like I was at preaching untill the the organ began [[moaning?]] then I felt as though I was at a party. I dont See where people get the doctrine of Music in churches, tis not in the Testament as I can find, if it is it is in Some unnoticed corner where my perceptions has never reached. Last Sunday I went to hear the Episcopal. They have quite a large brick church built on the Catholic plan of Gothic Architecture Superb and magnificent. The Parson came out of a closet in one corner with a robe on Catholic fashion, knelt by a desk a moment in Secret prayer where every body could See him; then began the Service. The Worship is read part by the preacher and members, he reading one verse aloud and all of them the next, in prayer he repeats a sentence and then the members all repeat it audibly after him. They Sing Psalms in stead of hymns which Sounded Very well, being diversified a little in the tune yet in perfect harmony. After Service followed the Catechism of the youthful members to See what progress they were making towards full membership; the repeating of the Creed &c, the Creed is identical with that of the presbyterians. [[illegible: words obscured by fold]] very good if they follow what they preach. Each Child is baptized in infancy, and two persons Standing by act as “Sponsors” Pledging themselves, in case the childs parents die or any other accidents happen that will render them incapable of taking care of the child, to take and raise or See that the child is raised in a proper and religious Manner. There is a great deal of form and Ceremony about their Worship resembling the Catholics a good deal. Preaching is tolerably plain, but there is so much fashion and Show about it that I dont much like it. I am pretty much the Same opinion as “Fanny Fern” on these matters; “True religion may go to Church in yellow gloves

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-129, followed by 09-131. Two columns read left then right. The fold interrupts the sentence about the creed. Accounts of denominational practice are the writer’s understanding, not editorially verified doctrine. A quotation he attributes to Fanny Fern begins at the bottom and continues on the next scan.

09-131 · Wealth, religious display, and George’s preference for modest dress

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 131

09-131-P01 and embroidered handkerchiefs, worth five hundred dollars but I dont believe it!” Though I do not know as I have any right to so judge the people of Houston because they are wealthy. I have noticed Several new Style Ladies Hats on the Street. The Kind I like best is high crowned narrow brimmed leghorn hats which does Some better I think than the old fashioned broad brims that used to [[deleted: illegible]] about So Conspicuously on the prairies. In my humble opinion however the old fashioned close Split bonnetts [[deleted: illegible]] the handsomest articles that ever a woman wore on her head. You may call that old fashioned and out of date in this day of Splash and dash when brilliants are all the [[rage?]], but it is modest, and that is the nicest quality which ever adorned a woman no matter what the world and the balance of mankind may Say to the contrary. above all things be modest.

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-130. Opening completes the quotation attributed by George to Fanny Fern; its wording is not corrected from an external text. “Close Split bonnetts” is retained as read, without silently substituting a fabric or garment name. The social judgments are the writer’s.

09-132 · Auctions, flour supplies, and Sherman’s move into Georgia

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 132

09-132-P01 Sunday night 11th — 7 Oclock. By candle light I resume to give a few more ideas in my usual disconnected Style of composition and flit. The boys are going to preaching to the Methodist Church So I will be alone, too cold for me to go without they would let music alone and have preaching instead of fun. There are auctions almost every day in town, dry goods of almost every description at very high prices though coming down a little, the figures are a little under what I wrote last. Flour is plenty in town by the wholesale or retail in lots to Suit purchasers. When asked where it all comes from the answer is invariably “Up the Country.” I have not heard of a great deal being Sold in that Country to Citizens, thought the Govt took all for the army &c &c. The latest news is Some little Stirring. Sherman has made a bold move into Ga much to the astonishment of all thereby creating a great Stir in military Circles. For once he outgeneralled Hood and all his advisers, [[lost: final words clipped]]

Editorial note. Continuation of the December 11, 1864 letter. Bottom of the source reproduction clips the last line. The writer contrasts flour for sale with his impression that the government had requisitioned it. This is not evidence of a specific theft or diversion.

09-133 · Guarded soldiers’ opinions, private gossip, and expected emancipation

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 133

09-133-P01 It is a mistake about Magruder being ordered back to Texas. It is Strange how men who ought to know Start and credit Such reports. Walker will still continue to Command here and furloughs will continue to jog along as usual. Spaight is doing his best to get all details ordered in, if all were present the Regt would number nearly one thousand. This is now about the largest Regt in the State. There is Somewhere in the neighborhood of a dozen home on leave from this Co now. Only one has thought enough of the fair to marry so far. If accounts be true Eddings, and old “bach” married a widow in [[Stewart?]] a few days ago, he has not yet returned to Camps. You were a little mistaken on Shialot on the war question, Soldiers generally profess more patriotism than they actually feel for they dont know what Kind of people they are dealing with, and always make sure to be on the Safe Side whether they are or not. On the Subject of Matrimony I confess I was no little astonished, though I am in the habit of doing things by fits and starts, but this Start Stumped me. I was not aware that She had ever done any thing disreputable. True I learned Henry had denounced his intentions but I thought this was merely a lovers or Something of that Sort. What else I learned merely Settled an opinion I long ago had formed, Viz; Lack of moral Courage and Self resolution. I positively know now nothing more than I knew three years ago, of what may or may not have happened Since I left home or even in the Service rather, I am totally ignorant; nor can I Say I care to know. So here the Subject must drop. [[He?]] had better let marrying alone and go to Mexico and get out of troublous times. The negro is bound to be freed before this war ends, and Jeff Wont give it up as long as he can get a white man or negro to fight for him. “Mr Southern is Some by himself.”

Editorial note. Continuation of 09-132. “Shialot” is the literal place/name reading; no identification is certain. Location of Eddings’s marriage and a pronoun near the bottom are tentative. The private discussion does not name the woman and George expressly disclaims knowledge; no allegation is treated as established fact. His expectation of emancipation is a prediction written in December 1864.

09-134 · Blockade running, conscription, and a cold room

George Douglas Papers Folder 6 - Correspondence.pdf · Scan page 134

09-134-P01 There is a Schooner at the landing on the bayou, just in from Tampico laden with merchandise. It belongs to [[Reichman?]] and Myers of this city. Quite a number keep out of the Service along the coast by blockade running, though they do not run on them themselves. A few men are around gathering conscripts and forwarding them to the front, they had better be gathering up loose & useless officers and putting them where they belong instead of bothering honest men. As it is late and cold having no fire in our room I will Close. I have to take this to the P.O tonight So it will get off in the morning to Millican. With best love to all I remain Your brother Geo Douglas.

Editorial note. Conclusion of 09-129–133, dated December 11, 1864. First merchant’s name is tentative. Claims about avoiding military service are the writer’s opinion, not a verified finding concerning every merchant or shipowner named.

10-045 · “Parody”: a rose offered in friendship, April 1868

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 45

10-045-P01 154 Parody.
10-045-P02 ’Tis the first rose of Summer Fresh blooming and fair Which sheds its sweet fragrance Upon the soft air; Oh! how sweetly it blushes Like a young maiden’s cheek When emotions are burning The lip cannot speak.
10-045-P03 I’ll not leave thee, thou fair one To bloom on the stem, But will gather thee gently The days sweetest gem; While the dewdrop yet lingers Upon thy bright leaves; As the tear on the lashes When th’heart fondly grieves.
10-045-P04 And soon will I give thee In Friendship’s true name To one who will prize thee Through life still the same; True hearts ne’er are withered Tho’ Youth’s bloom be gone And that Love is immutable Where Friendship first shone.
10-045-P05 April 1868.

Editorial note. Manuscript page 154. No author’s signature appears on this page. The heading “Parody” is retained without supplying an external source or attribution.

10-046 · “To Emma,” of Zephyrus Bower

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 46

10-046-P01 153 To Emma. Of Zephyrus Bower,—By “Moore” the second.
10-046-P02 Part First. Awake my sweet Lyre To Love I aspire Pure as the desire Of Angels above Hopes which I cherish Never let perish And cast a dark gloom O’er Fancy’s first bloom But live forever And flow as a river A torrent of Love. Then welcome the hour It finds Emma’s bower Where by thy sweet power I’m carried along; The Muses around Enchant The fair ground With Music’s sweet sound A heavenly Song. Then joy so complete While at Emma’s feet I softly repeat And for each word vouch That fondly I love her By all that’s above her And will till times over My dear Emma Couch.
10-046-P03 Part Second Awake my sweet Lyre Affections desire A heavenly fire Courses my veins Oh! let thy sweet sound Come floating around With gentle rebound In melodious strains; For Emma divine Will never be mine Unless I can shine By Poesy’s power. For no other score Will I go before A second “Tom Moore” To zephyrus bower, But that me will raise I fondly surmise And in Emma’s eyes Perhaps may succeed Then Life will be bright And joyous and light, And in young Love’s sight Elysium indeed.
10-046-P04 Part Third. Awake my sweet Lyre You know my desire; Oh! now go and fire Another young heart Thus you will prove That you can wake Love In Bower or Grove Wherever you start. Let Love’s sweetest Song Thy cadence prolong While moving along That verdant bower Whose perfumes shaken Emma will waken [[separate block: final two lines in the right margin]] To live the peerless Maid of thy bower.

Editorial note. Manuscript page 153, in two columns. Part Second runs from the bottom of the left column to the top of the right; Part Third ends in two rotated margin lines. “Moore” the second and “Tom Moore” are the poem’s own descriptions, not a verified attribution. “times over” is reproduced as written. The text names Emma Couch, but neither her identity nor a historical relationship is established here.

10-047 · “Bachelor’s Lament,” July 1875

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 47

10-047-P01 Bachelor’s Lament. July 1875
10-047-P02 O! where is the hope of the vine covered cottage The visions of Youth will so oft conjure up Forever ’tis gone, and now gray in my dotage I’ve drained to the dregs Life’s bitterest cup. And where is the dear One I’ve loved with devotion Thro’ life’s changeful scenes of unhallowed commotion With ever the same constant and changeless emotion Beloved at the first and beloved to the close.
10-047-P03 No answer comes back from my voiceless surroundings For silence and gloom are my comrades alway, I’m sad as if sunk ’neath the Sea’s deepest Soundings Where the [[deleted: uncoffined dead]] [[inserted: dead of the past]] lie mould’ring away, O! when will this cease here, this dread desolation Which binds my soul down in its deep tribulation And is there no season of calm consolation No morning unfolding again as the rose?
10-047-P04 Alone now I wander on life’s rugged byways The friends of my Youth I may never greet more For many have fallen on far distant highways And beckon me on to the Stygian shore; And ’neath yon low mound where the willow stands weeping My heart’s only darling forever is sleeping O! may the Death Angel make haste with his reaping And gather me there to a dreamless repose!
10-047-P05 Forever shall cease then those ties that are breaking And sweetly I’ll rest in the calm of the tomb. No storms can assail ’till the morn of awaking Shall beckon the dead back to joy or gloom— Around me shall linger no omen of danger Which compassed my way while a sad lonely ranger To all save a Peace—deep and dreamless a Stranger There calmly I’ll rest from my life’s gloomy woes.

Editorial note. A clearer version of passages also present in the faint notebook drafts at 10-021 and 10-026. The interlinear revision in stanza two is shown explicitly. No signature is visible. The poem’s references to aging, a lost beloved, and death are literary statements; they do not by themselves establish the author’s age, marital status, or a named person’s death.

10-048-P01 75 Thus Inez to me was the dross in the gold The Midnight’s dead shade o’er the hope of the soul The glowworm’s cold light where poison vines weep Their death dealing dews in the dark forest deep.
10-048-P02 But back thro’ the lapse of the shadowy years My Ida’s sweet smile ever changeless appears Ere the tempter invaded my Eden of Bliss And destroyed my sweet flower, leaving me this.

10-049 · “To Victoria”: welcome to Brushy

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 49

10-049-P01 74 To Victoria.
10-049-P02 Welcome Victoria! to Brushy’s green slopes The Cradle and Grave of my Bachelor hopes Here they opened and flourished and fell in decay As flowers nipt by a frost in the genial May.
10-049-P03 But why should I trouble you with Sorrows of Mine! For thousands have felt them, and thousands repine But may the kind Angel who is guarding thy way Protect you from them wherever you Stray.
10-049-P04 Thrice happy the hours since to Brushy you came For enjoyments exist now which were only a name; And sweeter than roses the converse we hold And the swift flying moments are brighter than gold.
10-049-P05 I speak not of Love, that fountain is dry Deception and Falsehood have quenched its supply Experience has taught me, the daughters of Eve The fairest the brightest were born to deceive.
10-049-P06 Sweet Ida was fickle, but still in my heart Her image is graven and will never depart, But Inez with falsehood has stained her young fame And the curse of a Douglas now rests on her name.
10-049-P07 Tell me why should the truthful one sympathy hold For that glittering dross which alloys the gold Or what what concord has night with the morn of the day The glow worms cold glare with the sun’s gentle ray.

Editorial note. Manuscript page 74. Continued at 10-048 (manuscript page 75), where the poem is dated July 1875. The repeated “what what” is retained. “A Douglas” appears in the poem, but it is not an author’s signature. Brushy is not assigned to a specific modern location here. The accusations about Ida, Inez, and women generally are the speaker’s rhetoric, not independently verified statements.

10-050 · “On the Banks of Brushy”: remembered childhood landscapes

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 50

10-050-P01 13 On the Banks of Brushy.
10-050-P02 Fair Brushy! again beside thy winding stream I rove again as in my childhood’s days And with ardor dream again each early dream Which once beguiled my young artless ways; O’er them still my Memory fondly strays Sweet treasures of the Past forever fled And doomed to rot in dark Oblivion’s maze Where all that’s pure and bright is tending fast To mingle with Earth’s common clay at last.
10-050-P03 Here first I heard the sky-lark’s warbling notes As it high ascended from its dewy nest: And here from a thousand other funny throats I heard the tones which swelled each tender breast Rising to Heaven as though they blest The great Creator’s name with guileless heart Who had all things in such beauty drest And given them here fair Freedom’s part Unstained by Man, with his dark wily art.
10-050-P04 Here too I culled the lovely flowers which grew In rich profusion on each verdant lawn Adding their charms of every varied hue Which could not be restored when they were gone Then with listless steps I wandered on To seek for others still more sweet Until the approach of evening’s dawn Homeward turned my wandering feet From many a pleasant flower adorned retreat.
10-050-P05 But ere from each pleasant landscape I withdrew I culled from many a lone mossy glen The lovely violets which in rich profusion grew In every woodland brake and tangled fen—

Editorial note. Manuscript page 13, continuing at 10-051 (page 14). “Funny throats” and “evening’s dawn” are retained as written. The speaker’s childhood landscape is called Brushy, but the poem alone does not securely identify either its author or the geographical location. The complete identified reading order is 10-050, 10-051, 10-060, 10-061, 10-052, 10-053 (manuscript pages 13–18).

10-051 · “On the Banks of Brushy”: flower battles and youthful ambition

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 51

10-051-P01 14 And naming each for earth’s illustrious men And counting signal numbers for each side, Vigorously began the mock battle—and when The flowery fight was done—and all but one had died O’er that Last victor my heart thrilled in boyish pride
10-051-P02 To think that I like it would triumph over all Who were arrayed against me as my foes That I would thus witness the last one fall Whom my right of sway would ever dare oppose. And of my life victory and peace would be the close Was the emblem which I saw in that flower And did not note how soon it died with those It had o’erthrown in battle’s stormy hour Yielding with them all unto a mightier power.
10-051-P03 But as those lovely flowers withering died Together in one fragrant floral heap So perished those early joys which were allied Unto the future where broad Fancy’s sweep Grasped the immortal and bade me keep An erect brow through swiftly coming years And clamber up Fame’s long wished steep Whose shaggy brow in the dim future rears Aloft above the rabble’s taunting jeers.
10-051-P04 But still those early scenes in freshness bloom Those brighter fancies of my childhood’s time Shine from afar, though intervening gloom And the wide distance gives them doubly the sublime Of Beauty, Glory, and Grandeur, which in their prime They wore unto my young enraptured eyes, As the measured feet of impassioned rhyme Lends dignity unto the writings of the wise Which Clothed in Poetry more majestically rise.

Editorial note. Manuscript page 14 continues 10-050 (page 13). It continues at 10-060 (page 15), then 10-061 (page 16), 10-052 (page 17), and 10-053 (page 18). The flower battle is explicitly a child’s game, not an account of a military engagement.

10-052 · Childhood morning, school, and play: “On the Banks of Brushy” sequence

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 52

10-052-P01 17 But once more the sun is in the glowing east, Once more the day has come beautiful and bright, Once more from Sweet Slumber’s bond released All Nature hails the grand return of Light. Once more unto my eager ravished sight The dew drops sparkle brightly on a thousand flowers From the pure crimson to the spotless white Which richly glow in Nature’s vernal bowers Adding sweetest perfumes to the returning hours.
10-052-P02 The lowing herds wandering forth to crop the grass O’er mead and hill in boundless pastures free The soft tinkling bells upon them as they pass Ringing on the morning air so merrily, And in a thousand brakes the song birds cheerily Hymning on High their Sweet discordant notes All forming [[deleted: the sweetest]] [[inserted: a Sweeter]] chorus [[deleted: which]] [[inserted: than]] ever we Have heard from any choirs of well trained throats As it through the Soft air, gently heavenward floats
10-052-P03 But the hour for School has come, we must along With Satchel and basket, and beneath the teachers eye Con our lessons over with a hum-drum Song With many a furtive glance at the bright blue sky And longing from the close School-room to fly To the cooling Stream or groves deep vernal shade Or o’er the flowery plain to chase the butterfly Where thro’ the long hours of morning it has Strayed Sipping the sweet from the flowers where it has played.
10-052-P04 Hail glorious playtime! for awhile set free With wild shouts we hail thee in the open air Happy as any class of mortals well can be Having to pleasure now our odd hour to spare,

10-053 · Schoolboy friendship threatened by cruelty and slander

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 53

10-053-P01 18 And laying aside every thought and care Which jocund joy might possibly impede And dividing into equal sides prepare For boyish games; and firing to nought else heed With laugh and shout the winged hours we speed.
10-053-P02 Thrice happy time! with no foreboding cares opprest The glowing hours in joy are winged away And present Hopes with full fruition blest Portend no shadows in Lifes evening day. Alas! that those should ever o’er us stray To blight young Friendship in the early bud And drown their first purest blessed joy Beneath dark Detractions turbid flood— Whose boiling tide inundates all that’s good.
10-053-P03 Oh! why should the Schoolboys path of flowers Be lined with thorns at every step he treads? Oh! why should his Life’s young gladsome bowers Conceal that Serpent in their floral beds Whose poisonous fangs obscured in hydra heads Of hate, malice, Scorn, Contempt, and pride, Strike with all their venom natively inbred Until the nobler passions of the heart have died Or with the baseness of Lucifer allied.

10-059-P01 61 Apostrophe To the Brazos.
10-059-P02 Sweet Brazos! Still thy murmuring waters lave Thy pebbly strand beneath yon Mountain height Whose summit crowned by an ancient Indian [[inserted: grave]] At once his nation’s pride and nation’s might, Some hundred years have winged their weary flight Since he was laid within the warriors tomb O! what a change hath been! What withering blight Has stamped the red man with an early doom— And swept him from the earth, to give the pale face room.
10-059-P03 But still thou flowest on as in days of yore With the same old tones, within thy Rocky bed The rugged cliffs still crown thy winding shore— Perchance an aged tree still rears its head; And saving these, all [[other?]] Scenes have fled, The Warrior proud and strong—his dusky Bride The stalwart Chief—and trusted Steed—are dead The Wigwam gone—with all the Red Man’s pride Swept with the flying years, [[illegible]] from their changeful tide.
10-059-P04 Though these are gone, still hearts as fondly brave And deeply true, still beat along thy stream, As those, thy long gone primal ages gave, Unto the world, and still as [[vainly?]] dream Of Love and Happiness, and fondly deem That they in after years will grasp the wand Of Human Bliss, whose rich illusive gleam Seen from afar but vainly leads them on Till Youth and health and strength and hope and life are gone.
10-059-P05 Tho’ this be so, O! still we’ll grasp the hour That beams with Love and Hope’s illusive smile We’ll woo its presence, and its cheerful power To be around us, tho’ for so short awhile

10-060 · “On the Banks of Brushy”: twilight and remembered youth

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 60

10-060-P01 15 Thus still those early scenes which first I knew Linger on the pages of the shadowy Past Which as Memory turns its leaves comes to view In pure unstained colors, which will last When the bands of Age are round me cast And earthly joys grow dim and fade away And Life’s last sands are ebbing fast And soon to mingle with earth’s common clay Where all at last must moulder and decay.
10-060-P02 How beautiful! when the garish day was done The sky appeared in twilight’s lovely hue When the last lingering rays of the glorious sun With amber streaked the deep heavenly blue Unto my boyish eyes the glorious view Seemed but the portals of a heaven on high Where from the horizon we might spring through And taste immortal bliss above the sky With those pure Spirits there which never die.
10-060-P03 And as still deeper glowed the tints of night Upon that horizon’s far distant west. The stars came forth with their lovely light And gazed on the earth like Spirits blest Watching it whilst it calmly sank to rest From the toil and cares of days passed here Whose fierce pursuits, pursued with eager zest By men, seeking for some altitude of power To dispense to mankind, curses by the hour.
10-060-P04 How softly falls, with the calm advance of night Its mild influences on mans stormy soul! Erasing the stripes of day, and bearing [[unsought?]] That boon of Heaven, whose high goal

10-061 · “On the Banks of Brushy”: childhood sleep and mortality

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 61

10-061-P01 16 Is fixed where Time’s billows can never roll Nor reach with their canker and decay The immortal Spirit’s far magnetic pole Around which it pursues its eternal way In the boundless light of an unending day.
10-061-P02 At length when all without was calm and still I would seek in slumber deep for childhood’s dream Softly lulled to sleep by the lone whip-poor-will Which sang its sweet song in nights soft beams And which to my young imaginations seems A lovely creature sent with pure nameless charms And matchless beauty, which in the starlight gleams Brilliant and bright, such as mightily warms A poets fancy when wrapped in Morpheus’ arms.
10-061-P03 How quiet are childhood’s slumbers! how free from all The stormy dreams of manhood’s feverish sleep! No wild unrest, no vain ambitions lofty fall! No withering hopes! o’er which to wake and weep But all is peace, and soft repose—and sweetly keep Their star watch o’er the young and tender frame Now resting in sweet unconsciousness so deep, That ’twere a pity, it should ever wake to claim A place again on the rough road to earthly Fame.
10-061-P04 Oh! it were better far in our earliest days Before we learn the torturing way of Sin, That in Death, should be quenched Life’s loved bright rays And we, sink into the tomb—though cold within Should be its cold vault—yet Oh! ’tis there Through that drear portal, and break the chain Of icy bondage there—and triumphing in The death struggle—returned unto Heaven again Resting the bliss of victory and Death of pain.
