10-070 · “Social Parties—What Are They?”: a critical account of local gatherings

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 70

10-070-P01 10 [[separate block: preprinted descriptive roll and enlistment headings, as at 10-068]] Social Parties—What Are They?
10-070-P02 The Social Parties as practiced by the Native and Adopted citizens of the younger class in this Section are in my humble opinion the most ridiculous amusements which it is possible for intelligent people to practice. Imagine a gathering of thirty or forty young people aged respectively from eighteen to thirty at some place selected for the contemplated performance. Having met and sat about rather indolently for awhile apparently very much embarrassed and seemingly very modest and very fearful of doing something contrary to the rules of Etiquette some venturesome character proposes a “play” The young gents capering select their partners and ere long promenading the floor in a circle by twos to the bewitching strains of “Old Sister Phebe” or “My pretty little love” or some other popular air sung in enchanting style by some one or two vocalists. No conversation worthy the name is ever carried on by any couple, those not engaged in singing keep profoundly silent or indulge in unmeasured laughter at some real or imaginary blunders of some one or more of the party. Tiring of the first or any other play each individual looks for a seat for him or herself, or a drink of water or something else. The girls congregate on one side of the house and indulge in apparently very lively and interesting chat if we are to judge from the many Smiling faces and little giggles which may from time

Editorial note. Manuscript page 10 continues at 10-071. This is the writer’s satirical criticism, not a neutral survey. The location and date become explicit on the following page: Ellis County, Texas, May 1866. “Native and Adopted citizens” here distinguishes local-born residents and newcomers in the writer’s wording; it is not an identification of Indigenous ancestry. Song titles are transcribed, not attributed to an external version.

10-071 · “Social Parties”: Ellis County, Texas, May 1866

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 71

10-071-P01 11 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form, as at 10-062]] to time be seen and heard. Poor things how they appear to enjoy themselves when alone but let a venturesome young Swain invade their circle an immediate Silence succeeds which generally makes a fellow feel as though he might have been the subject of the previous amusement and merriment. Thus the evening wears away varied by all the silly singing little plays with which the performers are acquainted until all get tired and break up by common consent. Each Swain takes his Sweetheart home if he has one and those who have none go home alone as [[illegible]]. Such is society in Ellis county Texas May 1866. Such is the manner in which the young deport themselves one toward another. What the Legitimate result of all this may be I have no way of determining it is to be hoped however that it will terminate in something more refined as well as Sensible And that a higher degree of Sociability may be attained than is at present [[afforded?]].
10-071-P02 Something loftier should be adopted for all confess when the point is urged that they feel ashamed of themselves [[when?]] participating in Such silly amusements. Then why not at once do away [[with?]] them and adopt something in their stead of which we will not be ashamed. Common sense could suggest many convenient ways of amusement which would be [[profitable as well as agreeable?]].

10-072-P02 ’Twas a brilliant affair for Texas at this stage of its intellectual development. Surpassing anything of the kind which has occurred so far in the history of this section of country. Nothing however Original spoken or performed on the stage, all derived from the brain of some foreign Genius.
10-072-P03 Eleven o’clock at night closed the fleeting pageantry and all I suppose went home satisfied judging from outside appearances—and some are doubtless delighted arguing from the same reason—but we have no right I suppose to surmise the secret history of any of the many palpitating fatty hearts that left that ground—if one did perhaps all that might be told would not be pleasant to hear.
10-072-P04 In common parlance the “Skirmish Line” was established & at least one Hymeneal affair was fully accomplished on this occasion of wit [[mirth?]]—May all at last leave all parties satisfied and happy and content to go on their way rejoicing—if not from the full fruition of their hopes and anticipations at least in the hope of a better day coming when they can at least call the [[beloved?]] [[illegible]] their own, if only Temporarily. [[deleted: illegible]] Sunshine and Shadow are strangely commingled in this [[mundane?]] Sphere. Those who are gay today may [[be sad?]] tomorrow, and those who are sad today may be gay tomorrow. It is doubtless [[more pleasant?]] to watch these transitions than to [[undergo?]] them—We will wait awhile and [[illegible]].

10-073 · Sixteen years in Ellis County and the difficulties of farming

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 73

10-073-P01 13 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] A residence of Sixteen years in this portion of Texas (Ellis County) has not made me fall in love with it by any means. ’Tis may be the easiest place to “get along” in of any other—yet the experience which I have had here in common farming life forces me to the conclusion that it is a hard place to make a living. The general mildness of the climate, and [[slowness?]] of the Summer have enervated the inhabitants to such a degree that they do not look forward with the proper foresight in regard to their pecuniary interests. Proper places for deposit of grain are not provided and frequently crops suffer [[deleted: from]] destruction to a considerable extent from this cause alone. We are poorly provided with machinery of all descriptions, There is not half mills enough in the country consequently instead of Competition we have Combination, and exorbitant rates of toll are charged which is detrimental to the farming interests of the country, but we farmers have to submit to an [[illegible]] which we cannot help and any hope [[illegible]] away change. I cite Millers [[illegible]] which [[inflict?]] upon the Community—Other professions do likewise as far as they are able. Self is the governing principle here [[to?]] the exclusion of all other and [[while?]] [[illegible]] [[localities?]] whose competition gives the farming class a chance to realize the full value of their crops from year to year [[would?]] surely be more desirable than [[illegible]] they are much the most [[illegible]].

Editorial note. Manuscript page 13 is unsigned and undated. The preceding page is dated July 4, 1866; this does not establish this page’s date or author. 10-074 · Home and the ties of childhood

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 74

10-074-P01 14 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] Home
10-074-P02 There are many pleasant associations connected with the word Home, It embodies at one group and in one view the leading features of our earlier days. Our first recollections, our first associations our first connections all spring at once to the mind at the mention of that one word. Our recollections of the innocent Sports that beguiled the days of our infancy, when lighthearted and joyous we played amid Sunshine and flowers, inhaling the wild free air and Spirit of nature, careless and gay as the bright plumaged birds which warbled their hymns of praise from every tree, Free as they from the follies and vices of the world nor dreaming of the blight of after years through which we would be called to pass—Our earlier associations with companions joyous as we, which can never be renewed, but which will linger in Memory, as one of the brightest periods of our existence; and to which we can always turn with pleasing emotions—Our earlier connections with parents, brothers, and sisters, fond endearing ties, woven in childhood years, and never to be forgotten, though separated by time and distance, far from the places where they sprung into existence—These remembrances all spring within the mind when Home is mentioned and as we contemplate them through the lapse of years they assume a hallowed purity, which no other scenes or associations can. They are holy because they belong to the past, they are sacred because they are pure and uncontaminated by vile connections, they are the tender ties of early love, mutually enjoyed and mutually reciprocated, they are the holy links which bind the family

Editorial note. Manuscript page 14 continues at 10-075. This is a general reflection, not a list of the writer’s own identified relatives. The following page says it was written at a young lady’s request at Seclusion, September 20, 1866.

The influence of such associations will always be felt no matter what may be our course through life, whether wild and dissipated, or gentle and refined, in one case, they will check us in our wayward career, and point to a nobler existence, in the other, they will be an incentive to a continuation in a life of well doing, ennobling our feelings and refining our natures, inspiring in our hearts a spirit of Charity and contentment which will be a perpetual wellspring of happiness to us, which the cares of Life cannot destroy. Written at the request of a Young Lady Seclusion Sept 20th 1866.
10-075-P02 Sonnet or, Blent Flowers, Adieu ye bright hopes that so fondly have hovered Around the light dreams of my earlier days When with feelings transparent and affections uncovered I faced the gay world in its meridian blaze Those visions of joy bright [[deleted: in]] [[inserted: all]] ecstatic Elysian Have faded before adversity’s cold gaze And nought now remains but those dreams [[deleted: of]] [[inserted: Life’s elysion]] Dimly discovered through memory’s dark haze But still they will linger on those dim distant pages And occasionally be read when a sunbeam there strays And fondly remembered as one of those happy ages That in Childhood and Youth deceivingly plays But will return not again in life’s varied stages Although we hope for it in Philosophy’s atherian ways Seclusion July 1866

10-078-P04 Every monday morning I understand All of your faults you have to own Then lay strong hold with both your hands And go to gnawing on this bone.

10-078-P07 Then comes the Sabbath pure and bright Its glories over earth are thrown

10-082 · To Miss M A A or fair Mary

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 82

10-082-P01 22 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] To Miss M. A. A.
10-082-P02 When Heavens blue arch so gracefully bending Above me brightly glows with loves azure hue And the mind with sweet thoughts calmly ascending Along that bright arch turns fair Mary to you.
10-082-P03 As the needle with magnet faithfully thrilling Still points to the pole so steady and true So the deepest emotions of my hearts fond instilling Drawn with true magnet fair Mary to you.
10-082-P04 And when on the green grassy banks reclining Of fair Red Oak, listening to its waters flowing there The entrancing shades, above it so gracefully entwining Fond Memory turns fair Mary to you.
10-082-P05 The voices of waters songsters in those bowers dwellying My wild restless Spirit does enchantingly woo But still while I listen to the wild choral ringing In rapture my heart turns fair Mary to you.
10-082-P06 And like the Sunflower its fair face Extending In the early morn ere it sheds the bright dew To meet the bold gaze of its bright god ascending So I open my heart fair Mary to you.
10-082-P07 In the morning of Life I am now joyously standing Before me is spread bright prospects sweet to view With the gay Charm of Hope my heart is expanding But they all point at last fair Mary to—you.

10-086 · Dutch Campmeeting in September 1866

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 86

10-086-P01 26 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] Dutch Campmeeting 1866. In 1866 in September I went to the campmeeting And as well as I can remember Received a very cordial greeting The first of social joys which I took Was a gentle sprinkling. Thus I caught a forward look And of what was coming got an inkling. ’Twas rain a shower and mud a heap And drabbled dresses plenty And I got many a sly peep At tapering ankles from ten to twenty. The camp accommodations were very poor And it did not suit the lasses To have to sit upon the floor On straw in lieu of grasses. Grasses they would have preferred beneath a willow Soft yielding green dewy sparkling ever And every lass of them a handsome fellow To twain bright garland posies weaving ever But alas! the difference, a preacher here Restraining the free flow of chat Between the gents and ladies fair A thing they all would fain be at. But after a while they bolder grew And some got in the passage And what do ye think they did do When they got the passage? Why they mixed all up together In a crowd huddle—

Editorial note. Manuscript page 26 begins a long satirical poem continued through 10-090. “To twain bright garland posies weaving ever” is unusual wording retained as read. The social and physical descriptions are the speaker’s often unkind judgments. This verse should not be treated as a verified report about identifiable people.

And now and then a softer word I spect was slyly thrown in And by the proper person heard Who never thought it a bit o’ sin. But this I do not know I only simply guess it But they had none to do A great deal in the way of chat Betimes they grew more confidential As they got into a livelier mood And some things were said potential Which by the way were very good. But I did not like the stile of compliments Which was peped around off from the fence Yet I do not think any one meant To give to any other any offence.

10-088 · The camp meeting poem on flattery and courtship

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 88

10-088-P01 28 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] How affectionate they looked so coy and sly With their bright eyes glancing about Seeming to say “if you will but try The kisses you may have with a pout!” By hokey! the favorite young devil Who was smart enough to get a few smacks Should I find him in manner quite civil I’ll endeavor to walk in his tracks! I will be all smiles and attention And specially notice their slightest needs Do everything that politeness could mention And think of all things that it cant. And always with the greatest deference Will I lift my hat when I speak to them And always manifest the greatest preference For any thing to which they take the whim. To please them so in a loving mood I will tell them lies by the score And if this does not do any good I will tell them twice as many more. Then if I see their brows gently reproving I will instantly recant all I have said And be so affectionate and loving They will bestow blessings by the forewarning head, In short I will bend as the willow To every slight breath of the wind And do everything in the world to pillow My head on their bosoms so kind!
10-088-P02 But I know there are some peevish creatures Who long since have lost their lovely features

10-089-P01 29 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] Who will censure me quite severely For all which I have here said sincerely, And will dubiously say “he is a devilish scamp And one too of the most outrageous stamp, And, the girls should not allow such capers, But give him at once his walking papers!” Should some thus talk I can only say That they have not known in lifes rugged way The glorious pleasure, the enraptured bliss That hovers around an endearing kiss They are such persons as an aged tale avers Of winning charms or gentle graces devoid Who have so far gone Lifes journey all alone To social joys and high vested bliss unknown, Who have this [[Cythera’s?]] bright congenial shores Plucked no fruits from its unrivaled bowers But withered them all beneath a misanthropic Sun Until their nobler feelings were forever gone And now they stand upon Lifes verge Whining to Youth and happiness a mournful dirge.
10-089-P02 But when we meet a beauteous girl The pride and envy of the world Whose matchless beauty and faultless grace Displays each lovely feature of form and face Where from a high and classic brow The raven tresses fall around a neck of snow, And from her dark eyes deep lustrous hue The beaming soul looks unimprisoned through, He who can these innumered there uniting art And not feel the fond effect of Cupids dart—

10-092 · Idle Hours concluded and memories of an oasis in life

10-092-P01 32 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] But so it is, with callous heart I face the world nor fear its scorn Conscious still that I can bear my part Though deeper in my bosom press the thorn. Seclusion Aug 23rd 1866
10-092-P02 [[separate block: a second poem, main text continuing into the lower right margin]] While backward gazing through the lapse of years A lone oasis in my early life appears Beautifully verdured and flowery fair And draped in brightness richly rare There Sunshine played o’er [[inserted: each]] happy scene And enchanting beauties shed their silver sheen Upon the vernal air, in bright relief To Lifes surrounding wastes of gloomy grief.

10-101 · The anonymous poet offers an apology

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 101

10-101-P01 41 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] And always overshot the mark,
10-101-P02 I every passion in one effort fling And aim to reach the goal at one bold Spring So ever thus my fondest hopes I blast By being just a little bit too fast.
10-101-P03 I am extremely sorry and would apologize For having written to you in this wise, If I knew how—but I cannot claim The honor of approaching you by name.
10-101-P04 But if I thought I could win your partial favor I would throw off my disguise and endeavor To rush to your presence half annihilated by fear And plead my case like a Lawyer at the bar.

10-103 · Trust as the strongest bond of friendship

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 103

10-103-P01 43 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] ’Tis Confidence, the first flower in the wreath of Love Which I now bestow a boon drawn from above Inspired by Heaven in thy Stainless truth, (The noblest gift now owned by mortal youth) Accept it, for within it lies The strongest links in Friendships holy ties.
10-103-P02 Then will the Social joys live again And within our hearts supremely reign And base Detraction hurled from his high seat Into the dust and trampled ’neath our feet Can rise no more in a hideous form To shake our trust or mar our joys so warm, Joys which will in long succession rise And date their birthright from the skies And through successive ages roll The light of life, the adamant of the soul Strengthening through succeeding years Erasing darkening doubts, dispelling gloomy fears.
10-103-P03 A Panacea for all human woes Which the unwilling future may disclose Leaving Nature in its purest mood When with pulses high and madly bounding blood The human breast by contending passions wildly driven Exiles Mercy from its home, defying Heaven Heaven with all its deep emotions pure Which requires no grosser props our to insure Through our downward march to Lifes ending scene Noble thoughts divine, deep, bright, and serene. Seclusion August 21st 1866

10-105 · A friend and companion of the poet’s youth

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 105

10-105-P01 45 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] Slowly the Shroud around him wound Its spotless folds Then deep was laid beneath the ground Affections holds. Friend and companion of my youth Though death has come It could not blast the lovely Truth That bore thee home. Though we shall meet no more on earth Thy memory In my hours of wildest mirth Shall sacred be. “And though I run Lifes mad career Wild as the wave,” I’ll pause, and drop, fond Friendship’s tear, Upon thy grave. When Spring in beauty bright shall come And robe the trees, The rose shall shed its sweet perfume Upon the breeze. The daisy on the verdant lea Shall sweetly blow And Natures wildest minstrelsy Joyously flow. No more with thee shall these bright scenes Pass in review For all that earthly pleasure means Has passed from you. No more with thee we’ll greet the morn When carols sweet On fragrant winds to Heaven are borne An offering meet

10-107 · Ad idem concludes with Courtesy and truth

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 107

10-107-P01 47 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] Drop here a tear with the broken hearted That live to mourn the loved and lost And the cherished hopes death has thwarted With the blasting blight of its early frost.

10-109 · Varying Moments questions human systems of thought

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 109

10-109-P01 49 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] Moments of Bitterness, deep and dark When wither each holier aim; Aims that rise as twere Spark by Spark From a lone and dying flame.
10-109-P02 These bitter moments congeal the Soul And cramp its warm desires Yet their way they onward roll Like fierce consuming fires,
10-109-P03 Fed by man with his isms wild That rack the brain, the Senses whelm, Distracting from his way each tender child That does not know who guides the helm!
10-109-P04 Oh! man, that tryest to lead the way Through Lifes temptations scenes, Canst thou, pour into a heavenly ray And tell us what it means?
10-109-P05 Canst make the darkened Spirit light Remove each load of care, And give us hopes forever bright While we may wander here?

10-110 · An album as a keepsake of absent friends

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 110

10-110-P01 50 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] For an Album,
10-110-P02 When young we treasure up some sacred Ties Of Lifes bright morn while all is gay Some garlands gathered ere the dewdrop dries Of beautys smile, too soon to pass away.
10-110-P03 We twine them in a pure and fragrant wreath And lay them on the heart in Friendships name And note how swift the sable wings of death Sweeps from us those flowers we loved to claim.

10-110-P05 These treasures are some thoughts to virtue given And traced upon an Albums spotless page By Youths careless heart ere by Sorrow driven— Or claimed by Death for his tutelage.
10-110-P06 So oer this page I now careless strew Some idle thoughts which may yet recall Unto thy Memory one you knew But who ah! too soon perhaps didst fall.
10-110-P07 Perhaps a lone tear from thine eye may start While thinking on his joyless career And a deep sigh escape thy tender heart To mingle with that gently flowing tear. February 1867

10-116 · Visit to Siloam

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 116

10-116-P01 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] Visit To Siloam.
10-116-P02 Twas on the first of Brumaire, (I like to be particular as to time So no matter when I go or where I will always know the occasion of my rhyme.) Twas on the first of Brumaire As I was just going to say That I brushed my shoes and sleeked my hair And promised myself a happy day. A western wind blew fresh and fair The morning clouds soon dispelled And as I faced the bracing air Its wild free spirit I inhaled.
10-116-P03 I mounted on a trotting horse And through the mud swiftly sped Unto Siloam I bent my course With poesy running in my head, Upon its grounds at length arrived And tied my steed unto a tree Then looked around at how things were contrived And to see such things as were to see. My heart beat high with hope elate While every thing propitious smiled With satisfaction I scanned my fate And with Hope the sunny hours beguiled. While stumping round through its verdant shades Oer heaps of logs and now and then a slab I came upon some of my old comrades Privately enjoying a lone confab.

Editorial note. Continues at 10-117. “Brumaire” is the word written, not silently converted to a modern date. The precise location of Siloam is not established here. The poem describes a social outing and should not be treated as a verified itinerary.

10-117 · Siloam companions and courtship banter

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 117

10-117-P02 Slowly at length spoke Prospect Hill “You are right about the emotion “And you may have it by whose laws you will “To us works out no ‘motion’ “I’m told the virgins of our Shrine “To day are coming to Siloam “One Sylph-like girl I’ll claim as mine “And with the rest you may freely roam.

10-117-P05 Thus I to him, “may you no ill betide “I would not do it for money “For you will be sure to ride “Home with a Parsons Honey.

10-121-P01 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] Hours of Bitterness. Oh there are moments when the past Comes oer me as a dream The scenes of youth—too bright to last That shed [[illegible]] a flickering gleam, Of happiness o’er my saddened heart Where not a ray of light now strays That could a moments bliss impart But what would ere the instant fade. I’ve grasped at Pleasures lively host That in swift groups swept by I’ve mingled in its wildest boast With pulses madly bounding high; I’ve seen its charms before me spread In bright succession far I’ve felt its influence when it led My way from Star to Star, Of Beauty that so brightly reigned Queen of every idle heart That blindly knelt in her bright train The centre of gay folly’s mart. I’ve seen the smiles of eager joy Play on the rosy lips Unstained by Arts deep dark alloy That Hope’s sweet fountains sips. I’ve seen the fondly loving eyes Meet eyes that loved again I’ve heard the softest earliest sigh Of the heart by Cupid slain. I’ve felt the hopes which fire the blood When prospective joys appeared,

10-122 · Hours of Bitterness: hopes that vanish

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 122

10-122-P01 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] I’ve felt the influence of a gayer mood When songs of revelry were heard. But what were they, a moment bright A minute like a flickering spark That upward leaps from a lone light Then dies and leaves all doubly dark.
10-122-P02 I’ve seen the hopes of Life decay Ere morning dews were dried I’ve felt my joys low with’ring lay Like garlands in the desert wide; All I have loved with trusting heart All I have hoped in early days. I’ve seen before me fast depart Like dews in mornings gaze. I’ve tried to win those pearly dews To keep within my heart I’ve hoped a gentler spirit to infuse With their pure and guileless art. I’ve tried to gather [[deleted: sweetest]] fragrant flowers That bloomed my way along To intertwine with happier hours And interweave in joyous song. Before my touch those dew drops bright Fled like morning mists away When the suns bold beaming light Proclaimed the Advent of the day. Those fragrant flowers of loveliness Like Snowflakes on the sea Reclined an instant on my breast Then swelled its storminess.

10-123 · Hours of Bitterness: loneliness and lost hopes

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 123

10-123-P01 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form; page read after 180-degree rotation]] Where e’er I turn for solid charms Where e’er I look with brighter hopes There is nothing which my bosom warms Or my hearts deep fountain opes. I’ve tried in vain from Purity To win her gems of priceless worth To wrench them from Adversity To illume my way on earth, Deeper in the dark recess Of the Souls night I’ve plunged my way And only found that nothingness Within its dreary portals lay. A chaotic void filled with gloom And stormy passions darkly driven Where light and beauty ne’er can come Or stray a single breath of Heaven.

10-125 · Hours of Bitterness: a voice promises rest

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 125

10-125-P01 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] Travelling—Where? without a mark By which we might surely go— Travelling in thro’ doubt and gloom Thro’ cankering cares on every side Behind, before, contentions loom And darkly rolls their murky tide; In vain for peace and sweet repose We gaze around with eager eyes And hope amid surrounding woes To see a ray of pleasure rise— Each distant scene which promise gives Of happiness in future days Alone in Fancy faintly lives And passes as the Summer haze; A moment bright it shines afar With varied brilliancy on high Glowing as a meteor star Amid the blackness of the sky And as quickly too it expires Amid the stillness of the night And backward hope as swift retires As it advanced to meet the light. Oh! even thus we hourly stand Twixt hope and fear, twixt joy and pain. Oft as we feel the heart expand As oft we feel it contract again!— Hark! a strange sound arrests the ear Borne on the swiftly passing gale. Hark! it rings again loud and clear And faintly echoes down the vale! “Lo! here is rest”, it is a voice Breaks on the stillness of the gloom,

10-129-P01 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] [[Blue Eyes?]] [[illegible]]
10-129-P02 The blustering rain loudly rattles on the roof Around the gables sadly sighs the wind And as I gaze into the fast thickening woof Of darkness far without all grows dark within.

10-130 · Oh! Let Me Forget: childhood and vanished hopes

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 130

10-130-P01 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] Oh! let me forget! In answer to—“Forget; Oh! never!”
10-130-P02 Oh! let me forget the [[inserted: early]] scenes of my childhood When careless I strayed brightest flowers among On the hills, in the valleys, by the stream in the wildwood, Inhaling their fragrance all the day long When my young heart expanded in the bright sunshine That fed the sweet flowers budding around And inhaled the pure emotions of the noble and divine Which haunted the ear at each joyous heart bound. Oh! let me forget!
10-130-P03 For those scenes in their brightness in Memory lingers Contrasting so vividly with with the dark gloom around Like the voices of Some distant melodious singers Which reaches us at times with a heavenly sound Which partakes not of earth in its mellowing sweetness But seems to proceed from a holier Sphere And with the rich bursts of its metrical sweetness Shows us the discords we always have here. Oh! let me forget!
10-130-P04 Oh! let me forget the hopes I have cherished In boyhoods bright morn, when all was so fair Ah! little I then thought they all would have perished And melted away like the mirage in air. But they have gone and all that was blooming Has rapidly faded before my eager gaze Which once was so brightly and sweetly illuming My varied wanderings in Lifes dreary maze Oh! let me forget!

Editorial note. Continues at 10-131–132, where it is dated February 1867. The title explicitly answers “Forget; Oh! never!” but no author of that earlier piece is given. Repeated “with with” and other grammatical irregularities are retained. The poem is unsigned on these pages.

10-131 · Oh! Let Me Forget: leaving home and the horrors of war

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 131

10-131-P01 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] Oh! let me forget the sad tears when I parted From home and its charms which I loved so well And the fond friends whom I left there broken-hearted When I spoke as I thought my last sad farewell. To go to that war whose Tocsin was ringing The death knell to thousands in our lovely land And from its distant bounds was rapidly bringing Those daring heroes the shock to withstand. Oh! let me forget
10-131-P02 Oh! let me forget the muskets horrid rattle Where brothers [[inserted: contending]] against brothers fell And the cannon’s loud roar in the din of the battle Portraying on earth a miniature hell. Where Death proudly riding rode on the breeze And fiendishly hurled his darts In the plain Or where the dark waves of the deep heaving Seas Her fiercely cast them again and again. Oh! let me forget
10-131-P03 Oh! let me forget those dark scenes of horror Which harrowed the soul with visions of dread And darkly foreboded that each coming morrow Would add a new list to the nations of dead, And the dark robe of crime gathering o’er us Racked the sad heart where the gospel light shone And with the prospect of oppression ever before us Prepared us to yield ere life was all gone. Oh! let me forget!
10-131-P04 Oh! let me forget the maid to whom I plighted The wild romantic feelings which burned in my breast And those heavenly ties which hourly invited

Editorial note. Continues 10-130 and leads to 10-132. The war is not named, nor are battles, dates of service or the woman in the final stanza. In the collection’s context the Civil War is a plausible referent, but this unsigned literary passage alone does not document a particular combat experience. “Her fiercely cast them” is retained as read, with uncertain syntax; the family version gives its apparent sense.

10-132 · Oh! Let Me Forget ends with grief and memory

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 132

10-132-P01 [[separate block: reused printed descriptive-roll form]] My wild erring Spirit to sweet moments of rest For the charms which encircled her, brought pain at the parting And saddens the long hours through each returning day And too often ’neath my eyelids the pearly tear starting Stains with effeminacy manhood’s stern way. Oh! let me forget!
10-132-P02 Oh! let me forget the varied Past and its pleasures Which never, never again in life can return With its hopes and its joys, and the hearts deepest treasures Which all moulder now in the Sepulchres urn. Like the Storm shivered tree alone on the heath Far from its mates in the forests so fair I stand and view my branches low scattered in death And pour my lament on the wild desert air. Oh! let me forget! February 1867.

Editorial note. Concludes 10-130–132, dated February 1867. The gendered judgment in “Stains with effeminacy manhood’s stern way” belongs to the text and is preserved, not endorsed. The sepulchral and shattered-tree imagery does not by itself establish the death of the unnamed beloved or particular relatives.

10-133 · A portrait in verse, dated May 31, 1861

George Douglas Papers Folder 7 - Poems Etc.pdf · Scan page 133

10-133-P01 She was not very beautiful if it be beauties test To [[deleted: with]] a Clasic model when perfectly at rest; And She did not look bewitchingly if witchery it be To have a forehead and a lip Transparent as the sea. The fashion of her gracefulniss was not a followed rule And her [[effervescent?]] sprightliness was never learnt at School And her words were all peculiar like the faeries [[inserted: fabled]] dialect, And her tone was ever Sweetest midst the cadences of grief. Said I she was not beautiful? Her eye upon your sight Broke with with the lambent purity of planetary light; And an intellectual beauty like a light within a vase, Touched every line with [[deleted: beauty]] [[inserted: glory]] of her animated face. Written May 31st. 1861 By [[Lizzie?]] Douglas

Editorial note. The separate sheet is sideways in the PDF and is read after clockwise rotation. The name after “By” is tentatively Lizzie Douglas, not assigned to George Douglas. “Written” may refer to copying rather than composition; original authorship has not been verified. An apparent canceled “with,” a correction within “effervescent,” the inserted “fabled,” and the substitution of “glory” for “beauty” are preserved. The irregular line “To a Clasic model” and repeated “with with” are retained. The woman described is unnamed.
